19923-the-ontario-readers-the-high-schoo:
The Ontario Readers served Canada's public schools for decades. The High School Reader of 1886 gathers prose and verse for older pupils. Its editors admit limited space prevents a complete anthology. They aim instead to show each author in characteristic moods. A fair perspective of the world of authorship is the goal. The selections present authors as a schoolbook can.

Provincial readers standardized English-Canadian schooling. Pupils from many small schools read the same set pieces. British and Canadian authors share these pages by design. The 1886 reader preserves that shared canon. Education historians trace taste and values through such books. A single volume shaped thousands of classroom hours.
21778-donahoe-s-magazine-volume-15-no-1-:
Irish Catholic America speaks in this January 1886 number of Donahoe's Magazine, a Boston monthly journal. The issue opens with an encyclical letter of Pope Leo XIII, then ranges across tales, biography, poetry, and history. A serial story, Dead Man's Island, promises the tale of an Irish country town. An affecting incident at sea and a valiant soldier of the cross fill out the fiction.

History and argument share the pages: chapters of Irish history, pieces on capital and labor, strikes, and Chinese labor. There is church news, council decrees, and word of Father Ryan's death. The magazine served readers who held Ireland and the Church together in one loyalty. This volume gathers the run from January to July 1886.
acts-pilate-walker-1886: The Acts of Pilate, also called the Gospel of Nicodemus, an early Christian apocryphal text. It imagines Pilate's report on Jesus' trial and the harrowing of hell. This edition preserves that ancient narrative. Its contents inform the historical record.
aeschylus-dramas-swanwick-1886:
Anna Swanwick translated all seven surviving plays of Aeschylus into English verse, and her fourth revised edition appeared in 1886. Aeschylus, the earliest Greek tragedian whose work survives, fought at Marathon and reshaped the stage of Athens. Swanwick's volume holds the whole of what time has left of him.

The Oresteia trilogy follows Agamemnon's murder and Orestes' revenge to its trial in Athens. The Persians mourns Athens' beaten enemy, while Prometheus Bound chains its Titan to a crag for mankind's sake. The Seven Against Thebes and the Suppliants complete the seven. Swanwick, a scholar of note, kept the verse stately and clear. Her Aeschylus was the standard Victorian rendering of the poet.
allbutt-wifes-handbook-1886: The Wife's Handbook, Allbutt's 1886 work. The wife's guide. This book preserves that manual. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
allibone-critical-dictionary-english-lit:
Volume Three of Allibone's Critical Dictionary, published in 1886, closes the set with authors from R to Z. It ends with Allibone's own colophon, dated 1870, a sign of how long the work took. The dictionary had grown alongside its maker for decades.

The final volume adds later authors the first volumes missed and corrects earlier entries. Quoted reviews let readers hear the period's own critical voices. Allibone died in 1889, his life's work complete. Later bibliographers built on his foundation, and his three volumes still serve anyone tracing a minor Victorian author's books and reputation. His prefaces explain how he gathered notices from sales rooms and private shelves.
arxiv-2510-00086:
Nemanja Antonic and four colleagues published this 2025 paper on reading the behavior of a tiny roundworm. The worm, called C. elegans, is one millimeter long and serves as a model animal in biology. Older tools need a clear view of the whole body to sort its movements into units. That view fails when many worms crowd together, which is exactly when social effects show.

The team instead tracks a single point, the worm's body center, over time and space. An automatic pipeline then cuts the motion into behavior units with no preset list. The authors compared those units with hand-designed ones and tested both in a simulated worm. Clear movement patterns emerged even from the single tracked point. The automatic method matched the real worm better, which frees studies of crowded worms from hand labels.
arxiv-2510-00386:
Ayush Jain, Andrea Montanari, and Eren Sasoglu published this 2025 paper on picking fine-tuning data when target examples are scarce. Fine-tuning works best when training samples mirror the target task's distribution. Usually teams hold the few target samples back as a validation set for scoring candidate data. The authors flip that arrangement in a method they call Train on Validation.

Their procedure fine-tunes on the small validation set, then re-scores the whole training pool. Samples whose predictions moved the most under that fine-tune get selected for real training. The insight is that samples most affected by the target data tend to help most on the target task. Experiments covered instruction tuning and named entity recognition benchmarks. In most cases the flipped method reached lower test loss than leading selection approaches. Theory in the paper backs why the signal should work.
arxiv-2510-00686:
Anisha, Biermann, Englert, and Mühlleitner explore a kinetic Higgs portal in this 2025 arXiv preprint on particle physics. The Higgs portal is a leading idea for linking known matter to a hidden sector that could hold dark matter. Their version adds non-standard momentum dependence, which arises naturally when the hidden sector interacts strongly.

The authors derive limits on this setup from four-top-quark production data and from precise measurements of Higgs couplings. Those limits matter most where destructive interference hides invisible Higgs decays from direct searches. They show the portal can still explain the observed dark matter abundance while evading current direct detection bounds. Future machines such as the high-luminosity LHC and a proposed FCC-ee collider could probe the remaining space.
arxiv-2510-00786:
Fedida strengthens a family of no-go theorems for pointwise quantum fields in this 2025 arXiv paper on mathematical physics. Textbook quantum field theory treats fields as operator-valued functions defined at each spacetime point. Classic results by Wightman and Wizimirski showed that this pointwise picture clashes with basic physical demands, but those results were proved mainly for scalar fields. Spinor fields obey different algebraic rules, so Fedida rechecks the obstructions for them.

Weak continuity of the fields turns out to be the decisive assumption. In globally hyperbolic spacetimes it rules out equal-time canonical commutation and anticommutation relations alike. In two-dimensional Lorentzian spacetimes it also kills fermionic microcausality, extending Wightman's theorem. Finally, a Poincaré-invariant vacuum precludes pointwise spinorial covariance altogether. The ban covers Weyl and Dirac fermions, photons, and gravitons, which underlines how hard pointwise quantization of gravity remains.
arxiv-2510-01186:
Shen and co-authors edit videos by swapping the appearance of chosen subjects while leaving everything else untouched. Editors often need several subjects changed at once, and earlier tools tangle masks at boundaries or demand retraining. Their framework, IMAGEdit, works training-free on any number of designated subjects.

Large pretrained models first supply rich descriptions and rough mask motion for each subject. A retargeting step sharpens those masks before a mask-driven generator renders the final video. The design plugs into any compatible generator rather than replacing it. On a new multi-subject benchmark, the method consistently beat current state-of-the-art editors. Time-consistent masks keep edited subjects coherent frame to frame. Prompt-side conditioning was the usual weak point this design strengthens. Non-target regions stay untouched by construction, not by luck. Benchmark clips stress crowded scenes with overlapping subjects. Editing power grows with subject count here.
arxiv-2510-01286:
Cebrian, Kito, and Castro Fernandez map a split personality in the language-model ecosystem, where making models decentralizes while judging them concentrates. Thousands of organizations now build models across many countries and licenses. Benchmarks, the shared yardsticks, tell the opposite story.

A small top slice of the benchmark network carries most of the influence paths. Three countries produce the overwhelming majority of benchmark outputs, and authority inequality is extreme. Simulations show new benchmark entry dilutes concentration, while anti-overfitting penalties barely help. The authors read concentrated yardsticks as useful coordination infrastructure with real, bounded costs. Two curated registries supplied the ecosystem data for the study. Betweenness centrality exposes which benchmarks act as bridges. Rapid inflows of new models can temporarily scramble coordination. Path dependence is the standing risk of shared yardsticks. Concentration and quality are entirely different questions.
arxiv-2510-01386:
Knowles, Ceballos, and Pena reduce the question of how a neuron computes to the sign and size of one number. Neurons switch between spotting matched inputs and summing them over time. Those two operational modes frame much of neural coding theory, yet their boundary stayed loosely drawn.

A stripped-down model captures the quiet dynamics of real membrane behavior. Its smallest curved term alone predicts which mode a driven neuron occupies. Transitions between modes follow from that term's value, not from simulation detail. The sorting may clarify disorders where the cell's firing itself breaks down. In vivo pulse patterns anchor the analysis in real drive. Scaling strips the units and yields the standard form being sorted. Potassium and calcium channel stand-ins supplied the two worked cases. One number replaces a shelf of simulations. Channel diseases are the medical shadow over the theory in the background.
arxiv-2510-01586:
Pan and co-authors train multi-agent systems to defend themselves by sparring with attackers that learn alongside them. Teams of language-model agents face jailbreaks, injected prompts, and unsafe teamwork that single agents cannot spot alone. Bolt-on guard modules add cost and become single points of failure when compromised.

Their framework co-trains attackers and defenders through adversarial reinforcement learning. Agents internalize safety through practice rather than obeying an external policeman. A shared baseline mechanism keeps the joint training stable while both sides improve. Defenses grown this way should generalize to fresh attack styles instead of memorizing yesterday's tricks. Cross-agent attack chains are the blind spot this training directly exercises. Co-evolution keeps pressure honest because yesterday's defense meets tomorrow's attacker. Northwestern-led authorship spans four universities on the author list. Safety practiced becomes safety retained. Public baselines steady the shared learning signal for all.
arxiv-2510-01686:
Xu, Mei, Zhang, and Patel present FreeViS in this 2025 computer vision paper on video stylization. Stylizing a video means redrawing every frame in a chosen artistic style. Doing that frame by frame causes flicker and uneven style. Training a dedicated video model avoids flicker, but it needs paired videos and heavy computing.

FreeViS needs no training at all. It feeds several stylized reference frames into a ready-made image-to-video model. Using many references curbs the error spread that single-reference methods suffer from. High-frequency compensation pins down layout and motion during generation. Flow-based cues keep style textures alive in plain, low-detail regions. In wide evaluations FreeViS beat recent baselines on style fidelity and smoothness over time. Human viewers also preferred its results, which makes the approach practical for creators.
arxiv-2510-02086:
Behnam couples a vision transformer with a diffusion process to segment brain tumors in this 2025 paper. Accurate tumor outlines on MRI scans guide diagnosis, treatment planning, and follow-up. U-Net style models remain the standard tool, but they see only local context. Long-range structure across a whole scan volume escapes them, and complex tumor shapes suffer.

The proposed model, VGDM, places a transformer at the core of an iterative denoising process. Global reasoning from the transformer steers each refinement step. That pairing improves volume accuracy and sharpens boundary precision. Voxel-level errors get corrected across rounds, recovering fine tumor detail. The design targets robustness on the irregular boundaries that trouble purely convolutional systems. Diffusion refinement, borrowed from image generation, turns out to suit medical imaging well. The paper offers a hybrid route for high-stakes clinical tasks.
arxiv-2510-02286:
Guo and co-authors automate the search for chat attacks that unfold over many turns. Their 2025 safety paper treats red-teaming as a planning problem. A red team tries to make a model break its own safety rules. Single prompt attacks miss how real attackers adapt. Skilled attackers steer a conversation step by step. The authors frame each dialogue as a tree of choices. Their system, DialTree-RPO, learns by reinforcement while searching that tree. It prunes weak branches and rewards paths that reach the goal.

Tests ran against ten target models. The method beat both single-turn and multi-turn baselines. It found varied attack routes without human templates. Results confirm that current models stay exposed in long conversations. Automated search gives safety teams a practical stress test. The authors flag the dual use risk plainly.
arxiv-2510-02386:
Wang and co-authors show that cheating on reasoning benchmarks is easy to hide. Their 2025 paper studies contamination in large reasoning models. Contamination means test questions leaked into training data. Scores then flatter the model unfairly. Many detectors hunt for memorization traces in outputs. The team contaminated models at two different life stages. Early contamination during fine-tuning was detectable at first. A short round of reinforcement learning erased the traces. The clipping style objective of that training caused the erasure. Late contamination with worked solutions left barely any trace at all.

Existing detectors failed across both stages in their tests. The authors call for new evaluation protocols urgently. Releasing intermediate training checkpoints would help outsiders audit. Detectors must move beyond simple memorization signals. Leaderboard trust depends on catching hidden training. This study shows current guards are fragile.
arxiv-2510-02486:
Tang, Adcock, and Mostert model how splashing waves throw large spray drops into storms. Their 2025 geophysics paper attacks a stubborn uncertainty in hurricane science. Spray drops up to two millimeters wide affect storm strength. Nobody knew well how waves generate those drops. Observations at sea are too hard to settle the question. The authors build the mechanism from first principles instead. Two liquid rims collide sideways in their basic picture. Ligaments form, merge, and pinch off into drops. Gravity cuts the whole process off at a set timescale.

Their theory predicts the drop size distribution from that contest. Existing experiments and simulations matched the predictions well. Sea state data can drive the full generation function. Few tuning parameters keep the model honest. Splashing may produce more spray than earlier estimates thought. Large drops break up in air into many small ones. Climate models gain a better spray recipe.
arxiv-2510-02586:
Bennett proves zero-one laws for targets and returns in systems that change over time. Her 2025 mathematics paper studies non-autonomous dynamical systems. The maps driving the system differ from step to step. A shrinking target problem asks how often orbits hit small balls. A recurrence problem asks how often orbits return near their start. Classical results answer such questions for fixed systems. Bennett extends them to the time varying setting. Uniform mixing yields a quantitative shrinking target theorem. The count of hits matches the expected sum with an error term. Inner function families supply applications.

Digit patterns in multi-base expansions fall under the results. Zero-measure laws govern recurrence in the changing case. For fixed systems, a zero-one criterion covers centered inner functions. Markov partitions and distortion estimates power that proof. One framework now handles static and evolving dynamics. Ergodic theory gains tools for real, nonrepeating processes.
arxiv-2510-02686:
Xu, Liu, and Ong make evolved scheduling heuristics readable by pairing them with language models. Their 2025 paper presents a framework called EvoSpeak. Genetic programming breeds tree shaped rules for hard scheduling jobs. The best evolved trees often grow too tangled to read. Opacity slows convergence and blocks transfer between tasks. EvoSpeak first learns from high quality evolved heuristics. It then extracts knowledge into language model form. Warm-start populations seed evolution runs from it. The model translates trees into plain language explanations. Preference-aware generation adapts rules to tasks.

Tests used flexible job shop scheduling. Both single and dual objective versions ran. EvoSpeak beat plain genetic programming in three of six scenarios. The other three matched without clear separation. Mean based objectives showed the clearest wins. Better heuristics arrived with less scatter across runs. Factories reschedule under changing conditions. Rules that humans can read earn trust on the floor.
arxiv-2510-02886:
Millán-Irigoyen and co-authors extend a tool that models star populations. Many galaxies hold stars poor in heavy elements. Distant young galaxies seen by the Webb telescope show the same trait. The HR-pyPopStar code builds model spectra for star groups. This second paper adds a full set of low-metal models at high spectral resolution.

The new spectra mostly match the older solar-metal set. Only the oldest ages differ, in bands tied to titanium oxide and carbon. The team reanalyzed sharp data on the globular cluster M 15. They found a better fit for its age and metal content. They also studied star-forming dwarf galaxies from the MaNGA survey. Their metal estimates by mass and light sat near prior values. Light-weighted values ran a bit higher than some studies found. Fuller data will be needed to settle those small gaps.
arxiv-2510-03086:
Lelarge teaches graph networks to align two graphs node by node. Graph alignment seeks the best match between unlabeled graphs. It is a hard combinatorial problem with wide uses. His method chains several networks in sequence. Each network refines the match scores left by the one before. Rankings from earlier rounds feed the next round as hints.

The networks judge node pairs rather than single nodes. Pair views capture global patterns that message passing misses. On hard synthetic tests, the chain won by a wide margin. Accuracy more than tripled against prior learning methods. Regular graphs, where every node looks alike, fell to the method alone. No rival approach could solve those cases at all. Adding classic optimization as a final polish helped further. That hybrid beat the best solvers on the standard benchmark. Chaining may carry to other hard matching problems.
arxiv-2510-03186:
Longon, Klindt, and Khosla show that tangled neuron codes hide how alike two networks really are. Neurons often serve several features at once in superposition. Two models may hold the same features in different mixtures. Standard alignment metrics then report a false mismatch. The authors build theory for how permutations interact with superposition. Toy models let them test that theory cleanly. Sparse autoencoders untangled the mixtures in those toys.

Alignment scores rose once neurons were swapped for disentangled codes. The same pattern held between real vision networks. It also held between networks and human brain data. Linear regression alignment climbed in both settings. Predictive mapping metrics seem biased downward by superposition. Untangling thus looks necessary before trusting such scores. Brain-model comparisons may have understated true similarity for years. It also suggests autoencoders as a standard preprocessing step. Alignment science gains a cleaner lens on shared representations.
arxiv-2510-03286:
Dzhivelikian and Panov present a 2025 arXiv paper on how a machine can build mental maps from its own memories. Their design copies ideas from the brain, where maps help animals plan routes and link one task to another. Most earlier models learn with global training rules that real brains do not use. The authors instead build a system that learns step by step, using only local rules much like real nerve cells.

Inside the system, stored episodes are grouped into levels. Groups form when memories share similar patterns of what tends to come next. In a partly hidden grid world, grouping by these patterns raised forecast accuracy well above random grouping. The map also gave a cleaner picture of how places connect. The system still trails classic training methods in raw accuracy. Even so, it shows how map-like learning could work in both brains and machines.
arxiv-2510-03386:
Yi and colleagues from universities and Google present a 2025 arXiv paper on guessing database query sizes before running them. Query planners need those counts to pick execution plans. Errors grow fast as queries join more tables, and classic rules of thumb rely on crude independence guesses. Heavy learned estimators fix accuracy but cost too much to run in practice. The team exploits the fact that real workloads repeat the same subquery shapes again and again.

Their system learns many tiny regressors, one for each repeated subquery pattern. A hash of the pattern's graph shape fetches the mini model instantly. Added to PostgreSQL, the method sped a movie database workload by over thirty percent in simulation, while its own learning overhead stayed under a minute in the same test. Accuracy rivaled far heavier learned systems. The design shows learned database parts can pay off without slowing the engine they serve.
arxiv-2510-03586:
Lan and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on sharpening high resolution brain diffusion MRI by correcting field unevenness slice by slice. Diffusion MRI maps tissue structure, but field distortions warp images, especially on head only scanners. Their method uses the fields of the scanner's gradient coils when computing correction settings. It also restricts the correction to brain tissue, segmented by a deep learning model. The team tested the approach on phantoms and volunteers using oscillating and pulsed gradient scans.

In phantom areas with strong gradient nonlinearity, field unevenness fell by seven hertz with that calculation. Image displacement shrank by ten voxels in phantoms and three voxels in human brains. Measures of water diffusion and fiber direction grew accurate in the upper brain, brainstem, and cerebellum. Cleaner diffusion maps support studies of brain wiring and disease. The method needs no hardware, only smarter use of fields the scanner produces.
arxiv-2510-03886:
Kang and colleagues at Yonsei University present this 2025 arXiv paper on helping image generators handle rare prompts. Modern diffusion transformers draw with high fidelity, but unusual concepts appear so rarely in training that outputs often miss them. A prompt like an Eiffel tower made of water can come out wrong. The authors show the needed meaning is already inside the model, just buried.

Their method, ToRA, widens the spread of text token embeddings before joint attention runs. This simple variance scale-up lets rare semantics surface in the generated output. It needs no retraining, no extra data, and no outside language model. It improved prompt alignment for rare concepts across text-to-image, text-to-video, and image editing tasks. The authors note the trick can occasionally misfire for some prompts and seeds. Even so, it offers a nearly free upgrade for models facing unusual requests.
arxiv-2510-04186:
Jiang and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on planning urban air mobility as a network integrated with ground transport, rather than a patchwork. Flying taxis promise relief for congested megacities, but infrastructure costs and complexity block deployment. The authors model a system reusing existing regional airports with a mixed fleet of aircraft sizes. Their LPSim framework uses multi-GPU simulation to co-optimize demand, fleet operations, and ground interactions at once.

An equilibrium search algorithm forecasts demand and picks the most efficient fleet composition. Applied to the San Francisco Bay Area, the model found over two hundred thirty thousand trips that would save more than twenty minutes each. Serving them took only two hundred forty-one aircraft flying five thousand daily flights. The authors caution that five thousand flights quadruple current Bay Area air traffic, straining air traffic control. Economic viability also remains untested in their operational analysis.
arxiv-2510-04486:
Aditya Gulati and three coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on whether quantum randomness tools can be built from each other. Classical cryptography rests on pseudorandom functions, objects that look random but run from a short key. Quantum versions come in three grades: unitaries, isometries, and function like state generators. Each grade implies the next weaker one, but the reverse directions were open. The team ruled out a class of reverse constructions.

A black box construction uses the weaker tool only as an oracle, without peeking inside. They built a unitary oracle world where the weaker tools exist yet the stronger ones cannot be reached that way. Their adversary rests on the quantum singular value transformation, a method of independent interest. The results do not close the equivalence question, since non black box tricks remain possible. They do show any equivalence proof must dig into internal structure.
arxiv-2510-04586:
Anshu Kumari and Nat Gopalswamy wrote this 2025 paper on a solar radio burst with a missing partner. Type II radio bursts usually trace shocks driven by coronal mass ejections. On November 2, 2023, telescopes caught a burst with split band structure and harmonic lanes. No ejection appeared in any space coronagraph at that time, though. A strong flare had fired before the burst instead.

Extreme ultraviolet images showed a disturbance expanding through the low corona at about five hundred kilometers per second. That speed matched the shock speed read from the radio data. The authors conclude the ultraviolet ejecta drove the shock low in the corona. The ejecta then faded or fell apart before it could register as an ejection higher up. The case shows that not every type II shock needs a surviving ejection behind it. Flare driven waves in the low corona can do the job alone.
arxiv-2510-04686:
Chenxiang Zhang and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on why some models merge well and others fail. Merging blends the weights of models with different skills into one model at no running cost. Two recipes average the weights or add task vectors built from fine tuning. Nobody had a rule for when merging will work. The team traced success to a quantity they call the effective noise scale.

That scale sums up how training choices stir optimization. Bigger learning rates, stronger weight decay, smaller batches, and data augmentation raised the noise. Merging success rose and fell as noise grew, with a sweet spot in the middle. The pattern held across architectures and data sets in their tests. Work linked training noise to the flatness of single solutions. This study shows noise shapes the landscape where merging happens. Knowing the sweet spot lets teams tune training toward models that will combine.
arxiv-2510-04786:
Jonas Hübotter and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on models that keep learning while being tested. People improve at a job by practicing its tasks. The authors give language models the same chance through test time curricula. For a task, the agent picks the relevant problems from a pool of training data. It then runs reinforcement learning on that built course. No human has to curate the set.

Across tasks and models, the approach improved results. One model doubled its try score on a math contest benchmark. On a coding benchmark its try score more than doubled. The ceiling rose: with eight tries, math success climbed from forty percent to sixty two percent. Coding success rose from twenty eight to forty three percent. The gains suggest models learn solution strategies during the test. Test time training joins reasoning as a way to buy skill with compute.
arxiv-2510-04886:
Adi Banerjee, Anirudh Nair, and Tarik Borogovac wrote this 2025 paper on finding which agent caused a failure in agent teams. When a system fails, engineers must locate the agent and the step that went wrong. Judging a trace at once is sloppy, and judging step by step misses context. Binary search over steps breaks when errors interact across traces. The authors propose ECHO, an algorithm built on ideas.

First, it organizes the trace into a hierarchy of context, so judgments happen at the level of detail. Second, it scores faults against objective criteria rather than vibes. Third, it decides by consensus voting among evaluations. Across multi agent scenarios, ECHO beat the attribution methods. It did best where rivals struggle: subtle reasoning slips and tangled interdependencies between agents. Reliable blame assignment is vital infrastructure for agent engineering. Without it, teams cannot tell whether to fix a prompt, a tool, or orchestration.
arxiv-2510-05186:
Hongpei Li and four co-authors rethink how giant language models train across many machines in this 2025 arXiv paper. Pipeline parallelism splits a model into stages that different devices process in turn. Idle gaps, called bubbles, waste expensive hardware time. Existing fixes offload memory by fixed heuristics and ignore fine trade-offs.

Their framework, OptPipe, casts scheduling as a constrained optimization problem. The model balances memory capacity, activation reuse, and bubble size together. Solving it yields fine-grained schedules tuned to each model and machine setup. Experiments cut idle pipeline time by up to 50 percent under the same memory limit. In some cases the schedules even fit larger models into tight memory budgets. The method complements, rather than replaces, standard offloading tricks.
arxiv-2510-05286:
Joel Wendin, Erik G. Larsson, and Claudio Altafini find hidden order inside trained neural networks in this 2025 arXiv paper. Every network defines a signed graph through the signs of its weights. Physicists measure such graphs with frustration, the distance from perfect structural balance. The authors compute that quantity for pretrained convolutional networks.

In every network tested, frustration came out lower than random null models predict. Lower frustration means the encoded disorder is smaller than chance would suggest. Functionally, the networks also behave closer to monotone functions than the null models do. The authors read this as a novel form of implicit regularization from training. Ordinary gradient training, it seems, quietly organizes networks toward order.
arxiv-2510-05486:
Huang and colleagues test how well language models can plan under real-world rules. Models are often used as planners that write out action steps directly. They also serve as formalizers that translate tasks into a formal language for a solver. Standard planning tests use plain, simple settings, which can flatter the models badly.

The team built CoPE, a benchmark that adds hand-written constraints to familiar planning tasks. The constraints span four defined types and are stated in rich natural language. They tested four top reasoning models across three formal languages and four datasets. Adding constraints cut performance roughly in half in almost every setting. Harder wording and longer problems hurt the models even more. Constraints also erased much of the formalizer approach's usual edge in robustness. The authors warn that lab scores may overstate how models would plan real jobs safely.
arxiv-2510-05586:
Kang and colleagues fix a quiet flaw in text-driven image retrieval. Vision-language models pool image and text features into global summary tokens. A few weak tokens can grab those summaries and drown out distinctive details. Their 2025 method, CalibCLIP, calms the dominant tokens without any retraining.

One part, the Contrastive Visual Enhancer, splits visual features into target and low-information regions. It then finds the dominant tokens and softens their representations on the fly. A second part sharpens the text side by separating general concepts from discriminative ones. Generic concepts get muted while telling details gain weight. Experiments across seven benchmarks and three retrieval tasks show consistent gains. Similar-looking images become easier to tell apart at search time. The code is public, so other teams can apply the calibration directly. The paper appeared at ACM Multimedia 2025 in Dublin.
arxiv-2510-05886:
Seiffarth and colleagues package live-cell imaging analysis into reproducible notebook workflows. High-throughput microfluidic setups record hundreds of parallel single-cell cultivations. Deep learning segmentation and tracking can mine those movies, but tooling stays fragmented. Their 2025 acia-workflows platform assembles pipelines inside single Jupyter notebooks.

The underlying acia library offers eight deep learning approaches for segmentation and tracking. Workflows bundle the pipeline, dependencies, documentation, and visualizations together. Over ten application workflows ship open source for real experiments. Demonstrations range from growth-rate comparisons across strains. Another tracks individual cell responses to changing oxygen at minute resolution. Reproducibility comes from packaging everything one workflow needs together. The design stresses customizability, robustness, and scaling to high-throughput screens. Routine biological research, not just specialists, is the intended audience. Three-dimensional segmentation support is planned as the next extension.
arxiv-2510-05986:
Gafni shows that blockchain fee mechanisms need only fear small collusions. Transaction fee mechanisms choose which transactions enter each block. Robustness against miner-user collusion defines the side-contract-proof hierarchy. His 2025 paper collapses that hierarchy above its second level.

A mechanism robust against a miner plus two users is robust against any larger collusion. The equality holds under a mild consistent tie-breaking assumption. Earlier work had separated the one-user and two-user classes. Beyond two, no further separation exists. A miner seeking a beneficial collusion needs only two co-conspirators. Payments can be burned in these mechanisms, unlike classical auctions. Ethereum's EIP-1559 is the prominent real-world mechanism of this type. The counterexample auction in the discussion shows where tie-breaking matters. Designers can therefore audit two-user collusions and stop there. Collusion, in coalitional complexity terms, turns out simple.
arxiv-2510-06186:
Miao and thirty co-authors present RECODE-H, a benchmark for research code development with human feedback. Language models often fail to produce correct, executable research code in one shot. Real development is iterative and feedback-driven, yet existing benchmarks ignore that loop.

RECODE-H holds one hundred two tasks drawn from research papers and repositories. Each task ships with structured instructions and unit tests. Agents work through multi-turn interactions with simulated human feedback, arranged in five levels from vague hints to detailed guidance. The authors built ReCodeAgent, a framework folding feedback into iterative code generation. They tested leading models including GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4, DeepSeek, and Gemini. Richer feedback produced substantial gains across the board. Even so, complex research code remained genuinely hard for every model. The benchmark gives the field a realistic yardstick for feedback-driven coding agents.
arxiv-2510-06486:
Kjønstad, Damour, Sharma, and Chan systematically improve trial states guiding phaseless quantum Monte Carlo in a 2025 chemical physics paper. Auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo needs a trial wavefunction to control its phaseless bias. Coupled cluster states are natural trials, but practice stopped at singles and doubles.

The authors extend coupled cluster trials to triples and quadruples. This creates an AFQMC/CC benchmarking hierarchy. The phaseless energy improved systematically at every level. It was typically far more accurate than the trial's own energy. One trend tempers enthusiasm. Relative improvement over the trial energy shrinks as the hierarchy ascends. A subtler result concerns in-simulation representation. Improving that representation does not always lower bias. It can fail even as fidelity with the exact ground state increases. Quantum chemists gain a stronger method and a warning against naive fidelity chasing.
arxiv-2510-06886:
Mancini, Metere, and Piazza, three algebraists writing with initials only, study how groups of symmetries act inside algebraic structures. Their 2025 paper works with hoops, which are algebraic systems tied to many-valued logic. The question concerns split extensions, a way of gluing two structures with a section back. Strong sections impose discipline on that gluing.

The authors characterize split extensions with strong section through strong external actions. For any hoop, a natural one-to-one correspondence links the two viewpoints. An extension can be described by a pair of maps obeying a set of identities. Those identities depend on which axioms the hoop family satisfies. The team extends the analysis to basic, Wajsberg, Gödel, and product hoops. One case collapses. For MV-algebras, the strong-section notion becomes trivial, which the paper notes as a remark. A link to semidirect products rounds out the picture for algebraists.
arxiv-2510-06986:
Jinho Cha and four co-authors read investors' hidden preferences out of the portfolios they actually hold. Their 2025 paper builds an inverse optimization framework for that detective work. The hidden traits include risk aversion, transaction cost caution, and ESG leanings. Observed allocations are treated as nearly optimal choices under unknown settings.

The framework blends robust methods with regret-based inference to handle wrong settings and market shocks. Tests ran on controlled synthetic data, where the true preferences are known. Transaction cost parameters came back accurately. ESG penalties proved only partly pinned down, an honest limit of the data. Regret grew sublinearly even under wild volatility and liquidity shocks. A real-data check used exchange-traded funds spanning 2007 to 2024. Transaction cost shocks hurt investor welfare more than volatility shocks there. The tool gives portfolio designers a rigorous way to infer what clients truly value.
arxiv-2510-07186:
Catanzaro, Garlaschelli, and Patil apply a physics tool to random networks. Their 2025 paper studies random graphs whose links influence each other. Here, the chance of one link depends on which others appear. The authors treat the model like a physical system with interacting parts. They ask which details survive when the network is viewed from far away.

A technique called renormalization answers that question by repeatedly zooming out. For the simplest case, the team derives an exact formula for how link chances change under zooming. More complex cases admit no such exact formula, echoing hard problems in lattice physics. Adding disorder makes the flow of probabilities match a known drift-and-spread process run backward in time. The upshot is that some pairwise link effects fade at large scales. Network scientists can use that insight to simplify sprawling models.
arxiv-2510-07486:
Luo and co-authors present AsyncSpade, a serving design that keeps long reasoning chains from choking on their own memory. Their 2025 paper targets test-time scaling, where models think longer to answer better. Longer thought means a growing key-value cache, and decoding becomes memory-bound. Sparse decoding methods drop unimportant cache pages, but their filtering depends on the current step and runs in sequence with generation, sometimes costing more than the generation itself. The team's key observation: the current query state can be predicted accurately from a short window of recent queries, with no training required.

A lightweight temporal-regression module makes that prediction. An asynchronous architecture then moves cache filtering off the decoding loop entirely, overlapping selection with the forward computation. The authors claim the first elimination of this sequential dependence without quality loss.
arxiv-2510-07586:
Chmura and a large team release TGM, a software library that unifies machine learning on graphs that change over time. Their 2025 paper addresses an infrastructure gap. Static graph learning enjoys mature frameworks, but temporal graph research is fragmented: libraries target specific architectures. The field's two cultures, continuous-time and discrete-time methods, barely share code, blocking comparisons and idea transfer. TGM is the first library to host both under one roof. It supports dynamic node features, conversions between time granularities, and link-, node-, and graph-level tasks natively.

The efficiency numbers are stark: on average nearly eight times faster training than the widely used DyGLib across models, datasets, and tasks. Graph discretization runs about one hundred seventy-five times faster than prior implementations. Beyond speed, the unified setting unlocks experiments that were impractical before, like dynamic graph property prediction and time-driven training paradigms.
arxiv-2510-08186:
Gómez-Ortiz, Bastogne, and Ghosez wrote this 2025 condensed matter paper finding topological textures in a structural order that is neither magnetic nor electric. Strontium titanate's oxygen octahedra naturally rotate in an antiferrodistortive pattern. Using second-principles simulations, the authors mapped the domain structures of those rotations. Besides the familiar ninety-degree twin walls, they found new metastable one-hundred-eighty-degree walls under compressive strain. Those walls resemble Bloch and Néel configurations, with the Néel-like form most favorable.

The team also stabilized vortex and antivortex structures in the rotation pattern. Each came with co-localized polarization vortices and a strain pattern, making the textures trimodal. The results extend topological ordering to non-polar structural degrees of freedom. Lattice-mediated couplings, long treated as background, actively stabilize these states. Strain-tunable textures in perovskite oxides suggest devices storing information in rotation patterns rather than charge.
arxiv-2510-08386:
Sourav Das, Aiman Khan, Francesco Albarelli, and Animesh Datta find the best possible precision for quantum spectroscopy in a 2025 arXiv paper. Spectroscopy probes matter with light to learn its energy levels and linewidths. Quantum light, such as single photons, can beat classical light at this task. Until now, the ultimate precision limit for single-photon probes was unknown.

The authors compute the maximum precision for estimating an emitter's linewidth and its detunings, the gaps from expected transition energies. The linewidth limit turns out not to depend on the emitter's internal Hamiltonian details. The detuning limits do depend on those details, a contrast they establish. They also identify the pulse shapes that reach these precision limits. Their results assume all photons emitted by the system are detected without loss. The work sets a benchmark for future quantum-enhanced spectrometers.
arxiv-2510-08486:
Lukas Novak constructs explicit equations for twists of elliptic curves in a 2025 arXiv paper in number theory. Let p be a prime and K a number field containing the p-th root of unity. He studies an elliptic curve over K with full p-torsion, meaning all its p-division points are already rational. Adjoining a p-th root of an integer d creates a related curve called a twist.

A cocycle built from two torsion generators defines which twist each integer d gives. Novak constructs generators of the twist's function field and writes down an explicit model equation for it. The model mixes powers of two variables with coefficients he determines. He also proves the twist is everywhere locally solvable for only finitely many integers d. Local solvability everywhere is a necessary step toward having rational points at all.
arxiv-2510-08586:
Vishakha Lall and Yisi Liu model stress in speech as a changing state rather than a fixed label in a 2025 arXiv paper. Detecting stress matters in high-pressure jobs, from emergency call handling to maritime operations. Prior systems mostly classify each clip independently, ignoring how stress builds or fades. The authors instead derive fine-grained stress labels from emotional annotations over time.

Their dynamic labelling strategy turns emotional label sequences into temporally rich stress annotations. Two cross-attention sequence models, a Transformer encoder and a unidirectional LSTM, then track stress progression. Accuracy rose over existing baselines by five percent on the MuSE data set and by eighteen percent on StressID, the authors report. The approach also generalized well to a custom real-world data set they collected. They argue temporal modeling is the key missing piece in speech stress detection.
arxiv-2510-08686:
Romina Ballesteros, Marcela Cárdenas, and Eric Lescano rethink scalar charge in black hole thermodynamics in a 2025 arXiv paper. They study four-dimensional Einstein-scalar-Gauss-Bonnet gravity, where a scalar field couples to a curvature correction term. Defining scalar charge covariantly for stationary, asymptotically flat black holes is subtle in this theory. Their differential-form framework exposes exactly where the usual definition fails.

Contracting the scalar equation with the horizon generator yields a scalar charge that is not closed. A bulk three-form measures the obstruction to closedness, encoding charge stored in the field outside the horizon. Under shift symmetry, the obstruction vanishes and the charge obeys a Gauss law from boundary data alone. The framework feeds into the Smarr formula relating mass, temperature, and charges. It also interprets spontaneous scalarization, where scalar-free black holes go unstable and grow scalar hair.
arxiv-2510-08786:
Voloch surveys progress on a conjecture about how closely special points can approach a curved subspace, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The setting is pure mathematics, in a branch that measures distance with p-adic numbers, a system based on divisibility by a prime. The special points are torsion points, points that return to the start after a fixed number of steps around a shape. Tate and the author once conjectured a single uniform bound on that closeness.

The survey traces what has been proved since, starting from the case of tori, which the original pair settled by reducing it to roots of unity. It then follows variants in nearby settings, including points that repeat under a repeated rule and special points on spaces of shapes. Voloch shows how results on these approximation questions tend to advance together with a famous family of conjectures about where special points can gather.
arxiv-2510-08886:
Wang and a large team build the first benchmark that tests language models on real financial auditing, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Company filings follow strict accounting rules and a branching taxonomy, a formal tree of categories, encoded in a structured data format. Models shine on loose prose, but nobody had measured them on this interlocking, number-heavy material. The benchmark, FinAuditing, is built from genuine filings that comply with United States accounting standards.

It splits auditing into three subtasks. One checks that meanings stay consistent, one checks relationships between entries, and one checks the arithmetic. The team ran thirteen leading models through all three with no task-specific training. Performance proved uneven, and accuracy fell steeply, by well over half in the worst spots, once reasoning had to span the taxonomy across several documents. The authors offer the benchmark as a foundation for financial AI that regulators could trust.
arxiv-2510-09086:
Falcón, Gutiérrez, and Jiménez Urroz translate a classic combinatorial object into algebra, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A Latin square is a grid where every symbol appears once in each row and column, the pattern behind Sudoku. When the grid size is a prime power, each square corresponds to exactly one special two-variable polynomial over a finite field. The dictionary between the two views had barely been explored.

The authors show that the polynomial's coefficients are pinned down as the zeros of an algebraic set, a system of equations over the same field. That yields a complete algebraic description of all such Latin squares through a single polynomial whose coefficients obey explicit constraints. Familiar square notions, including reduced and equivalent forms, get polynomial translations too. The paper works the theory out for orders four and five, and extends the dictionary to complete mappings and transversals.
arxiv-2510-09286:
Amarilli, Monet, and De Pretto prove that two standard clean-up rules for hypergraphs can be applied in any order without changing the final result, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A hypergraph generalizes a graph: its edges can contain any number of nodes. Before computing a hypergraph's minimum hitting sets, the smallest node sets touching every edge, practitioners shrink the input with domination rules. Edge-domination deletes an edge that contains another edge entirely. Node-domination deletes a node whose edges are all shared with some other node.

The question is whether deletion order matters, a property called confluence. The authors show the rules are confluent up to isomorphism: whatever sequence is chosen, the cleaned hypergraphs can be made identical by further rule applications. Hence a unique minimal hypergraph exists for each input, up to renaming. That justifies aggressive preprocessing, since no deletion order can corner the algorithm.
arxiv-2510-09586:
Fengming Lin, the sole author, measures research trends across more than twenty-six thousand conference papers in a 2025 arXiv paper. The survey covers accepted papers from CVPR, ICLR, and NeurIPS, 26,104 of them, between 2023 and 2025. Titles and abstracts were normalised and matched against a hand-built lexicon to assign up to thirty-five topical labels per paper, plus cues about tasks, architectures, and training regimes.

Three broad shifts stand out. Multimodal vision-language work tied to large language models rose sharply, reframing classic perception tasks as instruction following and multi-step reasoning. Generative methods kept expanding, with diffusion research gathering around controllability, distillation, and speed. Three-dimensional and video research stayed resilient, moving from neural radiance fields to Gaussian splatting. Within vision-language models, cheap adaptation such as prompting and LoRA dominates, and training now mostly fine-tunes strong backbones. The author releases the lexicon and method for auditing.
arxiv-2510-10186:
Tsygankov, Bulat N. Galimzyanov, and Anatolii V. Mokshin study bonding in liquid pnictogens in this 2025 arXiv paper in materials physics. Pnictogens are the nitrogen group of elements; the paper deals with molten arsenic, antimony, and bismuth near their melting points. In these melts, near-stable structures form, and why they hold together has no agreed answer.

The team measures how strongly atoms bond inside those structures, using a method that splits bond energy among pairs of atoms. Knowing which bonds do the holding tests the rival stories about the odd traits of these melts. The results matter for phase-change materials and heat-to-power devices, where bonding in the liquid shapes how well a device works.
arxiv-2510-10386:
Liu and a large team map dust and star formation in a distant supercluster in this 2025 arXiv paper in astronomy. The target is CL1604, a supercluster of galaxies at redshift 0.9, seen as it was when the universe was about half its current age. The survey uses the Subaru Telescope with two narrow-band filters.

Combining the filters lets the team detect both hydrogen-alpha and hydrogen-beta emission from the supercluster. Their ratio, the Balmer decrement, measures how much dust dims the star-forming regions. Degree-scale mapping shows how environment inside the supercluster regulates dust and star birth. Such maps test whether dense surroundings smother or trigger star formation at that era.
arxiv-2510-10586:
Giulio Ruffini argues that symmetry is the key to how intelligent agents compress the world, in this 2025 arXiv paper. In the algorithmic view, an agent is a program that tracks and compresses streams of sensory data. Ruffini proposes that the right prior is compositional symmetry: natural streams are captured well by local actions of Lie pseudogroups, families of symmetry maps, acting on low dimensional latent spaces.

Modeling the agent as a neural dynamical system leads to two kinds of constraints. Accurate tracking forces the agent's equations and readouts to respect the symmetry. Under steady inputs, the symmetry also creates conserved quantities, in the style of Noether's theorem, and confines the dynamics to smaller invariant surfaces. These surfaces form a layered stack matching the structure of the symmetry itself. Ruffini connects the picture to predictive coding, where higher layers receive only coarse prediction errors along symmetry directions left unresolved below.
arxiv-2510-10786:
Diana Shvydka and Victor Karpov model what happens inside tissue exposed to ultra high dose rate radiation, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such FLASH radiotherapy seems to spare healthy tissue, and the mechanism is debated. Their conjecture is that an electron-hole liquid forms in the water based tissue. Unlike the same phase in semiconductor crystals, the charge carriers here move sluggishly, so the liquid resembles an ionic melt more than a free electron fluid.

Coulomb coupling makes this liquid energetically favorable. That creates recombination barriers, which suppress the later structural changes that radiation damage requires. In particular, fewer secondary reactive species form, which limits biological damage and produces the sparing effect. The team shows the processes depend on tissue quality and on how the dielectric permittivity varies with frequency. They derive equations for the dose and dose rate that define the sparing thresholds, giving experimentalists concrete predictions to test.
arxiv-2510-10886:
Yashom Dighe, Youngjin Kim, and Karthik Dantu fix an information leak in how racing cars plan their laps, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A standard autonomy stack passes decisions from a global planner to a local planner to a controller. The global planner's rich sense of what is optimal gets compressed into a sparse set of waypoints. The local planner then reacts with little context, for instance when overtaking. The team asks whether time optimality information can be passed down in a usable form.

Their answer is QuayPoints: regions where leaving the optimal racing line costs significant lap time. By marking these regions, the local planner can judge when a deviation is cheap and when it is expensive. Integrated into an existing planner, QuayPoints consistently overtook opponents traveling at up to 75 percent of the ego vehicle's speed, across four race tracks.
arxiv-2510-11686:
Jens Tuyls and three co-authors ask a basic question about reinforcement learning for language models. Does it teach new behavior, or only sharpen skills the base model already has? Their 2025 arXiv paper studies deliberate exploration. That means rewarding a model for finding novel and varied answers. The bonus they test comes from the model's own hidden states. Those are the internal number patterns it forms while processing text.

At test time, the bonus raised solution rates across several models and reasoning tasks. It also more than halved the checking work needed for one large Qwen model. Added into training, the method beat both the starting model and standard reinforcement learning. On the AIME 2024 math contest set, the gain was striking. Their model matched in eighty attempts what a standard method needed two hundred fifty-six attempts to reach.
arxiv-2510-11786:
Kiran Adhikari Chhetriya sharpens a basic question in quantum computing: how many queries does an algorithm really need when something about its starting state is already known? Many quantum algorithms apply a function of a Hamiltonian to an initial state. Standard bounds ignore the starting state and price the worst case. Chhetriya's 2025 arXiv paper prices the actual case instead.

The key object is the spectral measure, which records how the starting state spreads across the system's energy levels. Chhetriya proves that the minimum number of queries equals the best possible polynomial approximation degree of the function, measured against that spectral measure. In plain terms, easy spectra need cheap approximations and few queries. The result ties Krylov subspace methods, a classical workhorse, and Favard's approximation theory directly to quantum query counts. It also explains when knowing the state yields large savings over designs built for the worst case.
arxiv-2510-11986:
Jasivan Alex Sivakumar and three colleagues spotlight a step that formal mathematics pipelines quietly skip. Before a problem can be translated into a proof assistant's language, someone must conjecture what the answer or bound actually is. Their 2025 arXiv paper argues this conjecturing step is where language models silently fail or succeed. They built ConjectureBench by augmenting existing datasets and redesigning the scoring to isolate the skill.

Testing foundation models including GPT-4.1 and DeepSeek-V3.1, they find headline autoformalisation scores are substantially inflated when the conjecture is handed to the model. Left to conjecture alone, models do possess much of the needed knowledge, but the pipeline wastes it. Their inference-time method, Lean-FIRe, treats conjecturing as its own task. It achieved the first end-to-end autoformalisation of thirteen PutnamBench problems with GPT-4.1 and seven with DeepSeek-V3.1. The authors urge the field to study conjecturing directly.
arxiv-2510-12086:
Ruijin Sun, Xiang Guo, Andreas Ruschhaupt, and Zhihai Wang learn to dial atomic teamwork up and down. When excited atoms emit together, their radiation can scale with the square of their number, a blaze called superradiance. Independent atoms, by contrast, add up only linearly. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies a cavity quantum electrodynamics system, atoms coupled to confined light, and asks whether the two scalings can be engineered separately.

They can. The atom-photon coupling significantly alters the emission behavior: it suppresses the collective superradiant scaling while boosting the scaling of individual atomic emissions. One knob thus trades group brilliance for solo brightness. The authors present this as a pathway toward controllable collective emission on modern experimental platforms.
arxiv-2510-12286:
Gagliani and a large team introduce trainable networks of coupled differential equations that can both classify and generate data, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Ordinary differential equations describe how quantities change over time, and each node follows such an equation coupled to its neighbors. Training shapes the connections so the system's evolution settles into a target state that depends on the input's class.

The authors plant stationary attractors, stable end states, into the system by design. Adding noise turns each point attractor into a probability distribution that can be computed with the linear noise approximation. Noise also hardens the system against adversarial attacks, and that robustness is written into the trained connection matrix itself. Feeding target samples into a companion network yields a fully generative scheme, and merging the two modes allows conditional generation. The authors also prove that isolated key features disentangle on their own in the learned representation.
arxiv-2510-12386:
Dhanoa and colleagues present Diana, a multimodal assistant that teaches people to use data dashboards by voice, text, or pointing, in a 2025 arXiv human computer interaction paper. Dashboards pack interlinked views whose interactions confuse new users, and author led onboarding sessions are time consuming to prepare and maintain. Language models now make self guided onboarding plausible.

Diana combines chat, audio, and mouse based interaction inside the dashboard itself. Users may pick any single modality or mix them, and each modality highlights the relevant dashboard features while explaining them, instead of confining help to a text chat box. The authors extend an existing process model of dashboard onboarding with these multimodal interactions. They then ran a qualitative user study to see how people use different modalities for onboarding tasks of varying complexity. The study informs when pointing, speaking, or typing best supports orientation and guided analysis.
arxiv-2510-12486:
Bhakta, Biswas, and Filippucci prove that certain elliptic equations with gradient dependent reactions admit only constant solutions on the whole space, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Results of this kind are called Liouville theorems. The equations involve the (p, q)-Laplacian, a diffusion operator with two growth exponents, and a source term depending on the solution and its gradient.

The approach splits into two strategies. When the reaction is controlled by a gradient power above a threshold, an Ishii Lions type technique applies. It shows every bounded solution, with no sign limit, must be constant. In the remaining cases the Bernstein method is used. Adapting it to the nonhomogeneous operator is nontrivial, because constant coefficients become possibly unbounded functions. The resulting gradient estimate implies the Liouville property. The work extends classical results for the Hamilton Jacobi and Lane Emden equations to this two exponent setting for the first time.
arxiv-2510-12586:
Lei and colleagues close the gap between image generators that work on pixels and those that work in a compressed latent space, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Pixel space models are harder to train and have lagged in quality and efficiency. Their two stage framework first pre trains an encoder to extract meaning from clean images while aligning its representations with points along the same deterministic sampling path.

In stage two the encoder joins a fresh decoder and the model fine tunes end to end, for both consistency and diffusion models. On ImageNet the diffusion model reached quality scores surpassing earlier pixel space methods by a large margin, rivaling leading latent models at comparable training cost. The consistency model achieved strong quality in a single sampling step, beating its latent counterpart. The authors note this is the first successful training of consistency models on high resolution images without pretrained components.
arxiv-2511-00486:
Pooja Singh, Shashwat Bhardwaj, Vaibhav Sharma, and Sandeep Kumar address machine translation for Bhili, a tribal language of India with almost no digital resources. They introduce the Bhili-Hindi-English Parallel Corpus, the first and largest of its kind. It holds one hundred ten thousand carefully curated sentences across the three languages, built with expert human translators. The topics span education, administration, and news.

The corpus anchors a full Bhili translation benchmark. Proprietary and open multilingual models were tested on translation both ways between Bhili and English or Hindi. A fine-tuned distilled variant of the NLLB-200 model performed best, showing multilingual models can serve very low-resource languages. The team also probed generative translation with in-context learning, measuring how well models generalize across domains. The resource opens a path for inclusive language technology.
arxiv-2511-00686:
Alex Inch, Passawis Chaiyapattanaporn, Yuchen Zhu, Yuan Lu, Ting-Wen Ko, and Davide Paglieri want image generators to surprise us on purpose. Text-to-image diffusion models paint beautifully but repeat themselves, a real limit for exploration and ideation work. Prompt tricks that chase beauty scores do not fix sameness. Their system, WANDER, imports novelty search, an evolutionary method that rewards difference itself.

WANDER evolves natural language prompts with a language model as the mutation engine, while CLIP embeddings measure how novel each image is. Special emitters steer the search into distinct regions of prompt space, widening the variety further. With a leading image model generating and a compact model mutating, WANDER beat existing evolutionary prompt optimizers on diversity metrics, and ablation studies confirmed the emitters carry much of the gain.
arxiv-2511-01086:
Vladimir Martirosyan and Rachit Kamdar compare employer reviews on two platforms with opposite credibility rules. Glassdoor allows fully anonymous reviews, while Blind verifies employment but keeps reviewers anonymous. The question is how that verification step changes what reviews say about company culture.

Using the Competing Values Framework, which sorts culture into clan, adhocracy, hierarchy, and market types, and a language model built for culture analysis, they study over three hundred thousand ratings. Blind reviews stress clan and hierarchy, while Glassdoor skews more positive and highlights clan and market. Verification, they conclude, does not remove bias; it shifts the cultural signal, so job seekers reading different platforms receive systematically different impressions.
arxiv-2511-01286:
Sivaram Krishnan and colleagues predict connectivity in flying ad hoc networks, swarms of drones that form their own wireless network while moving. Most machine learning for communications assumes static settings, but a drone network's topology changes constantly, so links appear and vanish.

They use data driven Koopman operator methods, which lift nonlinear dynamics into a space where they behave nearly linearly, to model drone trajectories and forecast link quality. Both centralized and distributed versions are proposed. In a surveillance scenario with drones on predetermined paths, the methods accurately predicted signal quality between drones and the isolation events that cause communication outages. Such forecasts could let drones schedule transmissions for moments when links will hold.
arxiv-2511-20086:
Vu, Thong, Nguyen, Nguyen, and Luu fight bias in AI multiple-choice answers by adding more of it. Their 2025 paper introduces BiasPrompting for language models. Models often pick answers with little real reasoning. Bare options invite shallow guesses and ordering biases. Context-free choices leave plausible answers unexplored.

BiasPrompting first makes the model argue for every option. A supportive reasoning is generated for each candidate answer. Then a second stage weighs those arguments together. The model selects the answer whose case survives scrutiny. Five standard question-answering benchmarks tested the framework. Accuracy improved significantly across the board. Ordering effects shrank compared with plain prompting. Performance held steadier across repeated runs as well. Hard questions, where rivals falter, gained the most. Experiments used seven-billion-parameter models like Mistral and Gemma. Compute costs stayed below heavier self-consistency schemes. Larger models remain untested.
arxiv-2511-20486:
Alvarenga and Fabris build a lopsided cosmos inside a modified gravity theory. Their 2025 paper uses non-conservative unimodular gravity, a variant of Einstein's theory. The Bianchi-I model expands at different rates along different axes. Its rules famously leave the cosmic history underdetermined. Extra input is needed to pin the dynamics down.

The authors impose terms on the sum of density and pressure. In the vacuum case the model mimics Einstein's theory plus a constant. Kasner solutions, the classic lopsided vacuum, survive in this theory. One new case with constant density-plus-pressure looks ghost-like. It suggests super-fast expansion needing a closer heat-based look. Other choices match standard lopsided cosmology well. The lopsidedness must stay near one percent throughout. That keeps the cosmos near fourteen billion years old, matching globular clusters. The lopsidedness fades to zero as expansion proceeds. Space grows smooth just as in Einstein's version.
arxiv-2511-21086:
Bryan E. Tuck and Rakesh M. Verma test in 2025 whether language models can obey letter-level rules in spelling puzzles. They ran 28 configurations from three model families, Qwen3, Claude Haiku-4.5, and GPT-5-mini, on 58 puzzles, for 1,624 experiments. Difficulty came from 10,000 solvers per puzzle.

Architecture mattered more than size: the best and worst families differed twofold, at 0.761 against a low of 0.343 on the F1 scale. An eightfold size increase within a family bought an 83 percent gain. Extra thinking budget helped models, adding 0.102 to a high of 0.136 F1 points, but mid-sized models saturated or got worse. Model difficulty ratings tracked humans, with correlations of 0.24 to about 0.38 across families. The failures were common words with odd spelling, like data, poop, and loll: humans solved them 86 to 95 percent of the time, while models missed 89 to 96 percent. The models lean on what looks plausible over what the rules allow.
arxiv-2511-21186:
Quantum physicist Loris Di Cairano takes a global look at entanglement, the linked behavior of paired quantum systems, in a 2025 theory paper. Entanglement is usually scored one state at a time, often with the von Neumann entropy of part of the system. Di Cairano instead studies the whole space of pure states at once, using projective Hilbert space equipped with the Fubini-Study metric, a standard way to measure distances between quantum states.

Within that space he groups states into surfaces of constant entanglement and defines a geometric entanglement entropy: the logarithm of each surface's volume, weighted by how steeply entanglement changes nearby. The quantity works like an entropy in statistical physics, counting how abundant each entanglement level is rather than scoring a single state. The framework lets researchers ask which entanglement values are common, rare, or split into distinct geometric regimes.
arxiv-2511-21386:
Chengshu Li examines a stress test of a famous law of nonequilibrium physics in a 2025 commentary paper. The Kibble-Zurek effect predicts how defects scale when a system is driven through a critical point, resting on the adiabatic-impulse scenario, where the system first follows its ground state, then freezes. Recent work by Wang and coauthors drove a one-dimensional model, coupling two chains, through a rarer tricritical point instead.

Li explains the two surprises that emerged. First, the adiabatic-impulse prerequisite breaks down near the tricritical point, yet Kibble-Zurek scaling survives intact, proving the effect broader than its usual justification. Second, the entanglement entropy follows a new dynamical scaling law that mixes two central charges, measures of quantum critical content, inside a single equation. Li supplies physical arguments for these scaling forms, which Wang's simulations corroborate, and maps what they mean for quantum simulators.
arxiv-2511-21486:
Biao Zhang reports, for the ALICE Collaboration, new measurements of how charm-carrying particles tug on ordinary ones, in 2025 conference proceedings. The tool is femtoscopy. When two hadrons fly out of a collision close in momentum, their correlation reveals the force between them. It works even for unstable particles that vanish too fast for direct scattering experiments. Charm hadrons were the missing case, and their interactions could explain exotic charm states and hypothetical charm-bearing nuclei.

Zhang presents final results on correlations between D mesons and light hadrons from proton collisions at 13 TeV, extracting the residual strong interaction between them. Theory expects these scattering lengths to be tiny, about 0.1 to 0.5 femtometers, versus 7 to 8 for light-light pairs. The proceedings also introduce studies of Lambda-c baryons against protons at 13.6 TeV, using fresh Run 3 data from the Large Hadron Collider.
arxiv-2511-21586:
Markus Banagl, Eric Leichtnam, and Paolo Piazza extend a classic symmetry theorem from smooth shapes to singular ones, in 2025. The Atiyah–Segal–Singer G-signature theorem links a space's signature, a topological fingerprint, to the fixed points of a group action. It holds only for smooth manifolds. Many natural spaces are Witt pseudomanifolds, stratified spaces with controlled singularities, where the classical formula did not apply.

Banagl and his coauthors prove the formula in this singular setting. When a group element's fixed-point set sits inside the space in a normally non-singular way, fixed-point data compute the signature there. Reaching it required a detailed study of fixed-point sets in Thom-Mather stratified spaces, yielding a sufficient condition with many examples. The proof follows Rosenberg's analytic route through KK-theory, and the work is dedicated to Georges Skandalis.
arxiv-2511-21986:
Garcia-Failde and colleagues generalize Mirzakhani's recursion from orientable surfaces to Klein surfaces, including non-orientable ones like the Klein bottle. The recursion computes volumes of moduli spaces, cataloguing all hyperbolic shapes of a surface. On non-orientable surfaces a natural volume form diverges when one-sided geodesics shrink to zero length.

The fix is to work on Gendulphe's regularized moduli space, where the systole of one-sided geodesics is bounded below by a positive parameter epsilon. So the divergent form integrates to a finite, well-defined volume that genuinely depends on that cutoff. Using Norbury's extension of the Mirzakhani-McShane identities, the team derives an explicit formula for the volume of moduli space of one-bordered Klein bottles. A recursion for arbitrary topologies that tracks the epsilon dependence exactly. They connect the volumes to refined topological recursion for Euler characteristic minus one, conjecturing it holds generally.
arxiv-2511-22186:
Termphaiboon, Kula, Fan, and colleagues in Thailand and Japan ask whether a small file changes how a software project behaves. SECURITY.md, the standardized place for reporting vulnerabilities privately, is now a recommended practice in open source. They compare PyPI projects with and without one. The team examines dependency trees and tracks how dependencies evolve over time, hunting for a link between adopting a written security policy and managing the supply chain more actively.

Projects with a security policy rely on a broader set of direct dependencies, while overall tree depth and transitive counts stay similar, suggesting more modular, feature-rich projects. Projects created after SECURITY.md appeared, especially later adopters, update their dependencies more frequently, with dependency-related commits concentrated in setup and project configuration files. The authors read the policy as a signal of stronger maintenance culture, and suggest policy-aware tooling could help maintainers spot needed updates.
arxiv-2511-22386:
Baccini, Christoff, Gierasimczuk, and Verbrugge defend the most cautious method of revising beliefs. Minimal revision accepts new information while changing one's beliefs as little as possible. Rivals such as conditioning change beliefs more boldly and are known to learn more: minimal revision can cycle and has memory limits, so it cannot learn everything they can. The authors ask how much it can still achieve.

Quite a lot, it turns out. Minimal revision can learn any problem that is finitely identifiable, meaning finite telling data pin down the truth. It can learn from positive and negative data whenever only finitely many possibilities are in play. The team characterises exactly which prior plausibility rankings make it work on finite spaces, and does the same for conditioning and lexicographic upgrade. One caveat: several results break down once incoming information may contain errors.
arxiv-2511-22486:
Burles and Camporeale review work using machine learning to close the equations of plasma physics. Simulating a plasma as a fluid is cheap, but the fluid equations form an endless chain, each averaged quantity depending on the next one up. Modellers must add a closure relation guessing the highest from lower ones. Hand-derived closures throw away kinetic effects, which often drive large-scale behaviour in space and laboratory plasmas.

The review collects the data-driven attempts, from neural networks imitating analytic closures or kinetic simulations, to equation-discovery methods such as sparse regression searching for formulas. Highlights include networks trained on two-dimensional particle-in-cell data, which struggled with off-diagonal pressure terms, and a study linking architecture to how local a closure is. The authors judge the methods viable on test cases and map out what closures still need, better kinetic training data chief among it.
arxiv-2511-22686:
Zhang and colleagues probe whether 3D foundation models secretly understand geometry they were never taught. These models predict depths, poses, and point maps from images, but are trained mostly on overlapping views. Tested on extreme, non-overlapping pairs, they show an emergent grasp of extreme-view geometry. For the pretrained VGGT model, nearly half of unseen-scene pairs yield rotation errors below 30 degrees in the reported benchmark, despite no shared content to match.

To sharpen this latent ability, the authors tune only some backbone bias terms, about 80 thousand parameters, four orders of magnitude fewer than the full model, leaving decoder heads frozen. This alignment substantially improves pose estimation under extreme viewpoints without degrading depth or point quality. They also release MegaUnScene, a benchmark of unseen internet scenes, with test splits for pose and dense reconstruction, arguing low-parameter alignment is promising for 3D perception from sparse photos.
arxiv-2511-22986:
Zanutto and a large team of water researchers present a competition problem: plan the future of a regional water distribution network under deep uncertainty. Even the range of future demand and conditions is not well known.
