The network is synthetic, built from real municipal and weather data where possible, and failures in its primary supply lines could cut service to thousands of people.

Competitors must stage interventions over a planning horizon of at least 25 years, choosing works such as new supply capacity. A desalination plant alone takes 5 to 10 years to define and build. They balance pumping energy, carbon emissions, household tariffs, and bond financing. Plans are re-evaluated at the end of each stage as uncertainties unfold. And an open-source evaluator lets teams test solutions before final submission, making the contest a test bed for adaptive planning methods.
arxiv-2511-23086:
Chattopadhyay and colleagues tackle statistical inference for a flexible family of probability models defined through their quantile function. The quantile function is the rule that maps a probability to a value, rather than through a density formula. Families such as the Tukey Lambda and generalized Lambda distributions can mimic many shapes with few parameters, but their density and distribution function have no closed form, which breaks standard estimation tools.

Approximate maximum likelihood in these models can converge at abnormal rates with non-normal limits, making even the bootstrap unreliable. So the authors instead build confidence sets by inverting distribution-free confidence bands for the empirical distribution function through the known quantile function. Simulations confirm the promised coverage. And the method is demonstrated on the two Lambda families with two real examples, a small twin-study dataset and a large Spanish household income dataset, showing it works at both sample sizes.
arxiv-2511-23386:
Du and colleagues tackle a core obstacle for unified multimodal models, the tokenizer. It normally forces a choice between continuous features that suit image understanding and discrete tokens that suit generation. Their VQRAE, a vector-quantized version of representation autoencoders, is built on a pretrained vision foundation model with a symmetric transformer decoder. It is designed to emit both kinds of representation from one tokenizer for the first time.

Training runs in two stages, first freezing the encoder while a high-dimensional semantic codebook is learned for pixel reconstruction. Then it jointly optimizes with self-distillation so understanding ability is preserved. Against the field's usual low-dimensional codebooks, their semantic codebook reaches a 100 percent utilization ratio at a dimension of 1536 in the reported experiments. VQRAE posts competitive results across understanding, generation, and reconstruction benchmarks with scaling in autoregressive models overall.
arxiv-2512-00386:
Sampling within a bounded region, rather than all of space, is a recurring task in statistics and physics. Tarika Mane examines the reflected Langevin diffusion for this constrained sampling problem in 2025. The diffusion is written as a reflected stochastic differential equation on a closed, convex domain.

Mane introduces a sequence of penalized equations that soften the boundary instead of reflecting from it. Their invariant measures converge to the reflected diffusion's measure, in Wasserstein distance and with an explicit polynomial rate. Explicit rates matter because users need to know how long to run a sampler before trusting its output. Closed convex domains cover many practical cases, from portfolios to physical containers. For folks who run such sums, the gain is a bound they can quote. Run the chain this long, and the drift left is small in a way they can state.
arxiv-2512-00486:
Heavy fermion superconductors often withstand magnetic fields far beyond the standard Pauli limit. Yan-Xiao Wang and Yin Zhong study that violation in 2025, tying it to nearly flat electronic bands. Exceeding the limit signals that paramagnetic pair breaking works differently in these materials.

Strong correlations and hybridized quasiparticle bands are essential to the pair-breaking process, the authors argue. Flat bands concentrate electronic states in ways that reshape how fields attack superconductivity. Understanding the mechanism informs the search for superconductors that stay functional in the extreme fields needed by magnets and quantum devices. That limit, where the effect at last gives way, is called the upper critical field. Hybridized bands mix heavy and light electrons, a hallmark of these materials.
arxiv-2512-00686:
Anish Lakkapragada wrote a 2025 paper on why modern neural networks learn in sudden jumps. A known puzzle is grokking, where a network does poorly for a long time and then, without warning, starts to generalize well. Phase transitions like this are hard to explain with classic learning theory.

Lakkapragada turns to singular learning theory, a framework borrowed from physics and built on algebraic geometry. Classic tools assume each setting of a model is distinct, but neural networks break that rule. Many different settings can act the same. Singular learning theory handles that mismatch, and the paper uses it to explain sudden learning shifts.
arxiv-2512-00886:
Antoine Galet wrote a 2025 paper on duality for higher local fields. A field is called d-local when it sits atop a tower of fields. Each field in the tower is complete with a discrete valuation, and the previous one is its residue field. The tower ends at a finite field. Such towers appear in number theory when several layers of local structure stack up.

Galet studies duality for these fields following the work of Kato and Suzuki. Duality pairs mathematical objects so each side determines the other, often turning hard counts into easy ones. Extending duality to higher local fields supports class field theory in higher dimensions, a deep area of modern number theory.
arxiv-2512-00986:
Zhihan Guo and nine coauthors introduce Dr.Mi-Bench in a 2025 paper on research agents. The academic literature now grows so fast that automated deep research agents are needed to read and synthesize it. Evaluating those agents is itself a hard problem, and current benchmarks have gaps.

Many older benchmarks focus on retrieval while neglecting planning and reasoning. They also favor general topics over the scientific domains where research agents matter most. Dr.Mi-Bench is a modular, integrated benchmark built for scientific deep research. It tests the full chain from finding papers to reasoning over them, giving builders a fairer way to compare agents.
arxiv-2512-01086:
Paolo Marimon and Michael Pinsker wrote a 2025 guide to topological reconstruction. Many symmetry spaces carry both algebraic and topological structure at once. The automorphism group of a structure, for example, is a group in two senses at once. It is also a topological group under pointwise convergence, where closeness means agreeing on more and more points.

The core question is whether the algebraic side alone determines the topology. The guide covers endomorphism monoids and polymorphism clones, two richer kinds of symmetry collections used in algebra and computer science. A clear guide helps researchers entering a field where topology and algebra constantly interact. It is written as a map for readers who know one side well and want to learn the other.
arxiv-2512-01286:
Mudit Gaur and co-authors study flow matching, a way to build data-making models. Such models learn smooth flows that turn noise into real-like data. They train fast and sample fast. But the theory behind them is still thin.

The team asks how many samples the method needs to learn well. That count is called sample complexity. A firm count tells builders how much data a task will take. It also shows when flow matching beats older diffusion models. Their bounds give the field a firmer base for claims about speed and cost.
arxiv-2512-01486:
Farzad Milani gives a firm frame for black holes that change signature. Signature tells how time and space enter the metric. In his setup, it flips at the horizon of a BTZ black hole. Inside, time acts like space. Such flips strain the math of gravity.

Milani shows how to smooth that flip in a consistent way. The BTZ case is a clean test bed in two space dimensions plus time. A sound frame lets scholars ask what physics could sit past such a horizon. It also guards past claims from hidden math flaws.
arxiv-2512-01686:
Patrick Kwon and Chen Chen visualize stories with layout-aware video models. Past story tools place subjects from text alone. Keeping art style and identity steady across frames is hard. Faces and outfits drift as the story goes on.

Their pipeline, DreamingComics, customizes subject and layout together. It builds on a pre-trained video diffusion transformer. That base brings time-space priors that hold style steady. Layout control lets authors place each subject by plan, not chance. Steady, placed frames serve comics and storyboards. Video priors beat image priors for comics, since panels imply motion and time flow that a still-image model cannot infer alone.
arxiv-2512-01886:
The Sun's chromosphere, the layer above its visible surface, is threaded with thin strand-like structures called fibrils, shaped by motions below. A 2025 observational paper by Reetika Joshi and eight co-authors examines these fine structures and the role they play in the behavior of solar magnetic fields.

Many such features are already catalogued, from filament feet to arch filament systems, yet high-resolution telescopes keep revealing forms that defy easy explanation. The team focuses on an active fibril singularity, a striking pattern in the observed data. Understanding these small structures matters because they channel energy through the Sun's atmosphere and shape space weather near Earth.
arxiv-2512-02486:
Zhongjian Qiao and seven co-authors return to offline reinforcement learning, where agents learn from stored logs. One dataset rarely covers every case an agent will meet. Borrowing logs from a related setting helps, but that setting may obey different dynamics.

Past work mostly guards against shifts in the training data itself. Deployment brings a second risk: the live setting may drift again after training ends. The team's dual robust method defends against both kinds of shift at once. Agents that stay steady under change are safer for real tasks like driving, robotics, and operations. Tests in the wild, not just in the lab, will show how far this dual guard holds.
arxiv-2512-02686:
Yuxing Liu and Yong Liu improve anomaly segmentation, the task of finding odd objects on the road. Self driving systems must detect things outside their known classes, since the open world always holds surprises. Real anomaly data is scarce and narrow, which limits how well models generalize.

ClimaOoD creates physically realistic synthetic anomaly data to fill that gap. Training on varied, plausible oddities teaches models to flag the truly unknown. Better anomaly segmentation is a safety issue: a system that notices what it does not know can slow down or hand over control in time. Fake odd cases must look real, or the model learns to spot the fake, not the road risk ahead.
arxiv-2512-02786:
Anton Emelyanov, Sergei Kudriashov, and Alena Fenogenova test whether a multimodal model secretly trained on your data. Membership inference attacks ask if one specific item sat in a model's training set. Many detectors exist for text models, but they falter on multimodal ones.

Extra vision parts and shifts across inputs make multimodal models unstable targets. FiMMIA scales semantic perturbation based inference across modalities, probing how outputs bend under meaning preserving changes. Such audits matter for privacy and copyright, where proving a model trained on protected work has legal weight. Probes that bend sense, not words, test the part of a tool that sees and hears, where leaks are hard to spot with text checks.
arxiv-2512-02886:
Doosung Park and Paul Arne Østvær compute a refined cohomology theory for spaces marked by logarithmic data. Syntomic cohomology links algebraic geometry with p-adic Hodge theory, a bridge used in modern number theory. The logarithmic version handles schemes with fine, saturated log structures.

The pair studies this theory for truncated polynomials and coordinate axes, concrete test cases. They also realize it inside the logarithmic motivic stable homotopy category of a log point. Worked examples anchor abstract machinery, letting number theorists trust the theory on the singular spaces they actually meet. Toy cases with known truth are how new tools earn trust, and this pair of toy forms plays that role for a hard field.
arxiv-2512-03086:
Translating code between languages needs good training data. Le Chen and a large team address a shortage of such data in this 2025 work. Language models do well at code translation, but they falter in rare fields like Fortran and new tools like CUDA.

The team builds a pipeline that makes training data through dialogue. Two models work as questioner and solver, guided by compiler and runtime feedback. That loop helps keep the code correct. More good data could help firms update old code and use new hardware without hand work. Compilers in the loop help keep generated code pairs honest, rather than merely plausible.
arxiv-2512-03186:
Grip strength is a simple sign of health. Colin Barry and Edward Jay Wang test a phone-only way to estimate it in this 2025 work. Grip links to mobility, frailty, surgery outcomes, and health in general.

Their method uses the phone's vibration motor and motion sensors. As a user grips, the phone's shaking pattern changes, and the sensors pick that up. A phone-based test could let people check strength at home with no extra gear. That ease could help clinics track patients between visits. A simple home test could also flag decline early, when exercise and care help most.
arxiv-2512-03286:
Naming cell types from single-cell data is a key step in biology. Min Huang and Rishikesan Kamaleswaran present SpikGPT for that task in this 2025 work. Annotation gets hard when data sets differ by batch or hold cell types never seen before.

SpikGPT blends cell embeddings from a model called scGPT with a spiking Transformer design. Spiking networks fire in brief pulses, like real neurons, which can save energy. The authors aim for accuracy that is also easy to interpret. Trustworthy labels help researchers read tissue and disease data correctly. Batch effects fool many tools, so robustness across labs is a central test for SpikGPT.
arxiv-2512-03486:
Synthetic voices need sharp critics to sound real. Nan Xu, Zhaolong Huang, and Xiao Zeng present a universal harmonic discriminator in this 2025 work. Vocoders based on GANs use a discriminator to judge the generated audio.

The team focuses on time-frequency discriminators, which often read a Short-Time Fourier Transform of the sound. Their harmonic design aims to judge voices across generators, hence universal. Better discriminators push vocoders toward natural speech. That helps text-to-speech tools used in apps, books, and accessibility. Harmonic structure matches speech, where pitch and its overtones define voice quality.
arxiv-2512-03586:
Domenico Caparello and Tommaso Tenna split gas flow problems between two solvers and stitch their clocks together. Rarefied gases need the kinetic ES-BGK model, while settled regions obey cheaper fluid equations. Their 2025 method detects which regime each region is in and assigns solvers by territory.

The hard part is time: stepping the two solvers with an implicit-explicit scheme usually breaks the method's high accuracy order. Their coupled IMEX strategy preserves that order across the internal borders. Two-dimensional simulations checked robustness and confirmed the expected high-order convergence in time. The payoff is kinetic accuracy only where physics demands it, at fluid prices elsewhere.
arxiv-2512-04186:
Clouds of tiny solid particles veil exoplanet and brown dwarf atmospheres, bending the light astronomers use to read them. Matt G. Lodge and colleagues ask how the shape of those particles changes the spectra, in a 2025 planetary science preprint. Their modelling code, Virga, tracks particle sizes with altitude and now handles aggregates, from fluffy chains to compact clumps.

The team computed transmission spectra for warm Neptune and hot Jupiter settings, plus emitted light for an L-type brown dwarf. Shape mattered measurably, most strongly at short wavelengths where morphology steers the scattering slope. Their rule of thumb runs both ways. When particles are small next to the wavelength, elongated chains give the highest opacities; when particles are large, compact shapes win instead. Formation dynamics and basic optics explain both regimes. Their advice: treat shape as a free parameter in retrievals.
arxiv-2512-04386:
Zhou Yang, Shunyan Luo, Jiazhen Zhu, and Fang Jin present MASE, a method that explains why a text model made a given call. Deep networks lead language technology, yet their choices stay hard to read. Word data pose a special snag, since older picture-based tricks do not transfer cleanly to text. Their 2025 arXiv paper seeks local explanations that work for any model, with no need to see inside it.

MASE nudges the hidden word vectors inside a model rather than the raw words on the page. Smooth random nudges, shaped by a Gaussian curve, reveal which inputs sway the output most. Those sway scores form a saliency map a person can inspect. In tests, MASE beat other model-free explanation tools, most clearly on a score that tracks how much the flagged words matter. Clearer explanations can help users trust and audit language tools.
arxiv-2512-04486:
Pratiksha Chauhan, Samir Shukla, and Kumar Vinayak work out the shape, in the topological sense, of certain complexes built from graphs. For a graph, the total cut complex gathers sets of vertices whose removal leaves a graph with no edges at all. These complexes came from work by Bayer and co-authors linking graph theory with algebra. Their 2025 arXiv paper extends that study to the case where two vertices are left standing.

The team focuses on three graph families: powers of cycle graphs, where each vertex links to neighbors up to a set distance, and grid-like products of complete graphs with paths. For each family they pin down the homotopy type of the complex, which says what kind of space it resembles up to stretching. Full answers for these families add to a growing catalog. Such catalogs help algebraists predict when related algebraic objects vanish or persist.
arxiv-2512-05286:
Katherine Pearce and Per-Gunnar Martinsson survey randomized algorithms for low-rank decompositions of tensors and matrices. Huge data matrices are often nearly low-rank, well approximated by a product of skinny factors. Classical decompositions like the singular value decomposition find those factors but can be too slow at scale. Randomization changes the economics: sketch the big matrix down to a small one, solve there, and lift the answer back.

The survey reviews the classical algorithms and how randomized dimensionality reduction accelerates them, including interpolative and CUR decompositions that keep actual rows and columns. It covers recent advances in fast sketching and sampling. Then it follows the ideas upward to tensors, the multi-way arrays behind modern data analysis, treating the CP and Tucker formats and their higher-order decompositions. For practitioners, it is a map of when randomness safely buys speed in numerical linear algebra.
arxiv-2512-05486:
Sakshi Gautam and Ram Pandey construct a new family of numerical methods for stiff differential equations — systems whose components evolve on wildly different timescales and punish naive steppers. Their methods are general linear methods, which blend multistep and Runge-Kutta ideas, built here with a symmetric order structure and a property called inherent quadratic stability. The schemes are designed under stability constraints that guarantee good behaviour on stiff problems, then optimized to minimize error.

The authors build implicit methods up to fourth order and test them on three real problems. They are the van der Pol oscillator, Burgers' equation, and the Gray-Scott reaction-diffusion model famous for its spot patterns. Observed-order checks and error-versus-step plots confirm the theory, and the schemes compete with existing general linear methods. The paper offers time-integration practitioners an alternative with stability engineered in from the start rather than verified afterwards.
arxiv-2512-05886:
A De Vita and fifteen co-authors map the electronic structure of a Dirac semimetal, BaMg2Bi2, and find states living on its surface that no one had reported. The material hosts a single, clean Dirac cone at the center of its momentum space, guarded by threefold rotation symmetry. Its strontium cousin is an insulator, so the pair may act as a topological switch. Earlier measurements used high photon energies, blurring comparison with theory.

Combining sharp, low energy photoemission with density functional calculations, the team now resolves the valence bands in full. The new surface states appear clearly, and prove topologically trivial. Knowing they exist reconciles longstanding mismatches between measurement and calculation. The full picture grounds predictions of how the material conducts. The switch case now rests on bands that are actually understood.
arxiv-2512-06086:
Matías Leizerovich, Susana Landau, and Claudia Scóccola give cosmology a better ruler for its favorite argument: how much do our datasets disagree? Dataset tensions, possible hints of new physics, are usually quoted pairwise. Their estimator generalizes the difference in means statistic to many datasets at once. It finds the disagreement's dominant directions.

For two and three datasets, the tension gets a geometric picture. Applied to the reported friction between the DESI survey and the Planck satellite, the framework tempers the headline. An apparent rise in tension between data releases reads, under the new effective measure, as a more modest shift. Tension claims drive headlines and telescope time. Such a metric guards against false alarms and missed discoveries.
arxiv-2512-06186:
Max Dupré la Tour, Manuel Lafond, and Ndiamé Ndiaye close an algorithmic loophole: you cannot even cheaply test whether a graph has the nice structure that makes hard problems easy. Bounded mim-width makes many hard problems polynomial. Variants, sim-width, omim-width, and linear forms, followed. Recognizing the smallest widths stayed open.

This work proves hardness all the way down. Deciding width one, for three parameters, is NP-hard; mim-width two as well. The reductions come from a quartet problem in computational biology. Heuristics must carry the load of finding the precondition. Theory needs such negative results to stay honest.
arxiv-2512-06586: Mikhail Zimin, Milyausha Shamsutdinova, and Georgii Andriushchenko adapt a factual consistency checker for Russian texts. Tools that grade whether a generated text stays true to its source exist mostly for English, leaving Russian writers and systems without a check. The team fine tuned a Russian language model with heads for classification and regression on Russian data and on translated English data sets. Their AlignRuScore matched the unified alignment approach of the original metric, showing the method can cross languages. They release the corpora, checkpoints, and code.
arxiv-2512-06686:
Ying-Jian Chen and Jun Nian bring quantum jitter and heat into a famous model of warped spacetime. The Randall Sundrum model places our universe on a brane inside a higher dimensional space, and it is often studied around a black brane. Close to that black brane's horizon, the geometry simplifies into a two dimensional gravity theory, Jackiw Teitelboim gravity, whose quantum fluctuations follow a Schwarzian action.

The authors feed those fluctuating modes back into the full metric. From the resulting equations they compute how the masses of the model's tower of heavier particles, the Kaluza Klein modes, shift under the quantum corrections. They also weigh what the corrections do to the Goldberger Wise mechanism, the piece that fixes the size of the extra dimension. The work gives a version of the model with both temperature and quantum effects in play, of use for cosmology and phase change studies.
arxiv-2512-06986:
Taehwan Jung and co-authors report a surprise in remote epitaxy, a crystal-growing trick where a film copies the atomic pattern of a base through an atomically thin sheet. Instead of copying cleanly, competing pulls from the sheet, the base, and the film's own rebuilding can frustrate the boundary layer. In films of a gadolinium-gold-germanium compound grown over graphene layers, the team found a self-limiting interface state with no long-range order.

The frustrated layer appears only at middling numbers of graphene sheets, and the film above it picks odd crystal orientations as the count changes. Magnetism tied to the interface grows strikingly strong, persisting above room temperature and scaling with the boundary rather than the bulk. Heating an orderly film drives it into the frustrated state, ruling out mere frozen disorder.
arxiv-2512-07486:
Niklas Dobberstein and Jan Hamaekers wrote this 2025 materials science paper on designing crystals with AI. Their system, Materium, is a transformer that generates new crystal structures. It turns a three-dimensional material into a sequence of tokens, much like words.

Each token sequence spells out the elements and their oxidation states. It also gives the atoms' fractional positions and the shape of the unit cell. Diffusion models, the usual rivals, nudge atoms into place over many slow steps. Materium instead places each atom at an exact position in one pass. Generation is therefore fast and easy to scale up. Training takes only a few hours on a single graphics card. Users can steer the output by naming target traits. Those traits range from density and symmetry to band gap and magnetic strength. Under single and combined conditions, the samples match the requests well.
arxiv-2512-07586:
Hongfei Shu, Peng Zhao, Rui-Dong Zhu, and Hao Zou wrote this 2025 mathematics paper in representation theory. Tensor product multiplicities count how often one representation appears inside a product of others. Those numbers are basic, yet they can be hard to compute directly.

The authors develop a new combinatorial formula for those counts. Their difference formula links the multiplicities to restricted occupancy coefficients. A shifted operator carries out the connection between the two. The method stretches further, yielding branching rules for subalgebras. A conjectural application reaches A-type Lie superalgebras, a wilder cousin family. The note is short, but it hands algebraists a fresh counting bridge.
arxiv-2512-07786:
Vinayak Joshi and Ashok Joshi wrote this 2025 theoretical physics paper on black holes without a crushing center. Regular black holes replace the singularity with a smooth core. The Simpson-Visser geometry, nicknamed the black-bounce, is a clean example of the idea.

The authors explore how such an object behaves as a thermodynamic system. They find a critical instability in its heat capacity. At the transition, that capacity jumps discontinuously rather than sliding smoothly. The jump signals a deep change in how the black hole evaporates.  The paper then pushes past the semiclassical picture of evaporation. A Hamilton-Jacobi tunneling method yields leading quantum corrections to the entropy. Those corrections refine the entropy counting. The nature of the final end-state gets a quantitative treatment too. Resolving the singularity, they conclude, is a thermodynamic event, not just geometry.
arxiv-2512-07886:
Hamoon Soleimani wrote this 2025 economics paper on a paradox at Bitcoin's core. Issuance follows a fixed, inelastic schedule set in advance. Demand for scarce block space, by contrast, swings wildly and elastically.

His Endogenous Constraint Hypothesis links those two facts into a feedback loop. Protocol throughput limits, he argues, choke the base layer's monetary velocity. The loop is nonlinear: friction bites only past a sharp threshold. He builds a Transaction Cost Index from on-chain data to measure friction. Threshold regression then hunts for the break in the relationship. Velocity grows robustly in calm regimes and sags hard in shock regimes. The net contraction in utility across the break is statistically clear. Instrument tests confirm the effect is regime switching, not a steady slope. Congestion also concentrates capital, as users swap active use for hoarding. Stagflation-like behavior, in his telling, is built into the protocol.
arxiv-2512-07986: S Yu Orevkov, a mathematician who works on complex surfaces and singularities, posted a short note on arXiv in December 2025. He studies germs of mappings between two copies of the complex plane, both fixed at the origin. The mappings branch along a germ of an irreducible curve whose image has a simple power form. Orevkov presents the note as an addendum to an earlier paper by Kulikov on the same family of mappings, and he gives a description of these germs.
arxiv-2512-08086:
Arup Singha, Shaili Sett, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Arindam Ghosh, and Rahul Debnath, physicists and materials scientists, posted an experimental study on arXiv in December 2025. Their device is a ferroelectric transistor built from twisted tungsten diselenide layers. The twist creates long range moire patterns with built in polarization at that same scale. Such devices promise low voltage, non volatile two dimensional electronics.

The hard problem has been controlling that polarization without trapping charge, which ruins stability. Using atomically clean layered interfaces, the team built a transistor that couples polarization to the channel efficiently and suppresses trapping. It switches at very low voltage, holds a stable memory window, and shows high mobility, matching advanced silicon devices. Electrical measurements, backed by Landau Ginzburg Devonshire modeling, point to very fast switching. The results present moire based ferroelectricity as a scalable route to clean, low power memory and logic.
arxiv-2512-08186:
Meng Wei, Chenyang Wan, Jiaqi Peng, and a large team of robotics researchers posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their system, DualVLN, is a foundation model for vision and language navigation, where a robot follows spoken or written directions through a space. Earlier models map images and words straight to short actions, yielding jerky motion, slow responses, and weak obstacle avoidance.

DualVLN splits the job between two systems that work at different speeds. A vision language planner thinks slowly, using image grounded reasoning to set mid term waypoint goals. A light diffusion transformer policy then moves fast, turning pixel goals and planner features into smooth paths. Training the parts separately keeps the planner broad knowledge while the mover stays quick. The system beat prior methods on all benchmarks used, and real world tests showed strong long horizon planning in busy, changing settings.
arxiv-2512-08286:
Liao Hu, Qiteng Wu, and Ruoyu Qi, software engineers in China, posted a systems paper on arXiv in December 2025 introducing SolidGPT. It is an open source assistant for developers that splits its work between the user machine and the cloud. Cloud tools reason well but expose private code and add delay, while local tools miss the full context of a project.

SolidGPT lets developers talk to their codebase, asking where features live instead of hunting through files by hand. It can also draft product documents, break work into tasks, build Kanban boards, and scaffold new web apps, with links into VS Code and Notion. Private code folders can be added, agent personas tuned, and the system run through Docker, a command line tool, or an editor extension. Because it runs locally first, teams keep control of their code and data, a privacy respecting way to speed real development work.
arxiv-2512-08486:
Ada Gorgun, Fawaz Sammani, Nikos Deligiannis, and colleagues, computer vision researchers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Diffusion image models are usually judged only by their final pictures, yet a picture forms step by step as noise is removed. The authors ask a sharp question: at what moment does a concept, such as age, enter the image and lock the rest of the process in?

Their framework, Prompt Conditioned Intervention, answers without any training or access to model internals. It inserts a concept at a chosen timestep and measures how often that concept survives into the final image. Applied across leading models and a wide taxonomy of concepts, the probe found varied timing patterns, with certain phases favoring certain concepts. Those maps also guide text driven editing, showing when an intervention bites hardest. Their edits balanced accuracy against keeping the original content, beating strong baselines.
arxiv-2512-08586:
Hang Zhou and coauthors study a subtle effect in thin superconducting films just above the field where superconductivity is lost. In that range, theory predicts fleeting clusters of paired electrons that rotate like early forms of vortices. Those clusters were long thought too fast and too weak to observe directly.

The authors show that the clusters should leave a clear mark in the high frequency electrical response of the film. They predict a strong rise in the imaginary part of the conductivity at a set microwave frequency tied to the field gap. For niobium, a common test material, that frequency falls in a range that modern microwave tools can reach. The result turns a hidden quantum fluctuation effect into a target that lab tests can check.
arxiv-2512-08786:
Mahmoud Srewa, Tianyu Zhao, and Salma Elmalaki study how to align large language models with diverse human views when learning happens in a federated setting. In that setting, data stays local, and each group scores model outputs to produce reward signals. The server then combines group rewards without seeing raw data, but standard combining rules can under represent some viewpoints.

The authors build an evaluation framework that tests how alignment quality trades off against fairness across aggregation rules. They compare simple rules that take the minimum, maximum, or average reward. They also introduce an adaptive rule that adjusts group weights based on past alignment performance. In question answering tests with a reinforcement learning pipeline, the adaptive rule gives better fairness while keeping alignment scores competitive. The work offers a practical path toward models that reflect plural views more fairly.
arxiv-2512-09386:
Peter Baile Chen and colleagues present CONCUR, a framework for routing each AI task to the computing strategy that fits it best. Tasks differ in difficulty. Varied combinations of models and decoding methods suit varied tasks. Most routing systems train one model over all strategies, so adding a new strategy means expensive retraining, and earlier continual routers generalize poorly.

CONCUR trains a separate small predictor for each strategy, so new ones slot in with little added cost. Its predictors also use several representations of both the task and the strategy, capturing more of what makes routing hard. The framework supports routing with or without a budget limit. On knowledge and reasoning tasks, both familiar and out-of-distribution, CONCUR beat the best single approach and strong existing routers. It had higher accuracy and lower inference cost, and it reduced training cost in the continual setting.
arxiv-2512-09486:
Manish Yadav and colleagues test a cosmological model that allows both curvature and evolving dark energy, using data from the DESI survey. The model, called wCDM, lets dark energy's equation of state differ from a pure cosmological constant and lets the universe's geometry be slightly curved. The question is which DESI release fits this framework better and what curvature does to the constraints.

They combine DESI's first and second data releases with Big Bang nucleosynthesis limits, expansion-rate measurements, and the Pantheon Plus supernova sample. The curvature results mildly disfavor the cosmological constant and lean toward a slightly open universe, though the deviations stay near the one-sigma level. Their fitted dark energy values favor the quintessence region, and their expansion-rate predictions from the fuller dataset sit comfortably with the Planck collaboration's results. Key distance measures also agreed better with the model under the second data release.
arxiv-2512-09586:
Prashant Kumar Choudhary and colleagues present a search for good variational quantum circuits, the parameterized circuits at the heart of near-term quantum machine learning. Designing such circuits by hand is a bottleneck, especially for complex data. Their system treats a circuit as a graph and improves it by mutation and selection.

A graph neural network acts as a surrogate model, predicting circuit quality and estimating how sure it is through Monte Carlo dropout. An expected improvement rule, borrowed from Bayesian optimization, then picks the best options to run. The test task is a hybrid quantum-classical classifier on a security dataset of firewall and internet-of-things telemetry, after feature selection and scaling for quantum embedding. Against a multilayer perceptron model, random search, and greedy graph picking, the guided optimizer found simpler circuits with similar or better accuracy. A noise study checked robustness across quantum noise channels.
arxiv-2512-10186:
Matthew Malkan, Lisbeth Jensen, and Lei Hao compare the narrow emission lines of Seyfert galaxies, active galaxies whose spectra mix a bright nucleus with its host. Seyfert 1 galaxies show broad lines from fast gas near the black hole; Seyfert 2s show only narrow lines. The team subdivided a large Sloan survey sample by how strong the broad component is, then compared the narrow lines against pure Seyfert 2s on standard diagnostic diagrams. For the strongest broad line objects, the narrow lines match those of Seyfert 2s. For the weakest, most spectra fall instead in the composite region shared with star formation.

A simple model explains the pattern: in the weakest Seyfert 1s, most narrow line emission comes from star forming regions, not the active nucleus. Dust reddening of the narrow line gas also grows steadily as the broad component weakens. The simplest unification picture is not supported.
arxiv-2512-10486:
Nicolás Cuello and a large team report ALMA telescope observations of the young binary star system L1551 IRS 5, part of the FAUST large programme. Twin young stars with discs are natural laboratories for the earliest planet formation. And rings or clumps in discs around such young protostars hint that planets may start forming sooner than models once allowed.

The disc around both stars shows two bright over-densities at the edge of its central cavity, the northern one somewhat brighter. The team mapped the disc's shape and motion to pin down the binary's orbit, then ran three-dimensional hydrodynamical models and compared synthetic views with the real dust and gas data. The match suggests the two stars themselves stir the disc, piling dust into the bright spots, where material could later grow further under the right conditions.
arxiv-2512-10986:
Lina Coulaud, Julia Santos, and Ko-Ju Chuang measure how oxygen molecules move and get trapped inside the icy material found between stars. Interstellar ice is mostly amorphous solid water with small amounts of volatile gases mixed in. Oxygen is an early and important ingredient for space chemistry, but its surface movement in such ice was poorly known.

Working in an ultra high vacuum chamber, the team used infrared spectroscopy and mass spectrometry to track the oxygen. A new fitting method let them measure diffusion even though oxygen itself is invisible to infrared light. Oxygen proved highly mobile, with a low energy barrier for movement. A share of it stayed trapped in the ice even at the highest temperatures tested, a result that matters for how volatiles persist in space.
arxiv-2512-12186:
Mohammad Taghi Dabiri and six co-authors design a road system that senses, locates, and talks at once in a 2025 paper. Fast traffic needs all three jobs done with no machine tracking. Older light based systems use point beams or cameras, which limit road coverage and update speed.

Their design pairs line lasers with reflector arrays on vehicles that can send data back. Two crossed line lasers scan along and across the road for wide, steady coverage. A math model links beam spread, scan shape, and dwell time. Tuning those settings improved coverage, link stability, and reliability in tests, all within one fixed scan period.
arxiv-2512-12286:
Zahra Ahghari and Mehrdad Farhoudi study cosmic inflation with a Higgs field in a 2025 paper. Inflation is a burst of fast growth in the very early universe. Their model adds a Gauss-Bonnet term, a correction from gravity theory, tied to the Higgs field through a dilaton like link.

Working in a standard expanding universe model, they derive the motion equations and use slow roll conditions. Since a key integral resists direct solution, they use a Taylor expansion plus plots and numerical work. Their values for the tensor to scalar ratio and the spectral index match recent data, notably ACT DR6. Without the Gauss-Bonnet term, results resemble chaotic inflation.
arxiv-2512-12386:
Swayam Bhanded presents SR-DiT, a fast training recipe for image diffusion models, in a 2025 paper. Recent tricks speed up diffusion transformers, but each was mostly tested alone. Combining them may give gains that single studies miss, or may clash. SR-DiT joins token routing, design changes, and training tweaks on top of representation alignment.

On ImageNet at 256 resolution, a model of only 140 million parameters reached FID 3.49 and KDD 0.319 after 400K training steps, with no classifier free guidance. That rivals 685 million parameter models trained far longer. Ablation tests show which mixes help and which clash, and the code is released as a baseline.
arxiv-2512-12486:
Tyler Becker and Zachary Sunberg extend AlphaZero style search to games where both players move at once in a 2025 paper. Many planning problems need simultaneous action, so turn based search fails; each tree node becomes a small game to solve. Their method, Simultaneous AlphaZero, targets two player, zero sum Markov games with continuous states.

A learned value function guides finite depth regret matching search at each node. Learned regret and average strategy functions warm start the solver when deployed. They prove error bounds for both parts, including how fitting errors spread through learning. In Dubins pursuit evasion and satellite custody tasks, guided search beat unguided search in head to head solver play.
arxiv-2512-12586:
Lixin Chen and four co-authors present StegaVAR, a privacy preserving video action recognition framework, in a 2025 paper. Action recognition reads what people do in videos, but raw videos leak private content. Past privacy methods distort the video, which draws attacker attention during transfer and destroys the space time features that accurate recognition needs.

StegaVAR hides the action video inside an ordinary cover video and runs recognition in the steganographic domain, a first for this task. The hidden video's information stays complete, while the cover looks natural. Two modules guide feature extraction with the secret video and suppress cover interference by cross band differences. Tests showed strong action recognition and privacy across data sets and steganography models.
arxiv-2512-13286:
Youssra Rebboud, Pasquale Lisena, and Raphael Troncy add causal reasoning to automated fact-checking. A claim often fails because it links events by a wrong cause and effect chain. Standard checkers rarely test those causal links directly, missing a chance for clear explanations.

Their method extracts event relations from text, computes semantic similarity, and applies rule based reasoning to spot mismatches. It compares the chain of events inside a claim with the chain inside the evidence. Tested on two fact-checking data sets, it sets the first baseline for fine-grained causal checking. The approach also makes verdicts easier to explain to readers.
arxiv-2512-13886:
Mohammad Mozaffari and co-authors introduce OPTIMA, a one-shot pruning method for large language models that uses quadratic programming. Pruning cuts inference cost, but simple weight zeroing hurts accuracy, while exact joint optimization is too costly at modern scale. SparseGPT sits between those poles with approximate updates.

OPTIMA recasts layer-wise weight reconstruction, after mask selection, as independent column-wise quadratic programs sharing one Hessian per weight matrix. Solving them gives the best per-column reconstruction under that Hessian, and the shared form batches well on accelerators. It improved zero-shot accuracy in 40 of 49 settings across LLaMA and Gemma models, with gains up to 3.97 points at 60% sparsity. It pruned an 8B model on one H100 in 40 hours.
arxiv-2512-13986:
Claude Zeller and Robert Cordery build an analytic framework for first-return statistics in radiative transport. A photon entering a scattering medium makes a three-dimensional random walk, set by the Henyey-Greenstein phase function, until it exits or is absorbed. They project that walk onto the axial direction.

The projection gives a one-dimensional alternating process whose peaks and valleys mark sign changes in the projected step. That reduction preserves first-return and first-passage events and leads to a Motzkin polynomial form. Boundary return terms appear as high-order integrals, handled with one truncation factor fit from Monte Carlo data. The factor follows a Cauchy distribution. Resulting first-return probabilities match full three-dimensional Monte Carlo within 2% for anisotropy up to 0.7.
arxiv-2512-14286:
Samuel Cruz Alegria and four coauthors present an additively preconditioned trust region strategy for machine learning in a 2025 paper. Training deep networks means solving large, highly nonconvex problems with rough objective landscapes, where plain methods can crawl.

Their method borrows additive Schwarz ideas from parallel solvers for large linear systems. The parameter space is split into subdomains, local nonlinear subproblems are solved in parallel, and their corrections are added together at each step. A classical trust region frame controls the step size. The authors report fast convergence and, thanks to the trust region design, much less need for hyperparameter tuning. The approach aims to scale network training across many processors.
arxiv-2512-14486:
Hiddo Algera and thirty-seven co-authors report the first systematic search for a key oxygen emission line in galaxies seen as they were within six hundred million years of the Big Bang. Using the ALMA telescope array, they observed four bright, gravitationally lensed galaxies that the Webb telescope had picked out. The line comes from ionized oxygen and traces star formation and gas conditions.

Two galaxies showed the line clearly, glowing about as expected from nearby-universe patterns. The other two, even more distant, showed none, and no dust appeared anywhere. One detection carried a broad extra component, the signature of gas blasting outward faster than star formation alone would suggest.
arxiv-2512-14586:
Muhammad Waseem studies a subtle optical effect that microwaves might switch and steer. When light reflects at an interface, its two polarizations shift sideways by slightly different amounts, the photonic spin Hall effect. Waseem models the effect inside a closed-loop atomic system of the lambda type, where a microwave field joins the optical controls.

At some settings the shift's size stays fixed while the microwave slides its angular position, which suits measuring microwave fields by comparison. At other settings the shift fades exponentially as the microwave grows, or peaks with the phase tuned just right. Phase changes even flip the effect on and off, pointing toward microwave sensors and optical switches.
arxiv-2512-14686:
Stochastic optimization drives most modern machine learning training, and its noise is often heavy-tailed rather than gentle. Recent work has pushed first-order methods from the classic bounded-variance setting toward noise that may not even have a finite mean, with gradient clipping as the key control.

The bias-variance trade-off of those clipped methods is the subject here: clipping tames wild gradients but also biases them, and the balance decides how fast a method can converge. Understanding that trade-off helps practitioners set clipping levels on principle instead of by trial. The analysis extends guarantees toward the messy noise that real training actually produces.
arxiv-2512-14886:
Jing Huang and a coauthor extend a classic family of graphs to the signed setting. Chordal graphs are prized because they admit neat descriptions: by forbidden subgraphs, by orderings of vertices and edges, by separating sets, and by tree like pictures. Signed graphs add a plus or minus label to each edge.

The authors define chordal signed graphs and chordal signed bigraphs, and describe each by the subgraphs they forbid. Signed graphs of this kind turn out to match strict chordal digraphs, a class studied by Hell and Hernández-Cruz, so old results translate over. For signed bigraphs the forbidden list looks similar, but the proofs are far harder and more intricate. The work completes the chordal picture for signed structures.
arxiv-2512-14986:
Carlo Bellingeri and a coauthor define a new integral for random processes that are rougher than Brownian motion. The Wick integral is built for processes with bounded p-variation for p below 2, which need not be Gaussian. The integrand can be a class of entire functions tied to the process itself.

For fractional Brownian motion with Hurst index above one half, the new integral agrees with the divergence operator of Malliavin calculus. It obeys a correction formula against the Young integral and an Itô formula, both with endless correction terms. Those terms come from integrating against the cumulant functions of the process, and they shrink to the familiar identities in the Gaussian case. The proofs grow from diagram formulas for Appell polynomials. The theory covers processes in the second Wiener chaos, such as the Rosenblatt process.
arxiv-2512-15086:
Hongjin Mi and three coauthors strengthen a neural method that learns to solve whole families of partial differential equations. Operator learning predicts full solution fields for new inputs fast, but models like DeepONet can demand huge datasets and wobble in their inner features. The authors borrow an old stabilizer: partition of unity, which blends local pieces into a whole.

Their network, PIP2 Net, adds a simplified physics informed partition penalty that keeps the trunk outputs of DeepONet coordinated and expressive. The penalty grows from a fresh take on an earlier partition based framework. They test it on three nonlinear equations: the viscous Burgers equation, the Allen-Cahn equation, and a diffusion reaction system. In each case PIP2 Net beat DeepONet and its physics informed and partition based variants in accuracy and robustness.
arxiv-2512-15486:
Mohammed Lalou and co authors study completely independent spanning trees in split graphs in a 2025 paper. Such trees share no edges and no internal vertices, so they give disjoint backup routes through a network. Split graphs, whose vertices divide into a clique and an independent set, are the setting here.

The authors link the existence of these trees to coloring problems on a related hypergraph, which yields bounds on how many such trees a split graph can hold. They prove that deciding whether two such trees exist is NP complete. The paper ends with a conjecture about the bipanchromatic number of the linked hypergraph.
arxiv-2512-15586:
Benjamin Minixhofer and co authors introduce Bolmo, a family of byte level language models, in a 2025 paper. Most language models read text as word fragments, which hides fine detail that matters in code or biological sequences. Models that read raw bytes avoid that loss but have lagged in performance until now.

Bolmo starts from existing subword models and converts them in two stages, with little extra training. The resulting fully open models beat prior byte level systems and shine on character level reasoning tasks, while staying competitive on standard benchmarks. Inference speeds are practical, and the low conversion cost lets others reuse the ecosystem around the source models.
arxiv-2512-16086:
Saeed Mahloujifar and three co-authors audit a common privacy trick in their arXiv paper from 2025. Photos shared for research often show faces and license plates, which must be hidden before release. The industry standard is Gaussian blur, but the team shows practical blur settings can be reversed enough to expose private details.

They compare four ways to hide image content: blur, pixelization, pixelization plus noise, and cropping. Privacy was tested with reversal and discrimination attacks, while usefulness was tested by training vision models on the cleaned data. Blur proved the least private of the four. Pixelization, with or without added noise, gave both privacy and utility at the right grain size. The authors released their methods and suggested settings in a software package called Privacy Blur.
arxiv-2512-16286:
Cassandre Lebot reviews a limit in fluid theory in their arXiv paper, posted in 2025. When flow speeds are far below the speed of sound, the Mach number is tiny, and compressible flow equations should simplify to nearly incompressible ones. Taking that low-Mach limit cleanly is a classic mathematical problem.

Lebot first surveys what is known for single-phase flows governed by the compressible Navier-Stokes or Euler equations. The focus then shifts to two-phase flows, mixtures like gas bubbles in liquid. Several model families are compared: pressure given by an algebraic rule or by its own equation, one shared velocity or two separate ones, and versions with or without entropy. The paper is a formal map of which limits have been justified and how the choices interact.
arxiv-2512-16586:
Shaohua Wu and three co-authors upgrade text-to-image generation in a 2025 paper on arXiv. Diffusion models build images inside a U-shaped network whose convolutional blocks see only local neighborhoods, which can blind them to long-range meaning in a scene. The team swaps those blocks for Swin transformer blocks in both encoder and decoder.

Text conditioning gets equal care, through a well-chosen text encoder and a careful way of feeding text embeddings into the network. An adapted time step search across diffusion stages improved inference performance by a further 10 percent. The model reached an FID score of 1.37 on the ImageNet generation benchmark, state of the art at the time, with no auxiliary models at any denoising stage. In side-by-side tests, people struggled to tell its images from human-painted ones.
arxiv-2512-16686:
Xinqun Mei, Guofang Wang, and Liangjun Weng study a prescribed curvature problem for convex capillary surfaces, which meet a flat wall at a set angle. They ask which such surfaces have a given Lp curvature, a blended measure of how the surface bends.

Using the support function, the task becomes a Hessian quotient equation on a spherical cap with a Robin edge rule. For p of one or more, they prove solutions exist under fit conditions on the data, with uniqueness in matching ranges. At the borderline exponent an eigenvalue problem appears, unique up to scaling. The results also cover capillary Christoffel-Minkowski and quotient curvature tasks in one frame.
arxiv-2512-17086:
Cole Wyeth and Marcus Hutter extend the AIXI agent, a flagship design in universal artificial intelligence, to a wider class of utility functions. A snag appears with hypotheses that predict only a finite history prefix, often read as a chance of death, the semimeasure loss.

The pair argue the same math reads as naturally as total ignorance, in the sense of imprecise probability. That view leads them to compute expected utilities with Choquet integrals and to chart the computability level of the result. The standard recursive value function returns as a special case. Yet their broadest utilities under the death reading cannot be written as such Choquet integrals, a split worth noting.
arxiv-2512-17486:
Luka Matijević and a large team weigh two forces tugging at the spiral galaxy NGC 2276. As the galaxy plows through thin group gas, ram pressure can strip and squeeze its own gas, like wind on a moving car. At the same time, gravity from neighbors can pull it out of shape by tides. Which force sculpts this galaxy's lopsided look was unsettled.

The team presents the first Hubble images of the galaxy and pairs them with hydrogen glow maps and infrared views. Young stars, up to about 100 million years old, crowd the leading edge and smear out behind it, the signature of gas being compressed by a headwind. Spiral arms also unwind with radius in a matching way. Ram pressure leads, though tides may still play a part.
arxiv-2512-17586:
Mahesh Keswani and Raunak Bhattacharyya test whether a safety method built for controlled settings survives contact with real driving data. The method, called SRPL, gives a learning agent a model that predicts future safety violations, so the agent can weigh reward against risk before it acts.

On the Waymo Open Motion Dataset and on NuPlan, SRPL improved the balance between reward and safety, with large gains in success rate and lower costs, both statistically significant. The benefit depends on the optimizer beneath it and on the data mix, and the method also held up better when sensor input grew noisy. Agents trained with it transferred to a fresh dataset without retraining better than agents without it, a sign the approach may carry toward real roads.
arxiv-2512-17686:
David Luce and three co-authors film the inside of a draining grain silo and find a wave running the show. As grains pour out, the bulk does not slide smoothly: a pulse of slowing starts near the outlet, beside the stagnant dead zone, and climbs toward the top of the pile. Acceleration maps of the flow make the pulse train plain to see.

Two traits surprised the team. The pulses come slower when the grains are stickier, a cohesion effect no simple model predicted. Yet widening or narrowing the outlet changed the pulse rate not at all. Engineers who design hoppers for grain, sand, and powders care, because such waves set the rhythm of discharge and the risk of jamming.
arxiv-2512-17886:
Laksha Pradip Das and four coauthors revisit particles that rain down when cosmic rays smash into the upper air. The IceCube detector, buried in Antarctic ice, sees more high energy muons than older models predict. Part of the excess may come from charm particles born inside the incoming cosmic ray itself.

Adding that charm source raises the predicted muon flow, but it also raises the flow of related neutrinos above a limit IceCube has set. The team tests several charm models and tweaks the share from plain mesons to ease the clash. The mismatch tells builders of air shower models where their physics still needs work.
arxiv-2512-18086:
J. López-Santiago leads a six author team reporting a steady beat in the light of GJ 3512, a small red dwarf star. The TESS space telescope caught a wobble with a period of 70 to 100 minutes. The signal lasted for weeks in one run and showed up again across three years of data, with no fade between big flares.

That long life rules out the usual flare echoes, which die in minutes or hours, and the star is too old for the known pulsing class. The team favors a corona based cause, such as repeated magnetic snapping in large active regions. No late type star has shown a sustained beat like this before.
arxiv-2512-18486:
Rajavardhan Talashila proves a uniqueness theorem for time-harmonic fields, the steady oscillating fields of electromagnetism. His paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, asks what boundary data pin down the field inside a spherical volume. The volume holds only perfect conductors and uniform lossless materials. The driving currents are given.

He shows the solution is fixed uniquely by two sets of data. The first is the radial parts of both fields, E and B, on the outer spherical surface. The second is the tangential part of either field on inner surfaces. The proof leans on the uniqueness of the multipole expansion outside the sphere. The result also frames the classic lossless theorem as a limiting case, as dissipation in lossy materials shrinks to zero.
arxiv-2512-18886:
Rhea Fernandez and six co-authors organize the young field of quantum education for school students. Quantum ideas are entering classrooms, but teachers face a scatter of approaches with no map. Drawing on a literature review and expert interviews, their framework, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and presented at a symposium on teaching Einsteinian physics, sorts the methods into seven categories.

The seven are Defamiliarization, Quantum Picturalism, the Spin-First and Einstein-First approaches, the Many Paths approach, the Historical Development approach, and Game-based Quantum Learning. For each, the authors summarize how it works and weigh strengths and weaknesses, stressing which concepts stay mathematically accessible to primary and secondary students. The result is a practical menu: an educator can pick a route that fits their class instead of improvising one.
arxiv-2512-19086:
Byung Gyu Chae models networks that feed their own output back in as input, a loop found in biological brains. His network is kept in balance by homeostasis, an internal control that resists drift. The goal is a clean theory of when such a system settles, reacts, or keeps reflecting on its own state.

The population dynamics collapse exactly to a one-dimensional radial flow, which reveals a fixed threshold for sustained reflective activity. A renormalization-group analysis then tracks how gain, stiffness, and reentry strength flow. All paths are drawn to a critical surface where leak and reentry balance. Three regimes appear, with a universal onset pattern.
arxiv-2512-19286:
Sameera M., Serena Nicolazzo, Antonino Nocera, and Vinod P. defend federated learning against poisoned updates. In federated learning, many clients train a shared model without sharing raw data. A malicious client can slip in crafted updates that drag the model down or bend it toward chosen errors.

Their shield, GShield, first learns what honest gradients look like, using clustering and Gaussian models in an opening round. Later updates are kept only if they fit that trusted pattern, which sidelines attackers and junk updates alike. The design targets the hard case where client data differ widely. A broad test campaign backs the defense, the authors report.
arxiv-2512-19586:
Diego Marques and Pavel Trojovsky mix geometric progressions with the Zeckendorf writing system, where every integer is a sum of non-consecutive Fibonacci numbers. The work is prompted by an Erdős conjecture about ternary expansions and by recent results on progressions meeting Cantor-like sets in ordinary bases. Forbidden digit patterns are the heart of the question.

Fix any finite set of forbidden binary patterns and any window onto the last digits. The authors prove the exponents for which a progression term's Zeckendorf expansion avoids those patterns in the window form a set that is either finite or eventually periodic. Wild avoidance, in other words, cannot continue in a chaotic way.
arxiv-2512-19686:
Zixuan Ye and seven co-authors fix a blind spot in AI image tools that think before they draw. Chain-of-thought prompting made such tools follow text prompts better. But the thinking mostly checks words against words. When a guide image is in play, the results often lose key traits. A face changes, an object shifts, or the style drifts.

Their method adds two habits. First, the model writes a checklist of visual traits that must stay fixed. Then it checks its own output against the list and refines it, round by round. Training teaches the routine, and a reward based on the visual check sharpens it. Tests show stronger visual consistency than plain models. They also beat models that reason with text alone.
arxiv-2512-19886:
Fawad Kirmani and six co-authors teach a neural network to spot a rare sight. The sight is a supernova split into two images by gravitational lensing. Such events fade fast. They are most often found because lensing makes them look too bright. This proof of concept reads the bent shape of the doubled image instead. It works from a single difference image. The split it hunts is under six tenths of an arcsecond.

Real cases are too rare to train on. So Hubble archive images fed made-up training and test sets. Priors from astrophysics set the splits, brightness ratios, and colors. Fake traps, like artifacts and plain supernovae, were added too. The network recalled 99 percent of the fake lensed events. It also split plain and empty images with care. The method aims at wide-field space surveys like the Roman Space Telescope.
arxiv-2512-20586:
Humza Nusrat and a clinical team test whether reasoning makes an AI planner safer for brain radiosurgery. Stereotactic radiosurgery sculpts dose tightly around metastases while sparing structures like the cochlea. Black-box automation has stalled clinically because planners cannot audit it. Their agent, SAGE, plans with a language model in the loop.

Forty-one patients with brain metastases, each treated with a single eighteen-gray fraction, were replanned by reasoning and non-reasoning variants. The reasoning planner matched human dosimetry on coverage, maximum dose, and conformity, while lowering cochlear dose below human benchmarks. Its traces show hundreds of prospective constraint checks and trade-off deliberations, behaviours absent in the standard model. Auditable reasoning, the authors argue, is the road to clinical trust.
arxiv-2512-20686:
Michael A Jones, Brittany Ohlinger, and Jennifer Wilson watch legislatures fill seat by seat. Divisor methods apportion seats by rounding scaled vote shares; because they satisfy house monotonicity, seats can be handed out sequentially as parties earn them. The authors focus on stationary divisor methods, defined by one rounding cutpoint.

With integer votes, the resulting apportionment sequences are periodic. For two parties, the authors characterize exactly which sequences can occur and tie their lexicographic ordering to the cutpoint's value. Pairwise sequences then extend systematically to any number of parties, and the count of distinct sequences is determined. A reframing of size bias emerges: large parties do not simply get more seats, they get their seats earlier. The Adams and D'Hondt extremes turn out to be intimately related.
arxiv-2512-20786:
F. Yusef-Zadeh and seven co-authors watched the black hole at our galaxy's center flare in three kinds of light at once. On 5 April 2024, the JWST, NuSTAR, and VLA telescopes monitored Sagittarius A* together. Its brightness changes reveal processes in the disk of gas swirling under strong gravity.

A strong X-ray flare arrived alongside a bright near-infrared flare, with radio brightening about an hour later. The team argue the X-rays came from infrared light scattered to higher energies. They propose an ejection much like a solar coronal mass ejection, with a magnetic rope and reconnecting sheet. One picture then explains the flaring across all three bands.
arxiv-2512-21186:
Tieguang Zi and Chang-Qing Ye forecast whether the future LISA observatory could detect a scalar charge on a small body spiraling into a massive black hole. A scalar charge is an extra field charge that some extensions of gravity predict. Real inspirals are messy: the small body plows through an accretion disk and a dark matter halo, not empty space. Both the environment and any scalar charge distort its gravitational waveform. The authors fold the charge into the energy fluxes and orbital evolution and compute its signal.

Under suitable parameters, the scalar-charge imprint stays distinguishable from the vacuum prediction amid the environmental effects. LISA could then pin the charge down with a relative error near ten percent. That forecast matters because a measured nonzero charge would falsify general relativity, while a tight null bound would discipline its rivals; the study shows astrophysics need not blind the test.
arxiv-2512-22286:
Ernest Fokoué develops a general theory of how ensemble weights should be chosen, arguing the usual story is incomplete. Textbooks credit groups with reducing variance, but that cannot explain why groups of already-stable methods, like smoothing splines or Gaussian process regression, still help. Fokoué formalizes groups as linear operators on a hypothesis space and puts geometric and spectral constraints on the weight sequences themselves.

A refined bias-variance decomposition shows structured, non-uniform weights can beat uniform averaging by reshaping approximation geometry and redistributing spectral complexity, even when variance barely moves. Optimal weights emerge as solutions of constrained quadratic programs. Plain averaging, stacking, and the author's Fibonacci ensembles all appear as special cases of the unified theory.
arxiv-2512-22686:
Kumar Sai Bondada, Daniel J. Jakubisin, and R. Michael Buehrer design a multistatic radar that syncs itself wirelessly instead of relying on GPS. Separate senders and receivers must share precise time and frequency references to locate targets jointly. Their protocol exchanges a two-tone waveform for frequency synchronization and a two-way exchange for time sync, keeping the network self-contained.

A Bayesian Cramér-Rao lower bound system gauges how leftover sync offsets degrade delay and Doppler estimates, and with them target position and velocity accuracy. Simulations from the analytical formulas show how much damage residual offsets do. With the sync-link parameters tuned, the multistatic layout can beat a single-unit radar and approach the ideal perfectly synced case. The required link parameters look feasible in practice.
arxiv-2512-22986:
Siyi Wang, Zifan Wang, and Karl Johansson study learning algorithms that must stay risk-averse while the world, and the right level of caution, keeps changing. Their setting is online optimization in a shifting environment, where risk is measured by Conditional Value-at-Risk, a statistic that focuses on the worst outcomes rather than the average. Two kinds of drift matter: the objective functions change, and the risk level itself moves.

The authors measure the first drift with a function variation metric and introduce a new metric for risk-level variation. They design algorithms for two information settings, one where gradients are observable and one where only function values are sampled, both under a limited sampling budget. Dynamic regret bounds are proved in terms of the two variation measures and the sample count, showing the methods adapt to non-stationary, risk-sensitive problems. Numerical experiments confirm the theory's predictions.
arxiv-2512-23086:
Teng Liu and a large team introduce eigen microstate entropy, a complexity measure meant to flag phase transitions before they fully arrive. The measure is built from the probabilities of statistically independent eigen microstates extracted from data. Its scaling behavior is first established in equilibrium systems and tested on classic critical models, the mean spherical, Ising, and Potts models, where transitions are well understood.

The payoff comes in nonequilibrium settings. Across very different systems, the entropy rose significantly ahead of the main transition, acting as a precursor rather than a symptom. It climbed before biomolecular condensates formed by liquid-liquid phase separation inside living cells. It also rose months ahead of El Niño events in climate data. The authors position the measure as a general framework for detecting and interpreting phase transitions in complex systems that never reach equilibrium, where traditional order parameters are hard to define.
arxiv-2512-23386:
Sunghun Ko and Jinsuk Park study bidding in Arbitrum's Express Lane Auction, a mechanism that sells speed on a blockchain network. The winner of each ahead-of-time, second-price auction gets a latency advantage lasting one minute, an edge for time-sensitive transactions. Building on a single-round model with risk-averse bidders, the authors hypothesize that priority access is worth less than a risk-neutral calculation suggests. Short-horizon volatility is hard to forecast, and bidders dislike that uncertainty.

They test the hypothesis by matching Express Lane bid records against high-frequency prices of Ether, the network's currency. The evidence lines up with the model: bids behave as if the value of priority is discounted for volatility risk. The study connects auction theory to a blockchain market. It shows how a one-minute advantage gets priced when the asset can jump before the advantage is used.
arxiv-2512-23586:
Marcin Markiewicz, Łukasz Pawela, and Zbigniew Puchała study twirling, the averaging of a quantum channel over a symmetry group until only its symmetry-respecting part remains. Twirling is a standard simplification tool, but doing it for channels rather than states is technically awkward. The arXiv record's title replaces the catalog's different working title, and the record governs here.

Working through the Choi representation, which turns a channel into a state, they give a constructive description of the averaging map for arbitrary input and output symmetries. A partial-transpose trick converts the hard mixed twirl into an ordinary Schur-Weyl twirl, yielding explicit formulas built from permutations. They also extend twirling beyond compact groups to reductive non-unitary ones, and give two finite constructions that realize channel averaging with designs.
arxiv-2512-23686:
Deepak Babu Piskala releases ProfASR-Bench, a benchmark for speech recognition in professional settings where mistakes carry real costs. In finance, medicine, law, and technology, speech is dense with specialized terms and formal registers, and an error on a critical name or number is far worse than an average word error. Existing benchmarks underplay those pressures. The arXiv record's title and framing govern over the catalog entry.

Each test item pairs a natural-language context prompt, a domain cue or speaker profile, with an entity-rich utterance to transcribe. Scoring covers ordinary word error plus entity-aware measures, reported by accent and gender slices. Testing Whisper and Qwen-Omni families under several context conditions, Piskala finds a context-utilization gap: even perfect oracle context barely improves recognition, meaning today's promptable systems underuse side information they are given.
arxiv-2512-23786:
Ankan Aich and five co-authors improve depth estimation for surgical cameras, a capability autonomous robotic surgery depends on. A single camera must infer three-dimensional shape, but models trained outside the body fail inside it: real operations bring mirror-like reflections off wet tissue and constant deformation. Training on noisy labels from real surgery causes boundaries to collapse. The arXiv record's title governs over the catalog's shorter one.

The team instead adapts the strong synthetic priors of a foundation depth model, Depth Anything V2, using a low-rank adaptation scheme with dynamic vectors. On the public SCARED benchmark they report a new state of the art, with squared relative error cut by over seventeen percent in the most reflective conditions. They also introduce ROCAL-T 90, the first validation set from real operations, with ninety endoscopic sequences and sub-millimeter ground-truth trajectories from CT alignment.
arxiv-2512-23886:
Sylwia Antoniuk, Andrzej Dudek, and Andrzej Ruciński ask how much randomness completes a dense graph's structure. Their graphs satisfy the Pósa-Seymour condition, a minimum-degree requirement slightly above a threshold fraction of the vertices. The target is a power of a Hamiltonian cycle: a cycle through all vertices. It is strengthened so each vertex also connects to its near neighbors along the cycle, up to a chosen power m.

Adding random edges one by one eventually forces such a power to appear, and the paper finds how many are needed. Two threshold types govern the answer, with the so-called over-threshold dominating once m grows. For each fixed degree parameter and all large enough m, the authors prove tight bounds, in the limit, on these over-thresholds, show the bounds coincide for infinitely many m. They also determine exact thresholds for several small parameter pairs.
arxiv-2512-24186:
Felix Zahner and five colleagues report a first sighting. Topological spin textures appear inside an intrinsic antiferromagnet. The setting is a single atomic layer. Skyrmions are whirl-like spin patterns prized for spintronics. Antiferromagnetic versions should move better in devices. Until now they were seen only in synthetic stacks.

The team used spin-polarized scanning tunneling microscopy. Manganese layers sat on a tantalum surface. The monolayer showed a spiraling antiferromagnetic pattern. The double layer showed a straight, collinear state instead. Half-skyrmions formed at the boundary between the two. Calculations and simulations backed the reading. The layout of the structure thus switches the film's state. Plain states and topological ones are both reachable. That control matters for future devices.
arxiv-2512-24386:
Gur-Eyal Sela and four colleagues cut the cost of live video analytics. Camera fleets run vision models around the clock. Inference with modern models is expensive. Choosing model size dynamically per segment could cut cost tenfold. The catch is judging accuracy without ground truth at runtime. Existing systems sample a few models, read their confidence statistics, then pick a size.

Prior systems generalize poorly to new workloads. Mobile videos and lower accuracy targets expose the failure. Sampling often costs more than it saves. Per-segment accuracy prediction is also unreliable. RedunCut answers with a measurement-driven planner. It weighs the cost and benefit of sampling before doing it. A light, data-driven model improves accuracy prediction. Across vehicle, drone, and surveillance videos, compute fell by wide margins at fixed accuracy. Robustness held under scarce history and drifting content.
arxiv-2512-24586:
Xian-Peng Zhang, Xiangrong Wang, and Yugui Yao build a small-scale theory of magnetoresistance, how the resistance of a magnetic material changes in a magnetic field. They treat free electrons and local magnetic moments as one open quantum system. Their method solves the governing formula with a projection method that tracks loss of spin order over time.
