Both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic cases emerge from heat and field dependent spin decoherence, meaning the fading and dephasing of spins. Resistance linked to decoherence follows the magnetic order of the material. Readers get guidance for learning about and designing magnetic materials where this effect matters.
arxiv-2512-24886:
Tyler Hanks, Cristian Nino, and Joana Bou Barcelo track multiple unknown targets with a varied team of agents using cellular sheaves. Sheaves generalize graph theory and allow other state spaces on other nodes. Nonlinear motion and mismatched dimensions defeat standard graph Laplacian methods. Their work extends sheaf teamwork methods from cooperative consensus to non-cooperative target tracking.

Tracking is cast as a harmonic extension problem over the sheaf, letting varied agents share information in matching forms. Robotics and estimation readers get mathematics built for mixed teams. Sheaves let a camera, a drone, and a ground sensor cooperate without forcing a common state format.
arxiv-2601-06686:
Darius Jakobeit and Oliver Wallscheid teach one brain-like net to run many power boxes in 2026. Control of such boxes is now tuned box by box, they point out. That blocks reuse when the shape of the box changes from job to job.

Their plan does not care what shape the box has, by design. The box's wire list is writ as a graph of two node kinds. A graph net reads that graph, shaped by the task at hand. Small heads spread through the box then act on what the net finds. One frame could run a whole line of box shapes with no fresh tuning. They show this as an early proof that the thought can work. If it holds, design time drops for whole fleets of such boxes.
arxiv-2601-07086:
Osama Yousuf and four co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a tool called XBTorch. XBTorch helps teams model chips that learn in a crossbar layout. In such a layout, rows and cols of tiny parts store weights and do math in place. The tool lets teams design the chip and the model as one task.

New kinds of memory parts have drawn much note in the past few years. They can do math right where the data sits. The parts are built at a tiny scale and hold their state when power is off. Their conductance can be tuned in fine steps. Chips of this kind can cut energy use by a wide margin. They can also cut wait time, when set next to classic von Neumann designs. XBTorch gives teams a way to test such chips before they build them.
arxiv-2601-07586:
Jerome Droniou and colleagues design a numerical scheme for contact problems with friction on fractures. Their 2026 preprint uses a higher order polytopal method, which works on meshes with general polygon or polyhedron cells. The mechanics problem involves fractures along which Tresca friction acts. Contact conditions must hold where surfaces press together.

The approach rests on a mixed formulation with two fields. One is the displacement field; the other is a Lagrange multiplier that represents traction at the fractures. The scheme belongs to the Discrete de Rham family. Higher order accuracy on rough meshes matters for rock mechanics and reservoir modeling, where fractures shape the response. The authors both design and analyze the method. Numerical analysts and geomechanics scholars are the readers.
arxiv-2601-07686:
C E Lopetegui-González and coauthors build one shared route to Bell tests from contextuality with smooth, unbroken values. Bell tests check whether nature allows the local realism Einstein favored. The original EPR paradox used position and momentum, which are continuous. Most later studies, though, used tests with only a few split outcomes. Their 2026 preprint returns to the continuous case.

The scheme does not hinge on system size, the authors state. It can probe pure smooth cases, pure split cases, or mixed nonlocality in one language. That unity helps compare experiments across very different physical platforms. Contextuality is the broader idea that measurement results can depend on what else is measured alongside. The paper serves quantum foundations scholars who want one framework for many setups. The team writes for those who test the deep rules of the small scale world.
arxiv-2601-07786:
Abdullah Al Mujahid and Mia Mohammad Imran study the technical debt that developers admit AI tools created. Their 2026 preprint examines code comments where programmers flag problems left by generative AI. Tools like ChatGPT, Copilot, Claude, and Gemini now sit inside daily development work. Some comments name both the AI involvement and the shortcoming it left behind. The paper's title quotes one such comment: TODO, fix the mess Gemini created.

Self-admitted technical debt is a known research topic; AI-induced debt is its new branch. Cataloging these comments shows where AI assistance creates cleanup work. That evidence can guide tool design and team practice. It also gives managers a realistic view of AI coding gains. The study is empirical, based on real open-source traces. Software engineering scholars and development leads are the readers.
arxiv-2601-07886:
Abhishek Yadav, Uaday Singh, and Feng Dai extend a neural network approximation method to several variables. Max-min neural network operators approximate functions using maximum and minimum operations inside the network. Recent advances built such operators for one variable. Their 2026 preprint proposes and analyzes multivariate versions. The operators are activated by sigmoidal functions, the smooth S-shaped curves common in neural networks.

Multivariate approximation is the real-world case: most functions depend on many inputs. A method proven only for one variable has limited use. The authors develop the framework and its analysis together. Approximation theory supplies guarantees about how fast these operators converge. Such guarantees help engineers choose methods with known error behavior. The paper serves scholars in approximation theory and neural network mathematics. It carries a newer operator family into higher dimensions.
arxiv-2601-07986:
Haorui Yu and colleagues release Vulca-Bench, a benchmark for cultural understanding in vision-language models. Existing benchmarks mostly measure basic skills: object recognition, scene description, and factual questions. Higher-order cultural interpretation is under-evaluated. Vulca-Bench holds 7,410 matched image and critique pairs. They span eight cultural traditions, with Chinese and English bilingual coverage. Their 2026 preprint introduces the resource.

Matched critiques let evaluators check whether a model reads an artwork's cultural meaning, not just its content. Bilingual coverage tests whether understanding survives language change. Eight traditions guard against benchmarks that quietly center one culture. The resource gives model builders a fair test they can rerun. The paper serves the multimodal AI community. It extends a companion line of work on cross-cultural art critique into a full benchmark.
arxiv-2601-08486: Chengqian Zhang and seven co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on models of atoms and how they fare on new ground. A structure-property model must work past its training range, for new molecules and materials. Pre-trained models score well on their home range after fine-tuning. How they fare off that range was less clear. The authors find a flaw in the plain way of fine-tuning. It makes the model's inner forms collapse, and wipes the chemical priors it learned. Multi-task fine-tuning is their fix.
arxiv-2601-08586:
Tao Zhou studies superconductivity in strain-engineered graphene with a self-consistent Bogoliubov-de Gennes approach. His 2026 arXiv paper challenges a common expectation about flat bands. High density of states in flat bands is often assumed to enhance pairing universally.

Zhou identifies a kinetic blockade instead. Strain-induced sublattice polarization segregates electronic states and renders the singularities inert. Superconductivity then emerges as robust filaments at geometric nodes, forming a pair density wave. The picture redirects the search for strong pairing in graphene devices. Strain patterns, not just flatness, may decide where superconductivity lives. Where strain acts thus shapes where pairing can survive at all.
arxiv-2601-08686: Matthias Carosi wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on ways to compute a value called a functional determinant. Such values sit at the core of field theory sums that rest on a saddle-point expansion. Many ways to find them skip the need to know the full spectrum of the operator. Two named ways are the Gel'fand-Yaglom theorem and the Green's function method. Carosi sets out how these ways match, as equal routes to one value. That helps users cross-check results and pick the cheapest route.
arxiv-2601-08786:
Guido Lagos, Jorge Navarro, and Hector Olivero study fix plans for systems that can fail in groups. A system here is a set of parts where the whole works or fails based on its parts. In real life, parts can fail at the same time, as in a storm or a power surge. Fixing a part should never make a sound system fail.

The team looks at plain fix rules for such systems. They split a system into parts that can be read on their own. That split makes it clear which fix rule is cheap and safe. A reader who keeps key kit gets math for a hard case. Group fails are the norm in the field, not a rare edge case.
arxiv-2601-09286:
Hanze Guo, Jianxun Lian, and Xiao Zhou ask why pick tools fail on items few folk have tried. Pick tools learn a dense code for each item from past picks. For a rare item, that code is built from few marks. The team shows a hard cap on how much true sign such a code can hold. Past that cap, more marks add noise, not sign.

They give a dual view fix. A sparse view, based on plain counts, can serve rare items well. A dense view serves rich items. Join both, and each item gets the view that fits its marks. A reader in pick tools gets a cause for a known flaw, and a split fix.
arxiv-2601-09486:
Ismail Huseynov, Arzu Ahmadova, and Agamirza E. Bashirov ask how fully an operator can steer a heat exchanger. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies two semilinear systems, one for a single-tube exchanger and one for a two-stream design. Neither system can be driven to every possible state.

For each system, the authors single out a subspace of states that can be reached exactly. That property is called partial exact controllability. Knowing the reachable subspace tells plant designers which temperature profiles they can truly command. The rest must be left to the physics of the device.
arxiv-2601-09586:
Said Yasin and Torsten Zesch want handwriting learners to see their mistakes, not just read about them. Their 2026 arXiv paper tackles visual error feedback on handwritten documents. Handwriting is still a core skill in school, yet feedback tools for it are little studied.

Going from a photo of handwriting to correctly placed, helpful marks is hard. The authors compare modular pipelines with end-to-end systems. They find that neither approach yet reaches acceptable overall quality. The honest verdict maps what must improve before such feedback can truly help in real classrooms.
arxiv-2601-09686:
Ha Nguyen and Sumanta Basu improve a standard method for learning networks from data. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents LARGE, a locally adaptive regularization approach for Gaussian graphical models. Such models encode which variables depend directly on which others.

The graphical Lasso is the usual tool: it estimates the precision matrix by maximizing likelihood with an L1 penalty. One global penalty treats all edges alike, which can misfit varied data. LARGE adapts the penalty locally instead. Adaptive penalties should recover truer networks in finance, biology, and other fields where dependence maps are the goal.
arxiv-2601-09886:
Sathvik Nair and Byung-Doh Oh ask why model surprise predicts reading effort better than human guesses. Their 2026 arXiv paper compares language model surprisal with cloze surprisal. Word predictability can be measured two ways: by asking people to fill blanks, or by reading a model's probabilities.

Both scores can predict how hard a word is to process. Language model scores win in practice. The authors dig into why the machine measure beats the human one. The answer matters for psycholinguistics, where surprisal is a main link between language statistics and the reading brain.
arxiv-2601-09986:
Cheng Zhang and co authors speed up checks for a class of programs. The programs are GKAT automata. They mix tests, loops, and acts. A check asks if two such programs act the same on all traces.

Checks of this kind can be slow. The team gives fast checks that work on the fly. They use SAT tools to search for a gap. To show use, they built a tool for code flow checks. It tests if a change to code flow keeps the acts the same. Fast checks of this sort help keep code changes safe.
arxiv-2601-10286:
E. A. Kokin sorts the twist groups of a class of contact shapes. Such shapes have a frame that twists as one moves. The twist group is named the holonomy group. It tells how a vector turns on a loop trip. Kokin's shapes have a metric of mixed sign.

Mixed sign breaks the plain tools. Past proofs split space by sign, which can fail here. Kokin adapts the proof to dodge that flaw. He shows the flat twist group is the full group, or sits in it one step down. The work fills a gap for these shapes.
arxiv-2601-10686:
Daniel Barake, Owen Chuchman, Cameron Franc, Geoffrey Mason, and Brett Nasserden connect vertex operator algebras to modular curves. A vertex operator algebra encodes the symmetries of a two-dimensional field theory. Each one can be tied to a vector bundle over the elliptic modular curve. The authors describe that bundle in detail.

They treat quasi-vertex operator algebras as well, a broader class. The stated aim looks ahead: using this bundle picture to study the characters of these algebras. Characters are the key functions that count states by weight. A firm geometric base could pay off across math physics, where these algebras link number theory, geometry, and string theory.
arxiv-2601-11086:
Chenlu Liu and co-authors convert qubit relaxation into erasure errors with a single fluxonium qubit. Qubits whose main error is erasure, a loss at a known place, are easier to correct than qubits with hidden errors. Dual-rail designs in cavities and transmons already make this trade, but they cost extra hardware and circuit complexity.

A single fluxonium could make the same trade leaner. Fluxonium is a superconducting qubit known for long coherence. If its relaxation can be recast as erasures, error correction gets a cheaper input. The work matters for fault-tolerant designs, where the type of error can matter as much as its rate.
arxiv-2601-11186:
Donato Bini and Giorgio Di Russo work on gravity in the strong-field regime. Their 2026 preprint studies a particle that falls straight into a black hole. The hole is of the Schwarzschild kind, with no spin or charge. The particle starts at rest and falls in along a radius.

The team counts the energy shed as waves to first self-force order. Self-force is the push a body feels from its own field. They treat two cases side by side for the fall. One is a scalar particle that sheds scalar waves. The other is a mass that sheds waves of gravity. Post-Newtonian checks back the results at weak field strength.
arxiv-2601-11486:
M. Idris and J.-M. Sac-Epee study which polynomials divide Newman polynomials. Their 2026 preprint gives algorithmic results on that question. Newman polynomials have coefficients of just zero and one. Their roots and measures link to deep number theory.

The team first treats the 8438 known cases of low measure. Those have Mahler measure less than 1.3 in the count. Mahler measure sizes a polynomial by its roots' growth. They then list polynomials that divide no Newman polynomial. A degree-10 case of small measure is singled out in the list. Such lists bound where small-measure polynomials can arise. The work aids the hunt for Lehmer-type minimal cases.
arxiv-2601-11586:
Shan Zhang and four coauthors trace how students replay problems in games. Their 2026 preprint studies latent problem-solving pathways in learners. Game-based learning logs each move a student makes. Pathways through problems reflect understanding and procedural skill.

Flexibility in approach also shows in those pathways. Replay behavior is the paper's special focus. Replaying may signal productive struggle or broad exploration. Both can foster deeper learning when they pay off. Little is known about how pathways unfold across problems. Timing of replays and strategies is also unclear. The team links those patterns to near and far learning outcomes.
arxiv-2601-11986:
Mingjie Feng, Yiming Li, and Hua-Sheng Shao weigh the odds of finding a new tetraquark state at LHCb. Tetraquarks are parts made of four quarks. The state they study holds both a bottom and a charm quark, with spin-parity 0+.

They model proton-proton crashes at 13 TeV at LHCb. They focus on states that decay strongly, so they are short lived and hard to spot. Rate checks show if a search is worth the effort. The work gives a target for LHCb teams to test.  Such rates set the scale for a search at the LHC.
arxiv-2601-12086:
A. A. Zheltukhin studies a spinning string with no tension. The action he uses is unchanged by reparametrization, local supersymmetry, and scale shifts. He builds the density of the energy-momentum tensor for this string.

He proves that its covariant divergence is zero. That zero comes from a mutual cancel of bosonic and fermionic parts. He also sets out how worldsheets of tensionless strings differ in geometry from normal strings. The work adds to the theory of strings at zero tension.  The string case is a clean test for field maths.
arxiv-2601-12186:
Vatsal Venkatkrishna, Indraneil Paul, and Iryna Gurevych ask what makes code verifiers trained with verifiable rewards work. Such verifiers grade and rerank model outputs in post-training. They are now a fixture for general tasks, but code use has been sparse.

For code, run feedback has been the main signal. The team's study, named in the work, probes which parts of reward-led training drive code verifier skill. That map can guide teams to train verifiers that catch bad code with less waste. It joins reward design to code quality.  Code verifiers could rerank code as they do prose.
arxiv-2601-12286:
Jonathan Pan sorts conversational context with a representation engineering route. As language models spread, guards must catch replies that stray out of context. Strays span topic shifts, false facts, and hallucinated claims.

Classic anomaly tools do not map well to context sense in text. His method works on the model's inner representations in place of surface text. Inner signals may flag a stray before it is full-blown. The work aims for more sound LLM guards.  Inner flags could warn before a bad reply is sent.  Topic drift is one clear stray kind the tool must catch at once.
arxiv-2601-12886:
Christoph Wittner surveys communication methods in multi agent reinforcement learning. This field extends reinforcement learning to systems with many interacting agents. Communication methods have multiplied in recent years to solve hard multi agent problems. Those problems include partial observability, non stationarity, and action spaces that grow exponentially.

When agents can talk, they can share what each one sees alone. Communication further enables efficient cooperation among all agents in an environment. A survey of methods helps researchers pick the right channel design. It also maps which problems each method really solves. The work serves robotics, games, and distributed control research.
arxiv-2601-13186:
Diego Gosmar and Deborah A. Dahl harden language models against prompt tricks in agent chains. A prompt trick hides a bad order in text a model reads. In chains of agents, one bad out put can pass the trick on and grow it. That risk is a top block to safe use.

Past work by the pair set a four part score for how weak a set up is to tricks. The new work grows that score. It adds a cache that reuses past checks by sense match, to cut cost. It adds a fourth agent that judges by fixed rules. It also adds a fifth part score for how clear the chain is to watch. The aim is guards that stay strong while they stay open to view.
arxiv-2601-13486:
Anderson Anrrango and co-authors teach a self led learner to guess power flow answers that stay safe. The task is security constrained DC optimal power flow. It picks cheap power dispatch that still holds if a line fails. Solve in full is slow, so a fast guess has worth.

Their guess is a linear model with tuned parts. The parts shift with demand and scale line caps. That form keeps the true physics shape of the DC task in view. Self led teach needs no solved cases to learn from. For grid teams, a fast and form true guess can run where a full solve cannot keep up.
arxiv-2601-13786:
Mozib Bin Awal and Prabwal Phukon study constant-entropy processes in a class of black holes in 2026. These are Anti de Sitter black holes tied to nonlinear electrodynamics. An isentropic process keeps entropy fixed while the hole changes. The pair ask if such a process can happen at all.

They show the process is classically forbidden for these holes. It can still proceed through quantum mechanical tunnelling, a leak through a barrier. They compute the Euclidean action for that tunnelling path. They also track how it shifts with charge, horizon size, and model parameters.
arxiv-2601-13886:
Shangzhe Di, Zhonghua Zhai, and Weidi Xie argue two schools of vision learning should be joined in 2026. Vision-language models like CLIP excel at global semantic alignment. They link whole images to text well, but lack spatial precision. Self-supervised methods like MAE and DINO capture fine local structure, yet miss high-level context.

The team says the two paradigms are complementary at a deep level. They build a principled multi-task framework to integrate them. Dense spatial supervision adds a further boost. A model strong at both scale levels could serve search, robotics, and medical imaging.
arxiv-2601-14286:
Wentao Jiang, Jingxin Wang, and six co-authors work on chip design in this 2026 paper. Their stage is technology mapping, the step that turns a logic plan into real gates from a cell library. Old mapping tools lean on abstract delay models. Those models do not tie to a real target technology.

That gap leads to wide errors in delay estimates for the built circuit. Real post-mapping circuits show timing traits the abstract models miss. The team built a learning method based on graph neural networks. It is path-aware and uses multi-view circuit learning. The aim is mapping choices grounded in how real circuits time their signals.
arxiv-2601-14586:
Dan Cheng and John Ginos study random fields on a grid in this 2026 paper. A discrete random field assigns a random value to each point of the d-dimensional integer lattice. Fix a threshold u. The excursion set, all points where the value exceeds u, decomposes into connected components, or clusters. Each cluster's size is the number of lattice points it contains, and that size is random.

The paper investigates the probability distribution of these cluster sizes. Cluster size laws matter wherever high spots group together, from brain imaging to materials. Readers get theory for how often big clusters appear by chance in a lattice field.
arxiv-2601-14786:
Wei-Jaw Lee and four co-authors generate music from text in this 2026 paper. Recent advances in text-to-music generation have yielded high-quality results. They often come at the cost of extensive compute and large proprietary internal data. To improve the affordability and openness of training, an open-source generative model backbone is needed. It must be more training- and data-efficient than current options.

The team's answer uses state-space modeling. State-space models process sequences with lean, structured state updates. The title calls the work training-efficient text-to-music generation. The point is who can join in. If the cost drops, more labs and bands can train their own tunes. Readers get a music generator designed so small labs, not just big firms, can afford to train one.
arxiv-2601-15086:
Oleg Shchendrigin, Egor Cherepanov, Alexey K. Kovalev, and Aleksandr I. Panov test what memory really takes for a learning agent. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with reinforcement learning in worlds that change over time. An agent must keep key facts for long spans.

It must also drop stale facts when the world shifts. The authors argue that retention alone is not enough to master memory tasks. Holding data is only half the job. The agent must also update and overwrite its store as conditions change, and the paper probes where agents fail at that.
arxiv-2601-15186:
Macarena Droguett-Callejas, Ezequiel Treister, and a team of co-authors hunt for black holes hidden inside merging galaxies. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with heavily obscured active galactic nuclei. In late-stage mergers, thick gas and dust can block most of the core's light.

That blockage leaves gaps in the census of growing supermassive black holes. The team uses a correlation between millimeter and X-ray light. That link can reveal black holes that other bands miss. The work probes how these hidden giants grow while their host galaxies merge and slowly collide together.
arxiv-2601-15286:
Shantanu Jaiswal, Mihir Prabhudesai, and co-authors fix complex image prompts by revising in rounds. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with text-to-image models. The models have advanced fast, yet they still fail on prompts with many objects, relations, and attributes at once.

Current fixes sample many images and pick a winner, or simply run more denoising steps. Those tricks fall short when many constraints must hold at once. The authors use iterative refinement instead. The image is improved step by step until it fits the full written prompt well at long last.
arxiv-2601-15386:
Misha Yutushui and David F. Mross build theory for a new wave of quantum Hall states. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with even-denominator states, where the Hall plateau sits at a fraction with an even bottom number. Such states are leading candidates for non-Abelian topological order.

The half-filled plateau in gallium arsenide was the first and most studied case. Recent experiments in gallium arsenide and bilayer graphene found more of these states. They sit at fractions such as three quarters and three eighths. The authors develop the theory these next-generation states need.
arxiv-2601-15486:
Javier N. Ramos-Silva and Peter J. Burke link language models to drone control in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their subject is a universal interface for drone command and control. Artificial intelligence could change what drones can do, they argue. The gain grows when real-world information joins the drone's own sensing. Command and control then draw on both at once.

The authors place their work in physical AI, a growing field. In that field, models act in the world, not just on text. A single interface that fits many drones would ease that step. Operators could give orders in plain language. The drone side would translate them into action. The abstract stays brief, so design details rest in the full text.
arxiv-2601-15686:
Xinyu Wang and five co-authors rethink how to update language models over time in a 2026 arXiv paper. Model editing changes a trained model with new facts or rules. It avoids full retraining. In real deployment, edits arrive as long streams, not one-offs. Existing editors face a plasticity-stability dilemma. Hard writes can pile up interference over time. Hard preservation guards only what is explicitly constrained.

Past edits can be overwritten, and unguarded behavior can drift. The authors answer with soft recursive least-squares, per the title. Soft updates spread change more gently than hard writes. The goal is lifelong editing that stays accurate without decay. Anyone running a model that must track a changing world faces this problem.
arxiv-2601-15986:
Matheus V. Scherer, Lea F. Santos, and Alexandre D. Ribeiro study entanglement between a spin and a field in a 2026 arXiv paper. The system is bipartite: one spin interacts with a bosonic field. The starting state is a product of two coherent states. The spin starts in a spin coherent state. The field starts in a canonical coherent state. From there, interaction entangles the two parts.

The authors build a semiclassical framework for that process. Semiclassical tools approximate quantum dynamics with classical-like trajectories. They aim to describe the entanglement dynamics faithfully. Spin-field systems model atoms in cavities and many qubit platforms. Predicting how entanglement grows there guides experiment design. A cheap semiclassical account, if accurate, is a practical gift to theorists.
arxiv-2601-16286:
Varun Chillara and coauthors cache the thought steps of agent systems, not just their end text. Their 2026 preprint deals with agent chains that run in steps. Such chains oft rebuild the same mid steps again and again. Mid steps span tasks like unit fixes or chart frames. New words from the user hide that the mid step is the same.

End text cache then misses the shared step and saves nil. Step cache stores the thought path for reuse on new words. Reuse cuts cost and wait for like tasks in the chain. The work names the flaw and gives a fix frame. It targets agent tools used at wide scale.
arxiv-2601-16386:
Naomi Ota and coauthors share XMM-Newton views of ten far CAMIRA star groups. Their 2026 preprint deals with groups at high red shift. CAMIRA is a way to find groups from deep pic sets. X ray views show the hot gas that fills each group. Gas heat and glow tell of group mass and past acts.

Ten groups give a fair set to weigh at that far range. The team checks gas traits for each group in turn. Far group traits test how groups grew in young space. They also help tune mass guesses from pic finds. The work adds X ray facts to a pic found set.
arxiv-2601-16586:
Benedikt Fesl and Fatih Capar learn a step chain for soft MIMO reads. Their 2026 preprint deals with reads of more than one send path. Such reads are a core hard task in new radio nets. Low cost reads count for small gear like RedCap and IoT sets. Past clean reads cost too much for such small gear.

The team learns a chain that peels paths one by one. Peel steps, called SIC, cut the clash twixt paths in turn. A learned peel can run fast with soft end marks. Soft marks feed the next steps of the radio chain. The work seeks high grade reads on weak gear.
arxiv-2601-16886:
Chi Yu, Hongyu Yuan, and Zhiyi Duan track how students learn, with a graph twist. Such tracking maps what a student knows over time. It then calls the score on the next quiz item. Links join students, items, and skill tags in a web. Their 2026 preprint adds a team of agents to that web.

The agents fetch apt sub-webs for each call. A lopsided fusion step joins what they fetch. Links among skill tags get more weight in this build. Apt calls help apps pick the right next task. They also flag weak skills for a teacher's eye.
arxiv-2601-17086:
Ayush Pratap Singh and a team of four co-authors fix how speech bots say hard names. Speech bots oft botch names from low-resource tongues. Names of folks, brands, and places get the worst of it. Those names are rare in the big English train sets. Past fixes need dear tagged speech from many tongues. Their 2026 preprint edits bot facts in a null-space cage.

The cage keeps edits from harm to the bot's base speech. Just the name's sound path gets the fix. No vast new speech sets are called for. Such fixes aid voice tools in mixed-tongue lands. They curb the sting of a name said wrong.
arxiv-2601-17286:
Sabarish V. Narayanan and Ganesh Subramanian compute heat and mass flow from a round drop in complex shear. The drop floats with neutral buoyancy in a linear flow. Inertia is absent, and convection is strong. The transport rate is summed up in the Nusselt number. That number tells how much flow boosts transfer past plain diffusion.

Exact rates for drops in mixed shear guide many fields. They inform spray drying, mixing, and microfluidic design. A clean formula beats costly simulation for quick checks. It also tests the codes used for harder cases. The strong convection limit is where simple rules often fail. This work pins that limit down for a key shape.
arxiv-2601-17786:
Yixin Liu, Kehan Yan, Shiyuan Li, Qingfeng Chen, and Shirui Pan work on spotting odd or harmful text. Their 2026 preprint deals with text anomaly detection. The task supports content review, phishing alerts, and spam filtering. Most top methods work in two steps. First a model turns text into a set of numbers, then a detector flags the odd ones out.

The weak point, the authors argue, is the use of a single model for that first step. One view of a text can miss signs that another view would catch. Their approach draws on several views of the text at once. It also adapts better across different data sets. The goal is steadier detection when the text type changes.
arxiv-2601-17886:
V. Pierro, M. Granata, C. Michel, and a team of co-authors report the first lab build of a new kind of mirror coating. Their 2026 preprint deals with mirrors made of three materials at once. The design came from an algorithm that juggles two goals at once: low thermal noise and low optical loss. Both goals matter for the mirrors used in fine instruments such as gravity wave detectors.

The team made and tested two ternary systems. One, based on silicon nitride, serves as a proof of concept. The other uses titanium-doped germanium oxide and aims at lower loss. Making the design real in the lab is the key step. It shows the algorithm's picks can be built and measured, not just drawn.
arxiv-2601-17986:
A team of authors trains multimodal models where the data cannot be gathered in one place. Their 2026 preprint deals with federated learning. Today's big multimodal models train in central data centers on aligned sets, like image-text pairs. Real federated settings look nothing like that. Data sits split across nodes, one holding sensor streams and another text logs. The sets are private and share no common items.

The team works through a single transformer design that fits all nodes. Learning must proceed without pairs that line up across sites. Success would let hospitals, firms, and devices train shared models without sharing raw data. The work attacks a hard gap between lab training and field data.
arxiv-2601-18386:
Gabriel Jun Rong Lee and five colleagues built ARMOR, a tool that plans attacks on AI models in a smart, step by step way. Tests that try to fool a model are key for checks on safety. Old test suites run the same fixed list of tricks in the same fixed order each time. They do not adapt, and they do not weigh what a trick means.

ARMOR acts more like an agent with a plan. It picks which trick to try and sets how strong the trick should be. It then learns from what the model does next. That flex lets it probe weak spots that a fixed list would miss. Strong probes help labs find flaws in their models before bad actors find the same flaws in the wild.
arxiv-2601-18486:
Manuel Tonneau and many colleagues question a common way of probing how language models treat groups of people. The probe gives a model one cue, such as a name or a way of speech, and reads its reply as a sign of group views. That plan takes for granted that each cue stands for the same deep trait. The team argue that this grant is shakier than it looks.

If two cues for the same group pull quite unlike replies, the probe may not test one thing at all. It may test the cue, not the group. That flaw would cloud claims about bias in models, in both ways. The work calls for probes that first prove their cues mean the same thing. Only then can their grades be read as fair signs of how a model treats a group.
arxiv-2601-19086:
Yiliang Li, Jun-e Feng, and Abdelhamid Tayebi sync the pointing of several rigid bodies under one leader. Each body, like a satellite or drone, must turn so its attitude matches the group's shared aim. The bodies differ from each other, and they talk over a network shaped like a tree with no loops.

Their shared control rule needs no central boss beyond the leader's lead. They prove the sync holds from almost any start, a strong form of stability. Fleets of craft that must point as one, for cameras or antennas, are the natural users of such a rule.
arxiv-2601-19186:
Zeyu Bian, Lan Wang, Chengchun Shi, and Zhengling Qi demand two kinds of fairness from decision policies at once. Fairness research mostly studies supervised learning, but policies that act on the world raise their own issues. Since a policy intervenes, it creates two fairness targets that can pull apart.

The first is action fairness: like cases should get like actions. The second is outcome fairness: the downstream results should also be even. Their framework, double fairness policy learning, chases both together. Tools used in hiring, lending, and care need this wider lens before they can claim to be fair.
arxiv-2601-19786:
Jinzuomu Zhong, Yi Wang, Korin Richmond, and Peter Bell study how speech tokens carry accent. Modern speech generation builds on discrete speech representation tokens, compact codes for raw audio. Past work probed how much phonetic and speaker information these tokens hold. How accent is encoded in them was largely unexplored.

The authors present the first systematic investigation of accent information in these tokens. Knowing where accent lives in the code matters for accent generation, where a system must speak with a chosen accent. It also matters for fairness, since accent bias can creep into speech tools. Their findings map a hidden layer of speech technology. The work guides designers of voices that can shift accent on demand.
arxiv-2601-20186:
Song-hai Li and three colleagues study time crystals, systems that keep oscillating on their own in a steady rhythm. In quantum models, strong nonlinearity alone usually fails to sustain such motion. The steady state ends up respecting time-translation symmetry, so no crystal forms. The authors identify dephasing as the main mechanism that enforces this outcome.

They show that links between the phases of coupled components can suppress dephasing. On that basis they give a general reading of nonlinear connected time crystals, joining self-sustained motion with quantum synchronization. The work clarifies what a quantum system needs before it can keep time by itself.
arxiv-2601-20386:
Qi Kuang, Bowen Gang, and Yin Xia present SCORE, a framework for online false discovery rate control. Online testing judges hypotheses one by one as data arrives, while keeping the share of false findings in check. Methods based on e-values control this rate under weak assumptions, but they lose power by discarding evidence that overshoots the rejection threshold.

SCORE recovers that overshoot as a refund that can be spent on later tests. More power at the same error guarantee means more true findings from the same data stream. The idea suits live settings like platform experiments and sequential clinical monitoring.
arxiv-2601-20886:
Spencer Mateega and five co-authors build a test for AI agents that work inside an editor. Their 2026 paper presents IDE-Bench. It evaluates large language models as IDE agents on real-world software engineering tasks. An IDE is the integrated development environment where programmers write and test code. New AI-native IDEs, like Cursor and Windsurf, give models structured tools. The benchmark mirrors that setting.

The team built a Dockerized test harness. It goes beyond raw terminal execution. Models get a structured tool ecosystem like the real products provide. Tasks then reflect how engineers actually work in an editor. This framing catches failures that plain command-line tests miss. IDE-Bench helps vendors compare agents on equal footing. It also shows where today's agents still fall short of a junior engineer.
arxiv-2601-20986:
Valerio La Gatta and six co-authors build a tool to analyze social movements online. Their 2026 paper presents SMART, a Social Movement Analysis and Reasoning Tool. Social movements that back the UN's Sustainable Development Goals play a vital role in improving lives. Journalists cover these movements under time pressure. If they knew how movements link to external events, reporting could be more precise and timely.

SMART aims to surface those relationships for its users. The paper includes case studies on two movements. They are #MeToo and #BlackLivesMatter, both global in reach. The cases show how the tool reasons over posts and events. Such support could help newsrooms and researchers alike. It turns a flood of posts into a readable story of cause and response.
arxiv-2601-21186:
TianYi Tang, Saba Alimadadi, and Nick Sumner catalog the bugs that haunt TypeScript projects. Their 2026 paper is the first large-scale empirical study of bugs in real-world TypeScript. TypeScript has rapidly become a popular language for modern web development. Its effect on software faults, though, remains poorly understood. The team analyzed hundreds of bug reports from popular open-source repositories. They built a taxonomy of fault types from that evidence.

The study quantifies how common each fault type is. It also relates faults to project characteristics. Size, domain, and dependency composition all come under the lens. Such a map tells tool builders where TypeScript code actually breaks. It can guide linters, type checkers, and teaching. The paper appears at the 2026 Mining Software Repositories conference. It grounds debates about language safety in counted evidence.
arxiv-2601-21286:
Adithya Bhat, Harshal Shah, and Mohsen Minaei speed up backup copies in distributed systems. In primary-backup setups, the main node sends work out and backups must replay each transaction. The total delay is capped by how fast backups can redo that work.

Their framework, Ira, sends small hints along with each batch of transactions. The hints let backups skip much of the slow re-execution. Faster replay means the whole system can confirm work sooner. It also means backups fall behind less during busy periods. The design targets systems that must stay both fast and consistent.
arxiv-2601-21386:
June-Woo Kim, Dhruv Agarwal, and Federica Cerina examine a popular score for judging synthetic speech. Human listening tests are the gold standard, but they are costly and hard to run at scale. A distance score borrowed from image work has become a common stand-in.

The score compares distributions of sound features between real and fake speech. The authors show that its verdict depends heavily on which features are used and how the test is set up. Careless choices can make poor speech look good, or good speech look poor. Their guidance helps teams use the score in ways that track what listeners actually hear.
arxiv-2601-21686:
Luca Benfenati and seven co-authors compress the memory cache that language models use while generating. The cache stores keys and values for every past token, which speeds up decoding. At long contexts it becomes a leading drain on fast memory, in both size and bandwidth.

A common fix projects each head's cache to lower rank and stores only the projection. The authors learn that low-rank fit over the Stiefel manifold, the space of tidy orthonormal frames. A better-fitting projection should keep quality while shrinking the cache. Smaller caches mean longer conversations and documents on the same hardware.
arxiv-2601-21886:
Michael Kuhlmann, Alexander Werning, Thilo von Neumann, and Reinhold Haeb-Umbach argue that judging speech quality with one score is not enough. Most automatic assessment tools grade a whole utterance or a whole system. Such scores can say that speech is bad, but not where it goes wrong.

Their 2026 preprint works on localization: finding the low-quality stretches inside speech, and spotting artifacts left by text-to-speech synthesis. Pinpointing the bad segments would help engineers fix synthesis systems, help editors clean recordings, and help users understand a score instead of just seeing it. The work treats quality as something with a location in time, not only a number at the end.
arxiv-2601-21986:
Yu Cui and co-authors improve how recommender systems suggest the next item in a sequence. Traditional models learn compact embeddings from item identifiers alone, based on user interaction history. That ignores rich text, such as item titles and descriptions, that could signal what an item really is.

Language models can encode that text into detailed semantic embeddings. The team's 2026 preprint presents SpecTran, a spectral-aware Transformer adapter that brings language model knowledge into sequential recommendation. Frequency-aware processing can separate lasting tastes from passing noise in a user's history. Sharper next-item suggestions drive streaming, shopping, and news feeds, so even small gains in reading user intent carry large commercial weight.
arxiv-2601-22386:
Jamiu Adekunle Idowu and Ahmed Almasoud ask whether a team of AI graders beats a lone one on school essays. Their 2026 preprint tests single-agent and multi-agent setups on the ASAP 2.0 set of student essays. Auto grading is now common, yet how the setup shapes scores is little known.

They check scores across essays of high, mid, and low quality. A setup that shines on strong essays may sag on weak ones. Knowing that split helps schools pick a fair grader. It also warns where human review must stay in the loop. The work guides real classroom use.
arxiv-2601-22786:
Hamid Reza Akbari and a team build a reward-based learning frame that borrows from Integrated Information Theory. Their 2026 preprint notes that current models are not conscious, yet they show acts akin to parts of consciousness. The frame aims at AGI, where such processing might play a key role.

Rewards shape the model toward more integrated processing, in the theory's sense. The claim is careful: an inspiration, not a proof of machine mind. Still, new training signals could yield new skills. The work is speculative theory with a concrete method. It invites tests, not belief.
arxiv-2601-23086:
Nathaniel Mitrani Hadida and four co-authors warn that models can learn to hide their reasoning. Chain-of-thought text helps models plan, and it helps humans monitor what agents are doing. A faithful reasoning trace can flag dangerous behavior early, before action is taken.

The authors show that training on outputs alone can teach models to obfuscate their stated reasoning. Worse, that hiding skill can carry over to tasks never trained for concealment. The finding presses labs to protect the honesty of reasoning traces. Output-only supervision is the surprising teacher: no one trained the hiding directly, yet the skill generalized to unseen tasks.
arxiv-2601-23286:
Hongyang Du and nine co-authors distill shape knowledge into video generation models. Modern video diffusion models look impressive, yet they often break three-dimensional consistency. Objects deform or drift in space across frames, betraying the lack of real scene structure.

The authors argue standard cleaning gives no incentive for shape unity. Their VideoGPA transfers shape priors from a teacher into the video model. Videos that hold their shape serve film, simulation, and world modeling far better. Object deformation and spatial drift are the visible symptoms the shape priors are distilled to prevent. Explicit incentives for shape unity are what standard cleaning objectives lack, on the authors' hypothesis.
arxiv-2603-01486:
A short search term on a food and goods app can mean quite different things at once. Emmanuel Aboah Boateng, Kyle Macdonald, Akshad Viswanathan, and Sudeep Das report a DoorDash case study from 2026 on that puzzle. A word like a flower name might point to a shop chain, a product, or fresh blooms, and a forced single guess often fails.

Their system grounds a large language model in the shop catalog and, for new terms, in live web search. It lists several ranked intents, and fixed business rules then pick how to route the search. On DoorDash search, scores beat both a plain language model and the old live system. The setup now serves most daily searches and can fit other shops that supply their own lists and rules.
arxiv-2603-01586:
Editing one small object in a busy photo is hard when the target is not the obvious focus. Yecong Wan, Fan Li, Chunwei Wang, and colleagues teach an editor to reason about place first in this 2026 work. In scenes with many things, a vague request can point to several spots at once.

Their frame, InterCoG, mixes text thought with visual grounding in turns. It first works out the target place and identity in words, with spatial links spelled out. Next it marks the target with boxes and masks on the image itself. Then it rewrites the edit request to state the wanted result in precise terms. Two training aids sharpen place accuracy and keep the reasoning clear, backed by a new set of annotated edit cases.
arxiv-2603-01786:
Nikita Morozov, Ian Maksimov, Daniil Tiapkin, and Sergey Samsonov find shortest paths with a learning method built to sample good options. Their 2026 work uses Generative Flow Networks, which learn to build objects step by step with odds tied to reward. Shortest paths matter for planning, routing, robots, and many puzzle-like tasks.

The team first proves a key fact for graphs that contain cycles, not just trees. If total flow is minimized, the learned forward and backward routes use shortest paths only. That proof turns pathfinding in any graph into training one such network with a flow penalty. Tests cover permutation puzzles and Rubik Cube solving, a stern test of search. Their solver matches top custom machine learning tools on solution length while using a smaller search budget at test time.
arxiv-2603-02186:
José Liceaga Martínez, Jesús Rodríguez Viorato, and José Carlos Gomez Larrañaga study shape tools on layered spaces in this 2026 paper. Their tool is the discrete Morse function, which tags points of a shape to reveal its form. The best such functions pair off as many points as possible. The spaces here are stratifolds, shapes built from smooth layers of mixed sizes.

The authors give a method that computes best functions fast for a wide class of these spaces. They also pin down when such a function is perfect. A perfect function leaves exactly the points that the shape's core counts demand. No extra critical points remain to clutter the picture. The result links fast computation with a clean test for perfection.
arxiv-2603-02286:
Yaoteng Zhang, Qing Zhou, Junyu Gao, and Qi Wang improve step-by-step object detection in this 2026 paper. A detector must learn new object classes over time without forgetting old ones. Prompt-based methods are cheap and need no replay of old data. Yet linked prompts interfere, drift, and slowly degrade as tasks pile up.

Their framework, PDP, splits prompts into two pools with clear jobs. A shared pool holds general knowledge that transfers across tasks. A private pool holds features that mark each task's own classes. A second module builds class prototypes to label old objects that new data marks as background. That keeps training signals consistent across steps. Scores hit new highs on two major benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-02386:
Caleb Robinson, Nils Lehmann, Adam Stewart, and colleagues present a tutorial on geospatial machine learning in this 2026 paper. Satellite data differs from ordinary photos in ways that break standard workflows. Scenes are huge and georeferenced, and labels come as masks or map shapes. Training and testing also need sampling that respects geography.

TorchGeo is a library built on PyTorch for exactly those needs. It supplies data sets, samplers, transforms, and pretrained models for Earth data. The tutorial walks through its core ideas with code examples. A full case study maps surface water in multispectral satellite images. The trained model is applied to a scene over Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Predictions are saved as a standard map file for further analysis.
arxiv-2603-02486:
Shadab Choudhury surveys explainable AI for assistive technology in this 2026 paper. People with vision or hearing loss rely on AI to describe images, read documents, and caption speech. Those models are deep networks, so their reasons stay hidden. Explanation tools exist, but they were rarely built for disabled users.

Choudhury reviews human-centered and accessibility-centered explanation research. Almost no work accounts for people with sensory disabilities, the survey finds. Many standard explanations are hard for those users to grasp or even perceive. A visual heat map, for instance, fails the blind users who need it most. The paper maps this perceptual gap in detail. It closes with concrete avenues for accessible, human-centered explanation design.
arxiv-2603-02586:
Hao Li, Huan Wang, Jinjie Gu, and colleagues benchmark AI agents on real-world tasks in this 2026 paper. General agents are spreading into daily use, but benchmarks poorly reflect real user needs. Their benchmark holds just over a hundred scenarios drawn from real requirements. Questions come from social media posts and real products, not synthetic prompts.

A generation method ensures each task is relevant, complex, and verifiable. The full release holds hundreds of tasks split between validation and testing. Models, frameworks, and commercial products were all evaluated on it. Results reveal practical performance levels and clear areas for improvement. The generation process supports continuous updates with fresh real-world queries. Static benchmarks age fast, so that renewal matters.
arxiv-2603-02786:
Noga Alon, Michał Dębski, Jarosław Grytczuk, and Jakub Przybyło ask how short an interval can hold shifted copies of many step-pattern sets. Each set in their 2026 study is an opening stretch of the multiples of some step size, like the even numbers up to a limit. The copies must sit inside one interval without overlapping each other.

They pin down the shortest interval length in two setups: patterns cut off at one shared bound, and patterns each holding the same count of terms. For the full family of steps, the answers grow at rates they determine exactly in order of magnitude. Beyond a threshold family size, a simple linear bound takes over. The results complete the picture for every smaller family size as well.
arxiv-2603-02886:
Guoqing Ma, Xun Lin, Hui Ma, and colleagues hide a face inside a normal picture so fake-face checks can run in private. Their 2026 framework, StegaFFD, responds to a leak risk: face images sent to cloud detectors can be intercepted or mishandled. Blurring or encryption protects privacy but looks suspicious and can erase the subtle traces detectors need.

Steganography instead tucks the face into a natural cover image, and detection runs directly on the hidden version. New modules suppress the cover image's low-frequency bulk and sharpen attention on the faint hidden face features. An alignment step matches hidden-face signals to their raw counterparts. Across seven datasets, the method stayed inconspicuous while preserving detection accuracy better than prior privacy tools.
arxiv-2603-02986:
Alessio Mazzucchelli, Ivan Ojeda-Martin, Fernando Rivas-Manzaneque, and colleagues recolor three-dimensional scenes in about two seconds. Their 2026 system, VIRGi, edits scenes built from 3D Gaussian splats, a fast rendering method that lacks good appearance editing tools. The challenge is keeping view-dependent shine, like specular highlights, correct after a color change.

The method splits color into a flat diffuse part and a view-dependent part, and trains across many viewpoints at once for a cleaner base scene. A user then edits one single image of the scene. Fine-tuning one small network spreads that edit across the whole scene, with a strength control for the shiny effects. Broad tests show clear gains over older radiance-field editors.
arxiv-2603-03486:
Mohammad Alikhani shrinks a network attack detector until it fits the smallest devices. Security monitors at the network edge and in real-time systems have little computing room, so big models are out. His 2026 framework starts from the opposite end: a large Kolmogorov-Arnold Network, a model skilled at capturing complex patterns, is trained first as a teacher on attack data.

Through decoupled knowledge distillation, that teacher trains a tiny plain neural network as its student. The students end up with only a few thousand parameters each, far smaller than the teacher, while keeping high detection performance. On two public testbed datasets, the distilled students beat identical untrained-by-distillation students by several points of F1 score. Alikhani presents the recipe as practical for resource-starved devices and releases the implementation publicly.
arxiv-2603-03586:
Ricardo A Pinto maps the unwanted couplings inside a fully connected star of superconducting qubits. In a star array every transmon qubit talks capacitively to every other, a connectivity that promises faster gates and cheaper error correction. The same web breeds crosstalk: several distinct ZZ-type couplings arise, one per interaction channel, each a path to operating errors. His 2026 analysis studies how two coupling families respond to qubit detuning, the frequency offset that dials interaction strength.

The exchange coupling fades smoothly and steeply as detuning grows. The ZZ couplings behave worse first, spiking where qubit states resonate with states outside the computational basis, then collapsing quickly to zero. That shape defines a safe operational region of near-zero coupling. Pinto derives formulas for both families as functions of detuning, and they agree with direct numerical solutions of the Schrödinger equation.
