Frederikke Malinovsky, Peter Brodersen, Berthe Fiil and colleagues characterized a plant protein tied to controlled cell death, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Programmed cell death is a normal part of life in multicellular organisms. In plants, one form is the hypersensitive response, a scorched-earth defense that kills cells around an infection site to wall off pathogens.

The protein Lazarus1, a member of the DUF300 family, contributes to that death program and to death seen in the mutant acd11. Naming the executioners of plant cell death helps breeders and biotechnologists tune crop immunity, since a defense that kills too much tissue can cost as much yield as disease.
plos-pone-0012686:
Berniker, Voss and Kording modelled how the brain mixes fresh senses with past learning. People blend what they see and hear now with expectations built over a lifetime. Their 2010 paper studies priors, the brain's stored guesses, and how a learner should set them.

They show how good priors can be learned rather than fixed in advance. Getting this right matters for theories of perception and for building machines that learn like brains. The work links lab findings on human judgement to a clean learning rule. The model also predicts when strong priors help and when they mislead.
plos-pone-0012786:
Murdoch, Clawson, Yue and co-authors linked a pattern in the cow prion gene to mad cow disease rates. Classical BSE, the cattle prion disease behind mad cow outbreaks, can pass to people through food. The bovine prion gene, PRNP, has stretches where variants travel together and other stretches where they mix freely.

Their 2010 study of European Holstein cattle tied one such pattern to how often BSE appeared. A gene pattern tied to risk could help breeding and surveillance programmes. It also sharpens the science of prion diseases across species.
plos-pone-0012886:
Li, Preuss, Rilling and co-authors compared the wiring of hand control in chimpanzee brains with their handedness. Most humans are right-handed and show matching left-right differences in the motor pathway from cortex to spine. Chimpanzees also favour one hand at the group level.

Their 2010 study used diffusion MRI, which traces fibre pathways, to measure both sides of this system in chimps. Matching brain asymmetry to hand preference tests how deep the roots of human handedness go. The comparison informs the evolution of brain sidedness itself.  Both chimps and their test scores came from research colonies.
plos-pone-0337786:
Yuri Russo and colleagues set healthy young adults walking a winding raised-stepping course while their eyes and steps were tracked, then added a mental task on top. Adaptive walking normally depends on looking ahead to plan each footfall. Twenty-three volunteers in their late teens and early twenties walked the L-shaped path alone and while thinking hard.

Dual-task walking slowed everyone down, lengthened the time both feet spent grounded, and scattered their gaze toward irrelevant spots with fewer, shorter looks at the stepping targets. Oddly, a sideways cross-step pattern appeared more often without the mental load. Even in the young and fit, the authors show, thinking steals the visual planning that safe walking needs.
plos-pone-0341786:
Paul Leavy, Blánaid Daly, John Ford, and Sara Burke published this 2026 interview study of dentists in Ireland. Private dentists can sign contracts to treat low-income adults under a state scheme, yet many hold back. Nineteen interviews with dentists, officials, and experts were used to build explanations of what drives that choice.

Low payment rates, an outdated menu of covered treatments, and heavy paperwork all discouraged participation, atop weak political backing for oral health. Leavy argues reformers can use these levers to draw dentists back in and widen care for poorer patients.
plos-pone-0342286:
Ye Liang, Louis Shuo Wang, Jiguang Yu, and Xin Zan stress-tested the standard formula doctors use to plan how many patients a new risk prediction model needs. They found it dangerously cheerful when the model aims to be very accurate. Their 2026 Monte Carlo study simulated model development across many settings. It measured the sample size actually required for the model's risk estimates to stay calibrated on fresh patients.

At moderate accuracy targets the formula held up. As targets rose, the true requirement pulled far ahead. At the highest target, the formula's recommended sample routinely produced extreme, unstable risk predictions. That is a separation problem, where the model becomes certain and wrong. The authors advise pairing formula planning with simulation checks whenever a high-accuracy model is promised.
plos-pone-0343186:
Shunsuke Yawata and colleagues asked whether intensive care units that order more blood gas tests in the first day see different death rates. Blood gas tests guide care for unstable patients, yet extra testing carries cost and harm. A Japanese registry covering nearly one hundred and eighteen thousand patients in eighty seven units from 2015 to 2023 was used, with test counts adjusted for patient mix.

Units varied widely in early test use. After adjustment, higher use showed no clear link with hospital death, though a gentle bend hinted at better outcomes at higher use without reaching certainty. More testing alone, the authors conclude, is neither waste nor cure; patient need should drive the count.
plos-pone-0346386:
Hailey Fazio, R. H. Khediri, and Nicole James look at how scientists think science ought to work, in a 2026 interview study. Their participants were postdoctoral researchers in materials science and chemistry, fields where testing a clear prediction is often held up as the mark of good work. Sixteen interviews were examined closely for how people described their own practice.

Most participants said prediction-driven testing defines good science, yet some admitted it is not always the most useful route in their own projects. That tension affected how they judged themselves and how they presented their work, pushing them to craft explanations that reconciled their practice with the textbook story. The authors argue that training should openly recognize many legitimate ways of building knowledge, rather than one master narrative.
plos-pone-0347186:
Clearing the breathing tubes of patients on ventilators follows strict guidelines, but intensive care nurses in Tanzania often cannot follow them fully. Loema Moshi Buyi, Rashid Heri, and Menti Lastone Ndile interviewed seventeen experienced nurses at Muhimbili National Hospital for this 2026 PLOS One study.

Three barriers emerged. Shortages of staff, equipment, and supplies came first. Next came knowledge gaps and habits that resist change. Finally, the guidelines themselves were hard to reach and felt written for richer hospitals. The authors argue non-adherence reflects a strained system more than careless nurses, and they call for guidelines adapted to local reality.
plos-pone-0347486:
Allison R Sherris and colleagues measured combustion chemicals in the urine of pregnant women in Nairobi, Kenya, and checked them against how their babies fared at birth. The chemicals, called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, come from traffic, cooking fuel, and burning, and most earlier studies of them in pregnancy come from rich countries. Just over three hundred and fifty mother and baby pairs took part, with urine tested late in pregnancy.

Nearly every mother carried measurable levels of all five chemicals checked. Most showed no link with birth weight or prematurity. One breakdown product stood out, tracking with slightly shorter pregnancies, and the link looked stronger for baby girls; it faded once home fuel and outdoor burning were accounted for. The authors call the effect modest and urge larger African studies of everyday air and fuel exposures.
plos-pone-0347686:
Jinxing Xu and colleagues studied how the colour of light during storage rewrites the chemistry of lily bulbs, work aimed at bulbs sold for their ornamental colour. Bulbs of a spotted lily subspecies kept under white, blue, or red light were profiled for pigments and for the activity of thousands of genes and hundreds of small molecules. Together these built a layered picture of the response.

White and blue light drove a fast build-up of violet-red pigments, multiplying the main pigment family many times over, while red light pushed the bulbs toward yellow-brown instead. The responsible gene chain switched on in sequence, early genes peaking first and late genes rising behind them. Temperature and packaging also nudged the outcome. The authors offer growers and breeders a light recipe for steering bulb colour on the shelf.
plos-pone-0347786:
Yuanyuan Fan designs a system to keep student data private inside online group learning platforms. Students leave names, grades, and study habits in these spaces, and leaks can hurt both rights and motivation. The 2026 paper blends several guards: noise added on the student's own device, searchable coding of stored files, and access rules tied to who is asking, all logged on a shared ledger.

Tests reported in the paper show the combined design beating older methods on accuracy, speed, and safety. A trial run inside a real learning platform checked that classes could still work together smoothly. For schools moving more teaching online, the design offers a way to share work without sharing more about students than needed.
plos-pone-0348086:
Zhiang Liu and co-workers compute how adding boron or nitrogen atoms to graphene changes its contact with atom-thin semiconductors. Such layered stacks are candidates for future tiny electronics, and the quality of the electrical contact decides how well they work. Their 2026 study uses first-principles physics calculations across ten partner materials.

Doping graphene shifted its energy level over a wide range. That shift could flip a contact from one charge type to the other, and in some stacks turned a blocking contact into a free-flowing one. Designers gain a dial for tuning barrier height on purpose rather than by luck. The results guide building sharper switches and better catalysts from layered materials.
plos-pone-0348186:
Karin Kiontke and colleagues trace the tail anatomy of male roundworms to learn how development channels evolution, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Male tails in these tiny nematodes carry sensory rays and a shaped tip that evolve again and again across species, raising the question of whether development limits which changes are possible.

Adding deeper-branching species to the family tree, the team watched tail organs form using fluorescent staining and laser removal of precursor cells. Tail tip formation was gained and lost repeatedly, while the early pattern of ray precursors stayed highly conserved. The picture is of evolution tinkering at the edges of a stubborn developmental scaffold, rather than rebuilding it.
plos-pone-0348286:
Samanta Tarquino González and Belfran Carbonell-Medina tested how far an axolotl, the Mexican salamander famous for regrowing limbs, can rebuild its lower jaw. Earlier work showed the jaw heals after side cuts, but surgeons remove jaw sections straight across when treating tumors, a much bigger loss. The team amputated the jaw completely across its width and watched the response.

Under the microscope, a blastema formed, the bud of growing cells that powers salamander regrowth, and new skeletal tissue followed. Cell division and gene activity matched that classic regrowth program. The researchers also found the response has a limit along the jaw's length. Knowing where regrowth works and where it stops is basic knowledge for any future jaw repair inspired by these animals.
plos-pone-0348586:
Touria Essayagh and co-workers measure how many Moroccan parents refuse the HPV vaccine for their daughters and what drives the refusal. The vaccine prevents cervical cancer, but uptake in Morocco lags. Their 2026 study surveys close to fourteen hundred fifty parents of girls aged eleven to fourteen at health facilities across several centers.

Nearly three in ten parents refused. Refusal tied to higher schooling yet lower income, weaker trust in the health system, and thinner knowledge of cervical cancer. Fear for daughters, missed past vaccine schedules, hard-to-reach clinics, and missing advice from health workers all added weight. Winning trust and giving clear information through clinics and media top the authors' list of fixes.
plos-pone-0348786:
Aychew Kassa Belete, Bantie Getnet Yirsaw, and Birhan Ambachew Taye pool what is known about physical inactivity among adults across Africa. Moving too little is a major driver of early death, yet African data sit scattered across small studies. Their 2026 review gathers thirty-four studies covering more than forty-one thousand adults and combines their results.

About forty-five in every hundred adults were not active enough, though rates varied widely between studies. Being female, older, heavier, or living in a city all raised the odds of inactivity. Depression and heavier drinking also played a part. The authors urge programs aimed at women, older adults, and city dwellers, where the need runs deepest.
plos-pone-0348886:
Fahman Saeed and Sultan Aldera present a deep learning model for forecasting creatinine, a key marker of kidney function, in hospital patient records. Predicting chronic kidney disease early is hard because each patient's course differs and risk factors tangle together. Their model is a transformer, the architecture behind modern language AI, reshaped by statistics drawn from the data itself.

Eigenvalue analysis of how clinical features correlate set the model's width, and the same math seeded its starting weights so it begins with real feature relationships built in. Tested on daily sequences from a large critical care database, it predicted creatinine with low error. The design also answers the black-box complaint: its structure is derived openly from the data rather than chosen by guesswork.
plos-pone-0349086:
Kathryn Lamoureux and Sheila M. Macfie ask how excess copper harms the root nodules where legume plants and partner bacteria turn air nitrogen into plant food. Copper pollution can poison plants, and this partnership is sensitive to chemical stress. Their 2026 study grows a model legume with its bacteria partner and doses the plants with copper at two levels.

Shots, roots, and nodules all shrank under copper, and nitrogen fixing dropped sharply. Yet copper did not build up inside the nodules, and damage markers there stayed flat. A defense enzyme's activity fell instead, hinting the nodules were aging early. The harm seems to arrive indirectly: a stressed host stops supporting its partners, which then shut down.
plos-pone-0349286:
Masato Kawashima and co-workers test whether gut microbes from fit, fiber-fed donor mice can help obese mice. Moving stool microbes between animals is a hopeful treatment idea for obesity. In their 2026 study, recipient mice stayed on a high-fat, high-sugar diet while receiving transplants from donors that had exercised, eaten added fiber, both, or neither.

The transplants did not improve body weight or blood sugar control in the recipients. Gut microbe mixes shifted only in part, and related gut chemicals changed little. A rich, sugary diet kept pressing on the gut seems to block helpful microbes from settling in. The findings suggest diet change may need to come first before such transplants can work.
plos-pone-0349386:
Mebuki Ito and co-authors swept one hundred and seventy-one sites across central Hokkaido, Japan, in a single spring season. They collected nearly ten thousand ticks and screened them for the diseases they carry. The haul included viruses behind encephalitis and newer fever illnesses, plus the bacteria of Lyme disease and relapsing fever, found almost entirely in two Ixodes tick species.

Computer habitat models, checked by leaving sites out one at a time, predicted where each tick and germ thrives with fair accuracy. Snow depth emerged as a key force separating the species' ranges, a very Hokkaido factor, since ticks shelter under the snowpack. The authors deliver fine-grained risk maps that local health officials can use to target warnings and vaccine advice valley by valley.
plos-pone-0349686:
Soo Hyun Seo and colleagues read the germ mix found under the gums of eighty-four people with gum disease, from mild to severe cases. The germ balance shifts as the disease worsens, but which germs mark each stage was not clear. The team read the DNA of plaque scraped from the teeth and taught five learning programs to sort patients by stage from the germ mix alone.

Two programs sorted the home sample with near-perfect scores, and a few germ types did most of the work. But on three outside groups the scores swung a lot, since mouths and test methods differ from place to place. A germ test tuned in one clinic may fail in the next, so local checks are a must before such tests guide care.
plos-pone-0349886:
Markus Gambietz and colleagues built a way to tailor movement models to a person's real body shape using phone photos. Standard models of the body are generic and then stretched to fit height and weight, which can skew estimates of joint forces. Their method scans the body's outer hull, infers the skeleton inside, and works out how bone, muscle, and fat are spread through each segment.

Tests against MRI-based models showed the photo-based models landed closer to the truth than stretched generic ones. The team also released two new average-body models so older datasets can use the method. Better segment weights mean better estimates of the loads joints carry, which matters for sports science, rehabilitation, and any work that reads meaning into how a body moves.
plos-pone-0350086:
Michaela E Larson and colleagues measured a sensitive heart injury marker in seventy two men in South Florida, grouped by HIV status and stimulant use. People with HIV face higher heart disease risk, and stimulants may add hidden heart strain. Blood tests used a high sensitivity troponin assay, with models split into whether any marker showed and how high it ran.

Men with both HIV and stimulant use had far higher odds of a detectable marker and higher average levels than men with neither. Amphetamine traces also tracked marker levels in a small exploratory check. Groups were small, so caution is due, yet combined risk flags a group that may need early heart screening.
plos-pone-0350186:
Yunkyeong Hwang and colleagues describe a protocol, with no results yet, for tracking safety of preventive treatment for silent tuberculosis in Korea. Preventive courses stop silent infection from waking into active disease, yet fear of side effects stalls starts in medically complex patients. Four university hospitals will enrol adults with kidney, lung, sugar, immune, cancer, or job related risks.

Blood tests will sort silent infection, and treatment will follow national guidance. Everyone, treated or not, will be followed for up to a year for side effects, adherence, and completion. A subset will give finger prick style blood samples for drug level work. Real world safety data could reassure clinics serving high risk patients.
plos-pone-0350286:
Alex Billingsley and colleagues tested timed chest imaging that freezes motion by firing X rays only at set points in breathing and heartbeat. A stationary scanner using carbon nanotube sources imaged a pig under several timing plans: breathing only, heartbeat only during held breath, both together, held breath alone, and free breathing.

Dual timing gave the sharpest heart wall and diaphragm edges by measure and by eye. Breathing timed scans matched held breath scans, and heartbeat timing sharpened the heart wall clearly. Every timed plan beat free breathing. Motion proof chest imaging could track lung change over time with far less dose than full CT scans.
plos-pone-0350386:
Julie Mortensen and seven colleagues compare contrast agents for scanning small animals in this 2026 imaging study. CT in small animals gives weak soft-tissue contrast compared with hospital scanners. Organs blur together, which hampers measurement and segmentation. The team tested familiar clinical iodine and gadolinium agents against a nanoparticle agent built for research. Phantom experiments first mapped brightness against concentration. Living mice then showed how each agent behaved in the body.

In phantoms, every agent brightened in clean proportion to its strength. At high dilutions the signal faded into background. In mice, clinical agents injected into the abdomen outlined the abdominal organs well. The research agent, given intravenously, pooled in specific organs instead. The practical verdict favours the cheap option. Ordinary iodinated contrast, delivered into the abdomen, offers small-animal researchers a cost-effective way to sharpen soft-tissue boundaries.
plos-pone-0350886:
Lei Feng and co-authors hunted for gene markers of liver cirrhosis in 2026, focusing on genes tied to white blood cells crossing vessel walls. Cirrhosis kills many patients, and early markers or drug targets are badly needed.

Public liver data sets were mined by combining network analysis with standard difference tests, yielding hundreds of candidate genes. A smaller hub set sat in inflammation and immune pathways. From it the team built a diagnostic chart for telling cirrhosis from health and screened possible drugs. Tissue staining checked key genes in patients. The work narrows a huge gene list to testable leads.
plos-pone-0350986:
Selemon Fakana, Fekadu Falta, and Abera Dofee map in 2026 soil loss in the Wolaita Zone of Ethiopia, where most people farm for a living. They combined a standard soil loss equation with satellite data and mapping software. Inputs covered rain, soil type, land cover, and slope, drawn from several public sources.

Most land lost soil slowly, but about one sixth faced high to severe loss, mainly in the wetter west with thin plant cover. Rates in the worst spots ran extremely high by farm standards. The authors point to contour farming, terraces, check dams, and tree based farming as responses matched to the mapped hot spots.
plos-pone-0351086:
Neelamberi Devi Klein and Kurt Hugenberg present this 2026 PLOS One study of how faces get judged as more or less fully human. Earlier work used only White faces. It found that attractive and smart-looking faces are granted more humanlike depth. Across two studies, the authors asked whether those rules hold when faces vary by race and gender.

Attractiveness predicted humanness for every group of faces. Perceived intelligence predicted humanness only for White faces. It did not do so for Black faces. The authors call this split intersectional dehumanization. They read it as proof that Black people's minds are discounted. Looking smart does not earn Black targets the same belief in a rich inner life. The result fits wider research on racial bias in mind perception.
plos-pone-0351886:
Caiyun Sun and three colleagues build a training system for cardiac rehabilitation nurses through expert consensus. Their 2026 study responds to a Chinese workforce gap. Demand for heart rehabilitation is outrunning the supply of trained professionals. Master's nursing students are the obvious talent reserve. Yet no standard framework existed for their training in this specialty. A modified Delphi process consulted twenty-two rehabilitation experts across two rounds. Agreement statistics and response rates tracked the consensus as it formed.

Engagement was near total in both rounds. The experts' authority ratings were solid, their agreement moderate but real. The finished system spans five domains and twenty-nine subdomains. Eighty-five competency indicators spell out what a graduate should be able to do. For universities, that converts a vague ambition into a checklist that can be taught, examined, and improved. The framework also gives hospitals a shared language for judging new graduates' readiness.
plos-pone-0351986:
Ho Nu and three colleagues optimise a surface treatment that makes titanium parts last longer. Their 2026 study concerns ultrasonic rolling of a workhorse aerospace alloy. Rolling with such vibration presses a beneficial squeeze, called compressive residual stress, into the surface. That squeeze resists cracks starting and slows fatigue. Both its size and its depth matter for how long parts last. Predicting them together is hard, because the metal deforms in tangled ways under the combined loads.

The authors built one analytical framework for the pair. Contact mechanics and plasticity theory supply the physics. A response surface method then searches the settings: static load, shaking strength, frequency, and ball radius. Published experimental stress profiles validated the predictions. Machinists gain a calculator instead of trial-and-error batches. For aircraft parts where a surface crack can become a catastrophe, optimising the invisible stress shield is money well spent.
plos-pone-0352186:
Mathé and colleagues asked whether hot weather raises cases of two serious blood infections in a 2026 German study. Records covered three years at six large hospitals, with thousands of infections caused by two common germs that can enter the blood. Daily weather data let the team count very hot days and compare them with infection rates.

Both infections followed a clear yearly rhythm, rising and falling with the seasons. The team modeled whether extra heat stress days added cases beyond that rhythm. Knowing if heat itself drives infections matters as summers grow hotter under climate change. Hospitals could use such patterns to plan staffing and lab capacity ahead of heat waves.
plos-pone-0352386:
Sascha Moreitz and seven colleagues mine a huge archive of masters swimming results in this 2026 study. Masters events let adult swimmers compete at high level for decades. The authors ask which nations keep appearing among the very best. Their unit of success is a place in the annual top ten. Every stroke, distance, sex, and age group counts. The archive covers nearly four decades of world championship racing, ending in 2024.

Over two hundred thousand long-course performances were extracted. Women contributed about ninety-four thousand entries, men about one hundred ten thousand. National differences were tested statistically across the full span. Such a long record shows more than who is fast now. It reveals which countries built durable masters cultures, keeping swimmers racing into old age. Federations can read the patterns as evidence for where lifelong competitive swimming truly took root.
plos-pone-0352586:
Chenping Zhao and co-authors propose in 2026 a network for clearing haze from a single photo, where haze depth varies across the scene. Their design recalibrates features layer by layer, refines local detail through a coupled residual block, and gathers context at several scales through widened filters. A redesigned attention block uses convolutions instead of dense layers to model channel and space together.

Tests on standard benchmarks gave top scores on both reference based and blind quality measures, according to the authors. The system handled real world scenes with uneven haze well. Clearer images help later tasks such as driving vision and photo editing in poor weather.
plos-pone-0352686:
Dominic Garza and seven colleagues catalogue viruses that infect Rhodococcus bacteria in this 2026 genomics study. These viruses, called bacteriophages, are everywhere and astonishingly varied. Fifty-six new phages were isolated using two Rhodococcus species as hosts. Some kill their hosts outright, others hide inside them. Genome sequencing let the team sort the newcomers alongside previously described relatives.

The phages fell into six clusters, plus sixteen loners matching nothing else. Genome sizes ranged widely, from about forty-four thousand to one hundred forty-two thousand DNA letters. Chemical composition varied just as much. Oddly, some Rhodococcus phages resembled phages of entirely different bacterial genera more than their fellow Rhodococcus phages. Such tangles reveal complex evolutionary histories of swapping and borrowing. Each new genome sharpens the map of viral diversity, and may someday supply tools against stubborn bacterial infections.
plos-pone-0352986:
Agha and colleagues studied social media priming for HPV vaccination in Abuja, Nigeria, in a 2026 paper. A health worker strike halted vaccination for about four months, then services reopened for just five days during a child health week. Exit surveys covered more than two hundred seventy caregivers of girls at vaccination sites.

Caregivers who recalled campaign messages on social platforms reported higher vaccination than those who did not. Official delivery counts matched the survey pattern. The gap shrank when scaled to all attending caregivers, but stayed meaningful. Priming audiences before a brief service window appears to help families act fast when doors briefly reopen.
plos-pone-0353186:
Yingxiang Xie and four colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One hospital study of a nerve block used during leg surgery in children with brittle bone disease. These children face high pain risk during operations to fix thigh bone fractures. One hundred twenty-six children were compared: half received an ultrasound-guided fascia iliaca block alongside general anesthesia, and half received general anesthesia alone.

The blocked group kept steadier heart rates and blood pressure during surgery, needed far less opioid painkiller, and woke up faster. Their pain scores in the first twelve hours after surgery were lower, inflammation markers rose less, and nausea and vomiting were less common. The authors conclude the block is a feasible, helpful part of pain control for these fragile patients.
plos-pone-0353486:
Yifan Gong and four colleagues teach machine-learning models to estimate spinal disease activity in ankylosing spondylitis from patients' own answers, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The standard activity score needs a blood test for inflammation, which clinics cannot always run quickly. Their data came from a Chinese registry of nearly four hundred patients, with thirty-four variables spanning clinical measures and questionnaires on pain, stiffness, function, fatigue, and mood.

Ten model combinations were built and tested on held-out patients. The best agreed strongly with the blood-based score. A reliable questionnaire-only estimate could let patients report from home between visits, flagging flares early and sparing stable patients unnecessary trips — though wider validation comes first.
plos-pone-0353786:
Chioma Okpalaora, Stephanie Young, and Tiffany Lee publish a protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026 for studying Canadian pharmacists who manage blood thinners around surgery. Patients on these medicines face a tightrope: stop them and clots threaten, continue them and bleeding threatens. Pharmacists are trained for exactly this balancing act, yet their actual role in Canada is barely documented.

The planned study will interview experienced pharmacists across the country, chosen to span regions and practice settings. Conversations will be transcribed and coded to surface what these pharmacists do, and what helps or blocks them. The authors hope the findings will shape training, service design, and policy for safer surgical care.
plos-pone-0354086:
Mowafy and colleagues, in a 2026 engineering paper, build a flat circuit that combines radio power from four sources into one output for radar. Radar transmitters stack several medium-power units to reach very high peak power, and the combining circuit must handle heat and load without waste. Their design reaches the kilowatt class on a flat board.

The circuit follows a layout called a Gysel combiner, rebuilt here in flat microstrip form, which is cheap and easy to make. The team tuned the design with computer models that account for current flow, heating, and the small errors that creep in during making. The built sample kept signal loss low, kept the four ports well isolated, and held the four signals closely matched in strength and timing across its band. Heat-spreading features dump stray energy safely when outputs mismatch. Radar builders get a compact combiner proven at high power.
plos-pone-0354186:
Candace Alagata and colleagues balanced the carbonate books for coral reefs at seven sites around O'ahu, Hawai'i. A reef grows when corals build limestone faster than other organisms and forces wear it away. Their 2026 census-based study used regional growth rates for each coral type and measured cover, diversity, and surface complexity.

Net production ranged from slightly negative at the weakest site to strongly positive at the best. Overall, production across the island's reefs came out net positive. The team also tested which reef traits best predict growth and erosion balances. Alagata and colleagues say such budgets give managers a single health metric that tracks whether a reef is building or crumbling.
plos-pone-0354386:
Mukesh and colleagues, in a 2026 study, forecast disturbances in the ionosphere, the charged upper layer of the air, during volcanic eruptions. Eruptions send waves up that stir this layer, which can bend satellite signals and throw off GPS positions. Their measure is the total count of electrons along a signal's path, drawn mainly from a station in Indonesia.

The team built a hybrid forecaster that averages two learning methods, one based on decision trees and one on memory networks. They compared it against each part alone and against two classic statistical methods. Six eruptions served as test cases, with data from other latitudes used to check that the model travels. Four error measures judged the forecasts. The authors aim to give satellite and navigation services warning time when an eruption is likely to scramble signals, so operators can plan around the worst hours.
plos-pone-0354486: Li and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on social media and false beliefs. The title states its main point directly: using social media has only a limited effect on what people wrongly believe. That cuts against a common fear that feeds are the main driver of misperceptions. The work adds evidence to debates about platform rules, media habits, and how false claims spread.
plos-pone-0354886:
Hasan Öncül and four colleagues published this 2026 study of blood groups and age-related macular degeneration, a leading cause of vision loss in older adults. Records covered nearly five hundred patients at a specialist center, classed as wet or dry degeneration, with major risk factors like smoking excluded. Blood group and Rh status came from medical files.

The overall blood group distribution differed modestly between the two degeneration types, while Rh status showed no link at all. Öncül calls the clinical meaning uncertain and asks for larger studies that adjust for many factors at once.
plos-pone-0355186:
Yanqin Liu, Miao Zhang, and Yuwen Peng survey doctoral students in 2026. They ask what turns drive into fresh academic work. The setting is research shaped by new AI tools. More than five hundred students took part. They rated self driven drive and pressure driven drive. They also rated having no drive at all.

Both kinds of drive linked to more fresh work. Having no drive linked to less of it. Good resources and support made the good links stronger. Belief in one's own creative skill helped too. Skill with AI tools helped as well. These factors also softened the harm of having no drive. Schools should pair drive support with real resources and sound training.
plos-pone-0355286:
Elena Galitsyna and colleagues work in 2026 on coaxing stem cells from human fat tissue to become bone forming cells. Their method silences a gene that holds back bone growth, using short RNA pieces carried into the cells. They compared several carrier products and several RNA designs to find a mix that entered cells well without harming them.

One common carrier worked best and stayed gentle even at high amounts. With it, the chosen RNA cut the target gene's activity and pushed the cells toward bone formation. The team frames the result as groundwork, with animal studies still needed before any clinical use.
plos-pone-0355386:
Bingtong Wang, Shunchao Wang, and Gaili He model in 2026 how drivers decide to merge onto a freeway when a lane change is forced. Their game based model treats the merging driver and the main road driver as two players weighing speed gains against safety loss. Ideas from the study of risky choice shape how losses loom larger than gains.

Real vehicle path data from two United States freeways were used to tune and test the model. It spotted the observed choices in more than nine cases out of ten. Adding the risk based view improved both accuracy and how well the choices made sense in human terms, the authors report.
plos-pone-0355486:
Paul Mellor, Stephanie Kendall, and Deborah Anderson screen drugs in 2026. They test a large set of approved drugs on a lung cancer. The cancer is hard to treat and has few targeted options. Cells were grown flat in dishes and as small balls. Drugs that killed flat cells were checked for strength. Ball models were checked for shrinkage after treatment.

Cells in balls resisted drugs more than flat cells did. Still, dozens of drugs worked in both models. Four stood out for one key reason. They hit a spreading form harder than its less spreading match. One was a hormone related drug. The other three are used against infections. Those four merit further study, the authors say.
plos-pone-0355686:
Selamawit Gebeyehu and colleagues explore in 2026 why young children in Ethiopia rarely get checks for early development during routine care. Their qualitative work in the Gamo Zone drew on interviews with health workers and parents of children under five. Discussion covered both giving the checks and reaching them.

Workers pointed to weak buildings, scarce funds, limited backing, and gaps in their own training. Parents faced low income, stigma, and local beliefs about delay. Trust in routine child health work and a clear referral route helped. Strengthening frontline skill while building on that trust is presented as the most workable path forward.
plos-pone-0355986: Aksen and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on abuse, impulse control, and drug use. They asked whether poor impulse control changes the strength of the link between sexual abuse and how often people use substances. The data spanned many countries and many gender and sexual identities. Knowing where that link is strongest can help target support to survivors at highest risk.
plos-pone-0356186:
Peng Liu and coauthors published a 2026 animal study in PLOS ONE on easing transport stress in piglets with astragalus polysaccharides, plant sugars from a traditional medicinal root. Transport is among the worst days of a young pig's life: crowding, fasting, vibration, and heat swings spike stress hormones, oxidative damage, and inflammation. Piglets were trucked with no supplement, or a low or high dose, and blood was sampled over the following week.

Unsupplemented piglets showed the expected surge: stress hormones up, reactive oxygen up, a key antioxidant enzyme down, inflammatory signals raised. Supplemented piglets blunted every move on day one, the high dose protecting more strongly, and by days three and seven their values drifted back toward unstressed controls. The supplement is proposed as a feed strategy for welfare around transport, when antibiotics are a poor substitute for prevention.
plos-pone-0356286:
Ville Kailankangas and seven colleagues in Finland profile gene activity in the blood of patients with invasive group A streptococcal disease in this 2026 study. Their aim was to learn why some die weeks after surviving the worst. Forty-five patients were recruited, with blood drawn in the first days after admission and again about a week later. Eight patients died within three months, half of them in the first week.

The gene patterns tied to severe disease looked markedly different between the two draws. At the later timepoint, high activity of genes involved in a form of cell death called necroptosis, together with low activity of immune-presentation genes, was associated with death. The authors caution that the group was small, so these signatures are leads about distinct mechanisms for early and late deaths, not ready predictors.
plos-pone-0356386:
Guangjing Wen and five colleagues follow patients through their first six months on maintenance dialysis to map how psychological resilience evolves, in this 2026 multicenter study from China. Nearly seven hundred people starting regular hemodialysis were assessed seven times, and modeling sorted them into groups whose resilience followed distinct paths. Starting dialysis is a profound life change, and the team wanted to know who adapts and who sinks.

Just over half stayed highly resilient throughout. About a third stayed low and flat, while a smaller group started high but fell fast. The falling group was marked at baseline by depression, anxiety, poor sleep, and more illness burden. The low group added older age, being unmarried, lower income, more hospitalizations, and less activity. The authors argue resilience screening belongs in early dialysis care, with support aimed at the groups most likely to struggle.
plos-pone-0356486:
Tuba Şafak and Ahmet Burak Erdem asked whether a quick bedside ultrasound can judge body fluid levels. Their patients were emergency cases whose blood sodium was dangerously high. Their 2026 study enrolled sixty adults at a Turkish hospital. It measured the width of the large vein returning blood to the heart. It also measured that vein's ratio to the aorta. Readings came before fluids and again three hours into treatment.

Patients whose sodium failed to improve early started with a notably higher vein-to-aorta ratio. The ultrasound measures separated early responders from non-responders fairly well. They were also quite sensitive. Pressure readings from catheters, by contrast, did not differ between groups. The authors suggest ultrasound can add fast, harmless information when deciding how much fluid to give.
plos-pone-0356686:
Oliver Ombeva Malande and a large team report a pilot quality project in Kampala, Uganda. It aimed to strengthen HPV vaccination for teenage girls who live with HIV. These girls face higher risk from the virus, yet uptake and course completion in the city were low and the reasons poorly understood. At two urban HIV treatment centers, several hundred girls were enrolled. They joined surveys on knowledge and attitudes. They also joined discussion groups and a vaccination drive. The team documented the drive's lessons.

Baseline coverage, knowledge gaps, and practical barriers were mapped before and during the drive, with a small number of families declining to join. Malande and colleagues use the pilot to show what a clinic-anchored vaccination push requires, from consent to follow-up, before any wider program for this high-risk group.
plos-pone-0356786:
Jutima Rattanakoch and colleagues tested whether a consumer-grade wearable motion sensor system can measure walking in people with below-knee amputations well enough for clinic use. A research-grade reference served as the yardstick. Their 2026 study fitted thirty-two unilateral amputees with both systems at once. It walked them through repeated trials. Hip, knee, and ankle angles were derived from each system. Trial-to-trial consistency and agreement between the workflows were checked.

Repeatability was excellent nearly everywhere. Agreement between systems was strongest in the forward plane of motion. There, knee and ankle readings differed by only a couple of degrees on average. Agreement ran looser for side-to-side and rotational measures, and for the prosthetic ankle. The transparent, low-cost workflow could let ordinary clinics quantify gait without a motion laboratory.
plos-pone-0356886:
Shuyi Tang and colleagues test whether a sugary coating shed by a yogurt bacterium can slow norovirus, the stomach bug behind much foodborne illness. No solid prevention exists for this virus, so food-based defenses draw interest. In lab dishes, mouse immune cells were infected with a mouse form of the virus, then treated with the bacterial coating, and virus levels and immune gene activity were measured.

Treatment after infection cut the amount of virus released by the cells. Gene readings showed the coating steered the cells toward antiviral alarm signals, boosting the very pathways that fight viruses. Tang and colleagues suggest the coating works by waking up innate defenses rather than attacking the virus directly, a route worth testing in animals next.
plos-pone-0357086:
Xiufang Hou, Yanglan Wang, Fangfang Wang, and Qiuping Li interview nursing undergraduates in a geriatric nursing minor about whether they would work in long-term care homes. Demand for elder care staff is climbing, but hospitals still win graduates' hearts. Fourteen students spoke in depth about their hopes and hesitations, and the team distilled their accounts into themes.

Three themes stood out. Interest in elder care is real but young, fed by the visible market need. Students doubt their own readiness, feeling their skills misfit the setting. And they see the wider support web of government, society, and family as underbuilt, alongside worries about status, workload, and thin career ladders. Hou and colleagues say fixing the pipeline means raising the setting's standing, not just recruiting harder.
plos-pone-0357186:
Georgios Bouloukakis and colleagues use artificial intelligence tools to chart and forecast world publication trends in microsurgery, the fine vessel-and-nerve repair specialty. Research fashion shapes funding and training, yet this field's output had never been projected formally. The team pulled metadata from twenty surgical journals across fifteen years, sorted true microsurgery papers with a keyword system checked against human review, and raced several forecasting models against each other.

From ninety thousand records, about eleven and a half thousand verified microsurgery papers remained, and yearly output grew by well over half across the period. A straight-line projection proved most stable for short horizons in their tests, and forecasts run to the decade's end. Bouloukakis and colleagues offer editors and societies a planning lens, with uncertainty stated openly.
plos-pone-0357286:
Kristina W Dreiås and five colleagues examine how often couples trying to conceive have intercourse, and how quickly pregnancy follows, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The analysis draws on Norway's large mother, father and child cohort, covering more than sixty-four thousand women with planned, naturally conceived pregnancies who reported their habits in the four weeks before conception.

Average time to pregnancy shrank as frequency rose, from just under five months for less than weekly to under four months for more than four times a week. The gain concentrated at the top: the most frequent group had about a sixteen percent higher chance of conceiving in any given cycle than the once or twice weekly reference group. Below that top band, frequencies barely differed from each other. The pattern held after accounting for body weight, prior children, cycle regularity, and endometriosis.
plos-pone-0357586:
Afsaneh Omidimorad leads a community-based survey of what Indigenous adults in Canada's Northwest Territories know about a common virus and its vaccine. The virus spreads through sexual contact and can cause several cancers, yet awareness in these communities had never been measured. Local trained assistants surveyed just over two hundred adults across eleven communities and also gathered open comments on why people skip vaccination.

About half had heard of the virus, and fewer than a third knew a vaccine exists. Schooling shaped awareness most: adults with less education knew far less, and women and younger adults knew more about the vaccine. Only about a quarter of the youngest adults had actually received it. Omidimorad and colleagues say outreach must be local, plain, and built with the communities.
plos-pone-0357886:
Jinze Li led a team of eight authors linking vessel aging and heart failure through one gene, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The gene, HMOX2, may drive shared processes as blood vessels age and hearts fail. The team combined bioinformatics, explainable machine learning, and lab validation to trace that crosstalk.

Li's multimodal approach is notable for testing computer findings in the lab rather than stopping at predictions. A shared driver names a treatment target at the crossing of two major killers. Explainable models also let other scientists judge the reasoning. Aging vessels and failing hearts are usually studied apart; work that joins them can reveal therapies that help both at once, which matters for older patients who have both.
plos-pone-0358986: Heo and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a fast test for pneumonia germs. The BioFire FilmArray panel names viruses and bacteria from one sample in about an hour. The team compared it with standard lab culture in hospital patients with pneumonia. They also judged whether the fast result changed care. Speed matters because the right antibiotic given early saves lives.
plos-pone-0359086: Park and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study using mini gut models grown from pig tissue. They added lipopolysaccharide, a part of bacterial walls that sparks inflammation. Then they watched the gut lining's barrier weaken and its alarm signals change. These organoids let scientists study gut injury without whole-animal tests, and the work may guide care for gut inflammation in pigs and people.
plos-pone-0360186:
Jwel Sharma and Ahmad Abdullah Mahdeen designed a candidate vaccine against Oropouche virus in 2026 using computer based immunology methods. Oropouche virus spreads through biting midges in parts of the Americas and causes feverish illness, with no licensed vaccine available. Their approach, called immunoinformatics, predicts which small pieces of the virus, called epitopes, the immune system is most likely to recognize.

The authors stitch several chosen epitopes into a single multiepitope subunit vaccine design. They then test the design in simulation, docking it against immune receptors and modeling how the body might respond and how stable the construct behaves. Computer first design cannot replace laboratory testing, but it narrows the field of candidates worth building.
pmc-13194186:
Yusuke Yamaga leads a 2026 case report of a brain abscess during leukemia treatment. The patient had acute myeloid leukemia and received CPX-351, a liposomal pairing of two chemotherapy drugs used to induce remission. During repeated fever with low white cell counts, the patient developed neglect of the left side as blood counts recovered.

Brain imaging showed a single abscess in the right parietal lobe. Drainage through a small skull hole grew Bacillus bacteria, and antibiotics followed, then endoscopic removal of the abscess, leading to gradual recovery. Leukemia remission was achieved. The drug's long immune suppression may favor such infections, the authors warn, so new nerve symptoms need fast imaging.
pmc-13194686:
Mohamed ELGabry is first author on a 2026 study of earthquake resilience in Egypt's Great Pyramid of Khufu, built in the Old Kingdom over four thousand years ago. The team ran a noise survey at thirty-seven points. Points covered its chambers, its blocks, and nearby soil. The method compares horizontal and vertical vibration.

The pyramid vibrated at a nearly uniform natural frequency across all its parts, showing it behaves as one coherent structure. That frequency band differed clearly from the surrounding soil's, preventing resonance build-up between ground and building. Shaking grew with height but eased inside the pressure-relieving chambers. Foundation soil scored low for seismic vulnerability, confirming strong bearing capacity.
pmc-13196986:
Qing Ma and colleagues present a 2026 model of a closed-loop supply chain for new products. In such a chain, used goods return for recycling or remaking. The team added two kinds of buyer regret: regret after buying, and regret after swapping an old item for a new one.

Their game model covers makers, sellers, and third-party recyclers over time. It solves for best prices and return effort at each stage. Regret after buying cut sales and long-term profit for makers and sellers. Regret after swapping did the reverse, drawing more buyers in. Both kinds of regret kept products on the market longer. Recyclers' profits were not swayed by either kind of regret.
pmc-13197886:
Pei Pei Heng and colleagues studied how soon smokers light up after waking in Malaysia in 2026. Time to first cigarette is a strong sign of nicotine dependence. A quick first cigarette means deeper dependence and harder quitting, so the team sought its drivers in a national survey.

Data came from a 2023 tobacco survey of more than four thousand adults. About twenty-nine percent of current smokers lit up within thirty minutes of waking. Starting smoking before age eighteen raised the odds of a quick first cigarette. So did never having tried to quit and feeling quitting would be hard. Smokers not worried about health harms had about double the odds. Targeted help may suit these groups.
pmc-13198786:
Abhishek Man Shrestha and colleagues present a 2026 case report on Collet-Sicard syndrome from a skull base tumor. The syndrome knocks out four lower cranial nerves where they exit the skull, harming swallowing, voice, shoulder lift, and tongue motion. Tumors are the usual cause, but benign paragangliomas, nerve-cell tumors, rarely are.

Their patient was a 58-year-old woman with worsening trouble swallowing. Exam showed weakness of all four nerves on the right side. Scans revealed a lobed, strongly enhancing mass centered in the canal for the tongue nerve, reaching into the vein opening and neck artery space. The picture fit a skull base paraganglioma. The authors stress full nerve exams and early scans for such signs.
pmc-13198886:
Dimitrios Karamanidis and colleagues present a 2026 case report on bloody nipple discharge in pregnancy. Bloody discharge often raises fears of cancer or duct growths. In pregnancy it can instead be a benign quirk from richer blood flow and fast duct growth, nicknamed rusty pipe syndrome.

Their patient was a 31-year-old woman in her first pregnancy, at sixteen weeks. Both breasts leaked blood from several ducts, with no lump or pain. Ultrasound showed only normal pregnancy changes, and cell tests were benign. Care stayed watchful, with no invasive steps. Symptoms held steady through pregnancy and cleared ten days after birth. The authors back a stepwise, non-invasive workup that keeps mother and baby safe.
pmc-13202686:
Bacteria in the mouth may mirror lung cancer severity, and a 2026 prospective study headed by Vanessa DeClercq tests that link in surgical patients. The research article profiles saliva microbes from patients undergoing curative surgery for non-small cell lung cancer, using full-length gene sequencing.

Samples from sixty-four patients were compared across cancer stage, tumor subtype, and survival outcomes. Most diversity measures were lower in stage III disease than in stage I, suggesting the oral community thins as cancer advances. Two genera, Haemophilus and Solobacterium, differed reliably in abundance at the later stage. The authors caution that the sample is small and call for confirmation in larger cohorts.
pmc-13206286:
More schooling may genuinely lower some cancer risks, and a 2026 genetic study by Mengdan Miao tests that claim with Mendelian randomization. Using inherited variants as instruments, the analysis probes whether educational attainment causally affects endometrial, ovarian, cervical, and vulvar cancers, and which traits carry the effect.

Higher education was linked to lower risk of endometrial, ovarian, and cervical cancers in the genetic analysis. For endometrial cancer, much of the protection ran through body weight, body fat, insulin, and hormone-related traits that education also influences. Body mass index and age at menopause partly mediated the ovarian finding too, suggesting prevention targets for women with less schooling.
pmc-13240986:
Lange and colleagues at the University of Southern Denmark protocol a school trial trading screen time for face-to-face play. Eighteen Danish schools joined the cluster-randomized Screen-Free Time With Friends study. Children aged nine to eleven and their parents take part. Five components mix classroom activities, family meetings, and community workshops.

Six hundred eighty-five children enrolled at baseline, about half with a parent answering surveys. Parents report peer interaction time through short text-message questionnaires. Follow-ups run past the first year, with a process evaluation tracking how delivery unfolds. Results are expected by the end of 2026.
pmc-13241486:
Guo's team at Southeast sort single cells inside droplets by looks alone, no dye labels. Their system snaps each droplet, spots its contents, and zaps chosen ones aside with current. Liquid-metal electrodes keep the required voltage low and droplets intact. Algae and particles served as test cargo.

Spotting topped 98 percent while sorting captured over 85 percent of targets. Single-cell droplets grew several-fold after one pass. Mixed algae samples sorted nearly as well by shape. Guo pitches the platform for fast screening where labels are awkward or unwanted. The runs used no labels at all.
pmc-13241586:
Ali and a world team review the healing chemistry of the Indian banyan, Ficus benghalensis, a mainstay of folk healing. Parts of the tree carry flavonoids, terpenoids, sterols, and phenolic acids. The authors pull together plant-chemistry, drug-action, and mechanism studies. Listed effects span antioxidant, microbe-fighting, diabetes-fighting, swelling-fighting, and cancer-fighting action.

Bark and leaf extracts killed germs and fungi broadly in lab tests. Effects on diabetes involve blocking starch-splitting enzymes and boosting glucose uptake in cells. Cancer cell lines died through cell death pathways, cycle arrest, and oxidative stress. The review closes with gaps: how dosing behaves in the body, standard dosing, and human trials all remain missing.
pmc-13242386:
Sanjai's team in Ooty review neurotrophin receptors as drug targets against nerve-cell loss. Today's standard drugs top up transmitters while the neuron loss beneath goes on. Nerve growth factor and BDNF signal cell survival through Trk and p75 receptors. The native proteins, however, make poor drugs in practice.

Small mimics aim to trigger the same survival cascades more narrowly. Such drugs could also drive cell change and synaptic plasticity pathways too. The review maps receptor biology from early forms through to downstream signaling. Disease change, not mere symptom masking, is the stated aim. That goal drives the whole review.
pmc-13242486:
Emilio Sebastia-Forcada and co-authors reviewed outcomes of reverse shoulder replacement for locked shoulder dislocations in older patients. Their series appeared in the Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery in 2026. A locked dislocation leaves the ball of the joint jammed against the socket rim rather than seated inside it. The team traced ten patients treated at their center between 2007 and 2023, with an average age of sixty-eight.

Every patient improved on standard shoulder function and pain scores after the reverse prosthesis was implanted. Results were similar whether the dislocation pointed forward or backward, a useful finding given how uncommon the injury is. No complications occurred during or after surgery in this small series. The authors conclude the operation is a workable option for patients over sixty with this injury. They stress, though, that each case still needs individual assessment before choosing it.
pmc-13242586:
Wenhua Hu and colleagues investigated whether fat-related hormones help cause lung cancer, focusing on the leptin receptor. Their paper appeared in Cancer Informatics in 2026. They combined Mendelian randomization, which uses gene variants as natural experiments, with tissue staining and cell experiments. Six adipokines were tested against lung cancer and its subtypes using large public genetic datasets.

Only the leptin receptor, LEPR, showed a causal link, and only with lung squamous cell carcinoma. Tumors of that type carried more LEPR than nearby normal tissue, and higher levels tracked with worse survival. In two cell lines, silencing LEPR slowed growth and invasion and pushed cells toward death. No other adipokine showed a similar association. The authors propose LEPR as both a risk factor worth watching and a possible drug target for this lung cancer subtype.
pmc-13247086:
Liu, Yang, Wang, and co-authors report a switchable chemical route to two prized ring systems in this 2026 Nature Communications paper. Nitrogen-bridged bicyclic scaffolds are valued in drug design as rigid stand-ins for common rings, with better drug-like properties, but each scaffold usually needed its own synthesis. The team found that a palladium-catalyzed reaction joining cyclobutenols and amines with carbon monoxide could be steered either way.

Changing only the ligand on the catalyst flipped the product between the two ring cores, from identical starting materials. The method tolerated varied substrates and was used to build twenty derivatives of bioactive molecules. The authors present it as a modular platform for generating scaffold diversity, a persistent bottleneck in designing new nitrogen-containing drug candidates.
pmc-13247986:
Chen and co-authors charted two pig viruses across China in this 2026 Transboundary and Emerging Diseases surveillance study. Porcine circoviruses 2 and 3 cause reproductive failure, wasting, and complex disease in swine worldwide. The team tested more than eight thousand clinical samples from twenty-eight provinces collected between 2022 and 2025, then sequenced hundreds of viral genomes to reconstruct evolution and spread.

Circovirus 2 was far more prevalent, peaking in autumn and reaching its highest loads in systemic wasting cases, and its 2d genotype overwhelmingly dominated nationwide. Type 3 ran quieter, favoring swabs, semen, and milk, with the 3c lineage ahead. Both viruses evolve mainly under purifying selection, and spread patterns differed: type 2 radiated from a Hebei hub while type 3 diffused from several centers. The maps give vaccine and control programs current targets.
pmc-13249986:
Surmann and co-authors checked whether a family of matrix proteins predicts ovarian cancer survival, in a 2026 study. Small leucine-rich proteoglycans help build the scaffolding around cells, and laboratory work had hinted they steer tumor behavior. The team measured their gene activity in ovarian cancer cell lines and public cell data, then compared activity levels with patient survival curves for the serous form of the disease.

For most family members, lower gene activity went with better prognosis, the opposite of a simple tumor-promoter story. Network analysis linked the proteins to known drivers of tumor spread in other cancers. The authors suggest the family as candidates for deeper study, while stressing that treatment relevance needs functional proof.
pmc-13250186:
Joly and co-authors map what research says about doctors' emotional skills and the quality of their medical reasoning. Their 2026 BMJ Open scoping review defines emotional competence as the ability to spot, understand, express, manage, and use emotions. The team searched three major databases plus hand-found sources, with no date limits.

From more than twelve thousand records screened, ninety-eight studies met the rules for inclusion. Emotional skill helped most with handling uncertainty, quick intuitive judgment, and performance during life-threatening emergencies. Benefits were strongest under heavy stress, likely because calming emotions frees mental capacity for reasoning. Evidence outside emergencies, and evidence for patient outcomes, stayed thin, which the authors flag as the key gap for future work.
pmc-13250386:
Isoda and co-authors test whether a clinical decision support tool lifts medical students' quiz performance. Their 2026 Journal of General and Family Medicine pilot ran online across Japan in November 2024. Student teams first answered case questions using any resource except UpToDate, then answered again using only that tool under tighter time limits.

Seventeen teams finished, and average scores rose modestly in the second round. Confidence in using the decision support resource climbed sharply, while confidence in other resources barely moved. The authors caution that the volunteer sample was small, so the results may not generalize to all students. They call for studies on real learning outcomes and how such tools fit into medical curricula.
pmc-13252786:
Hassan Gharayagh Zandi and colleagues test a therapy-based activity programme for inactive teen girls in this 2026 trial. Many adolescents stall on exercise through low confidence and discomfort, and the programme drew on Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, which builds flexible, value-led action.

The trial enrolled 132 girls aged 13 to 18 who were physically inactive, split between the programme and a control group. Seven sessions worked through the therapy's core processes. Afterwards, the programme group showed stronger inner motivation and sense of choice, less deadened motivation, and better activity levels, fitness, and both felt and measured movement skill. The authors back adding such programmes to schools and communities.
pmc-13252886:
Anirudh Gudlavalleti and colleagues review training for community health workers in diabetes care in this 2026 paper. Poorer countries carry most of the world's type 2 diabetes and lean on community workers to fill care gaps, but whether training those workers actually helps was murky.

The team screened over 3,000 studies and found only four solid enough to include, covering about a thousand patients. One trial showed a small but real fall in a long-term blood sugar marker, though sugar control was not its main goal and most patients had near-normal levels. Other studies showed non-significant falls. Bias concerns were moderate to serious. The authors call the evidence limited and indirect at best.
pmc-13253186:
Hidalgo-Arteaga and co-authors design surfaces that absorb terahertz waves from one side while letting them pass from the other. Their 2026 iScience study builds arrays of tiny tilted germanium disks and pillars that hide special resonances called quasi-bound states. Terahertz control matters for sensing and future communications.

At a matched angle, one disk design absorbed nearly all incoming terahertz light of one polarization, while staying transparent from the opposite angle. Pillar arrays reached a bit over half absorption for the other polarization under similar conditions. The surfaces also acted as sharp polarization filters, passing one polarization almost perfectly while blocking the other. The authors outline fabrication by angled growth and ways to tune the working angle actively.
pmc-13253586:
Sudhir Kothari and colleagues follow a stubborn dizziness condition in this 2026 study. Persistent postural-perceptual dizziness leaves people feeling unsteady for months, driven by the brain's mishandling of balance signals rather than ear damage, and it often travels with anxiety or depression.

Seventy-five patients at their clinic were assessed with disability and mood questionnaires plus a balance platform test. Nearly nine in ten had a mental health condition, most often anxiety with depression, yet balance machine scores were mostly normal despite strong felt disability. After three months of balance retraining, talking therapy, and low-dose antidepressants where mood scores warranted, disability and mood scores improved dramatically. Clear explanation by the neurologist anchored the package.
pmc-13253786:
Cristian Mendico offers a 2026 method for mapping how the brain routes a response to a stimulus. Past models measured the cost of moving activity on a fixed network but did not infer the routing map itself. Mendico combines brain scan signals, electrical recordings, and fiber maps to set start and target activity.

A branched transport model, which favors shared neural highways, then infers the route map. Maps built this way aligned with brain anatomy, and costs that follow fiber direction reshaped the routes versus plain baselines. Adding a dynamics model also showed trade-offs between route efficiency and how well activity can be controlled.
pmc-13253986:
Javeria Taj and co-authors review osteosarcopenia in older adults in a 2026 narrative review. The syndrome joins osteoporosis, weak bones, with sarcopenia, loss of muscle mass and strength. The team searched PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar for work on its causes, diagnosis, and treatment.

The syndrome affects about 18 to 20 percent of older adults, more often women, and raises risk of falls, fractures, and death. Shared drivers include long-term swelling, hormone decline, and poor nutrition. Care centers on resistance training, protein and vitamin D, and bone drugs, yet no treatment targets both parts at once, a key gap the authors flag.
pmc-13255386:
Alexandre Klopp and colleagues test a kidney marker in the very old in a 2026 cohort study. Creatinine in the blood is a standard kidney measure, but muscle loss and frailty in very old patients may blunt its meaning. The team studied 952 intensive care patients aged 90 or more in Hamburg between 2008 and 2019.

Death rates were 28.5 percent in hospital, 42.2 percent by 90 days, and 57.1 percent by one year. Admission creatinine did not predict in-hospital death, but higher values did predict death at 90 days and one year. Removing the kidney part of a standard risk score did not weaken it.
pmc-13256486:
Peter Baldwin and co-authors report a 2026 single-arm trial of Healthy Mind, a self-guided web program for mental health made for people with intellectual disability. Single-arm means every participant got the program, with no comparison group. People in this group face rates of mental illness up to three times higher than others, yet often miss out on care. Australian residents aged sixteen and over with mild-to-moderate anxiety or depression symptoms took part.

Eighty people enrolled, with a mean age of 27.8 years, and 61 percent chose a supporter to help them. The program did not significantly change depression, anxiety, distress, or functioning scores. Use was low: 42.5 percent never opened it, and users finished a median of seven modules. Still, the trial showed online recruitment and follow-up can work for this group.
pmc-13261086:
Swekchha Adhikari and co-authors report a 2026 pediatric case in which low blood counts revealed a blocked portal vein. Extrahepatic portal venous obstruction blocks the vein carrying blood to the liver. It is a leading cause of high portal pressure in children, usually showing as gut bleeding.

Their patient was a 13-year-old girl with pancytopenia, an enlarged spleen, and easy tiredness, but no gut bleeding or liver disease. Her bone marrow was underactive without cancer, first suggesting a primary blood disorder. Tests excluded nutritional, infectious, autoimmune, and cancer causes. Abdominal imaging then showed the main portal vein was not visible. A web of collateral vessels had replaced it, confirming long-standing obstruction. Endoscopy found grade III esophageal varices, treated with band ligation and non-selective beta-blockers. The authors urge imaging whenever a child has low counts with an enlarged spleen.
pmc-13262586:
Mohammad Ali Alshrouf charts three decades of osteoarthritis in Germany and projects two more. Drawing on Global Burden of Disease data in this 2026 analysis, he tracks new cases, total cases, and years lived with disability. Aging, growth, and true rate changes are teased apart.

Between nineteen ninety and twenty twenty-one, cases climbed by roughly a third to a half across measures. Men's burden rose faster in relative terms, yet women still carried far more cases in absolute numbers. Knee osteoarthritis dominated, passing seven million sufferers. Population aging drove most growth, and forecasts see the load swelling through twenty forty-one.
pmc-13263286:
Akif Mirioglu and co-authors explore a protein as a warning marker for bone tumor return in a 2026 journal article. Giant cell tumor of bone is locally aggressive and often comes back after surgery, but predictors are weak. They stained tumor tissue from 34 patients treated with scraping surgery between 2002 and 2016, scoring the protein HtrA1 separately in giant cells and in single-nucleus cells.

Patients whose giant cells scored high but single-nucleus cells scored low had the highest return rate, above 70 percent. Other patterns returned in roughly a third of cases, and the sole patient in the remaining pattern had no return. The differences were not statistically significant, so the authors call the signal preliminary and in need of larger studies.
pmc-13263486:
Xuming Zhang and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on placing a heat-expandable metal stent in narrowed ureters after kidney transplantation. The ureter is the tube carrying urine from kidney to bladder, and narrowing can damage the graft. Six women received a Memokath 051 stent using scopes passed from both directions at once.

All stents were placed successfully, with operations averaging about one hundred seventy-three minutes and hospital stays under nine days. Kidney swelling from backed-up urine eased in every patient, and kidney function improved measurably. One stent shifted and was repositioned, and one patient had repeated urinary infections controlled with antibiotics. All stents stayed open at final follow-up.
pmc-13264386:
Bell Raj Eapen, Oladimeji M Adaramewa, and Xiaoqing Li present a 2026 paper on Clinical Quality Language, a code used to state health care rules. That code works well on neat, coded data but not on free text notes. Their fix puts a large language model inside the run loop.

They changed a common CQL engine so it calls the model when a rule points to free text records, while coded data runs as before. Tests with two local models gave accuracy of 72 percent and 93 percent. The full tool is free and open source, with settings for model, prompts, and controls. The authors say this widens CQL use while keeping old rules intact.
pmc-13264986:
Daiji Nagayama and co-authors wrote a 2026 study on whether albumin, the main blood protein, predicts arteries stiffening over time in the general Japanese population. Low albumin links to heart disease death, and loss of lean muscle mass may be part of the path. They used three years of health screening data from more than 5,000 urban adults.

Among blood proteins, albumin tied most strongly to a stiffness index of the arteries. Each standard rise in albumin linked to lower odds of high stiffness, even after counting age and classic risk factors. People with higher starting albumin stiffened less over three years, a pattern not seen for age groups. Change in lean body mass carried a small part, 3.4 percent, of that link. The authors suggest nutrition care that builds muscle may help prevent vessel disease.
pmc-13266586:
Mehmet Okçu and colleagues wrote a 2026 study on safe needle depth for injections near the shoulder blade. Such shots treat trigger points, tight painful spots in muscle. A needle placed too deep could pierce the lining around the lung and collapse the lung.

The team read chest CT scans from 1,015 patients treated between 2017 and 2019. They measured skin-to-muscle and skin-to-lung-lining depths at four points near the shoulder blade. Depths differed by age, sex, and body size. In women the lung lining was closer to the skin at most points. The authors give tables to guide safe shot depth for each patient group.
pmc-13270586:
Simon Ueberschaar led a 2026 journal article on patients with allergy to wasp or bee venom who turn down venom immunotherapy. That therapy is a long course of shots. It lowers the risk of a severe sting reaction. The patients had tested positive and been advised to take the treatment.

Of 1,163 treatment candidates, 271, or 23.3 percent, declined or delayed for at least a year, and full records were reviewed for 166 of them. Those declining were more often female and had milder first sting reactions. Most cited time cost or feeling treatment was not needed. Over a median five years, 39.2 percent were stung again, and 13 of 65 re-stung patients had a severe allergic reaction.
pmc-13271486:
Saul Martin-Rodriguez is lead author of a 2026 Policy Forum article on what it calls a data transparency crisis in research. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses, studies that pool other studies, underpin clinical guidelines and health policy, yet reviewers often cannot access the underlying data sets or analysis code behind them.

Forced to rely on patchy summary numbers, reviewers use guesses and uncheckable assumptions that can distort results and mislead care decisions, the authors argue, citing past cases such as hormone replacement therapy. Despite widespread data-sharing policies, compliance stays low and enforcement weak. The article calls for enforceable sharing rules, with clearer checks built into journal editorial workflows.
pmc-13271586:
Kun He is lead author of a 2026 cross-sectional comparative study on using large language models, boosted with authoritative textbooks, for public health medical education in Tibet. The region, formally the Xizang Autonomous Region, is high-altitude and low-resource. Old textbooks lack accessibility and interaction, while general AI models can invent facts in specialised medicine.

In the first stage, four public models, from OpenAI, Google, DeepSeek, and Tencent, answered an 80-question benchmark on high-altitude public health, written by specialists. Each question was asked three times, giving 960 outputs, and two blinded panels of eight physicians scored the first replies for completeness, accuracy, clarity, and relevance. A second stage tested adding textbook retrieval to the models.
pmc-13272586:
Z. L. Abo-Shanab leads a 2026 study that changes waste polystyrene so it can improve bitumen, the sticky binder in asphalt. Plain polystyrene is stiff and low in polarity, so it mixes poorly and stores badly. The team grafted acrylic acid onto it, then reacted it with an amine to make a new form.

Tests confirmed the new groups were added, and the changed polymer bonded well with bitumen through hydrogen bonds. At 7 percent by weight, storage stability was much better than with plain polystyrene, and elastic recovery rose from 25 percent to 55 percent. Resistance to rutting also improved, raising the grade from 70 to 76.
pmc-13273286:
Joel Pires leads a 2026 study identifying a brain enzyme called STEP as a developmental brake on synapse formation. Synapses are the junctions where nerve cells pass signals.
