Balance between adding and removing phosphate groups on proteins controls how synapses form and mature, and STEP removes such groups.

Suppressing STEP, by genes or by drugs, promoted synapse formation through a mechanism on the sending side of the junction. That reveals a previously unrecognized role for STEP in early circuit assembly, beyond its known role in weakening mature synapses. The authors suggest STEP as a possible target for correcting synapse problems in Fragile X syndrome.
pmc-13274186:
Mariano Paracuellos wrote a 2026 journal article measuring dialect change across Almería in southeastern Spain through local bird names. The province sits where eastern Andalusian and Murcian speech meet, but that claim had rarely been tested with numbers. He analyzed folk bird names recorded across the province's seven districts.

Name patterns split the districts into southwestern and northeastern groups, matching the pull of neighboring Granada and Murcia. The Filabres Mountains may have limited mixing between the two sides. A second split ran coastal versus inland: coastal districts named more species, while inland districts kept more varied names per species. He links both patterns to landscape, habitat variety, and how people historically moved and talked.
pmc-13274586:
Koomok Lee and colleagues present a 2026 journal article demonstrating voltage-controlled magnetism in tiny dots of a special ceramic. The material, bismuth ferrite with cobalt substituted in, is both ferroelectric and weakly magnetic at room temperature, and its magnetism is yoked to its electric polarization. Flipping one should flip the other, promising memory chips written with voltage instead of current.

Working on a structure just 190 nanometers wide, the team scanned it with a biased probe tip and watched both orders with two microscope methods. The polarization flipped from net-down to net-up, and both sideways and vertical components of the magnetization reversed with it. They call this direct proof of full electric-field magnetization reversal at device scale.
pmc-13274786:
Qingtao Yang and a large team present a 2026 journal article on melatonin protecting rats from erectile problems caused by a scrambled body clock. The team disrupted rats' light cycles with rapid two-hour light and dark alternation for four weeks. Some rats also received daily melatonin, the hormone that normally rises at night, at low or high doses.

Clock disruption measurably weakened erectile function and damaged the spongy penile tissue, while melatonin preserved both. The harm ran through oxidative stress, which switched on a fiery form of cell death called pyroptosis. Melatonin revived a protective pathway, Nrf2 and HO-1, cutting the stress and the cell death. A separate antioxidant reproduced the benefit in human vessel cells.
pmc-13274886:
Siti Watiqah Samsuddin and colleagues report a 2026 journal article charting how four mood-stabilizing drugs were prescribed in British primary care from 1995 to 2018. The drugs, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, lithium, and valproate, treat epilepsy and psychiatric illness. Using anonymized records from a national primary care database, the team tracked new starts and overall use by age and sex.

Carbamazepine prescribing fell sharply from the early 2000s, while lamotrigine starts climbed from 2005 and led among adults under forty by 2018. Valproate starts dropped steeply, though its ongoing use in younger men stayed comparatively high. Lithium remained the least prescribed throughout. Prescribing of all four ran higher in more deprived areas, for both new starts and ongoing use.
pmc-13275786:
José Ángel Martínez-Huertas and Emilio Ferrer present a 2026 methods article on tracking how several traits change over time. Studies of growth often follow different age groups for short spans, then stitch the results together. That design leaves much data missing by plan, which makes full growth curves hard to estimate.

The authors test a mixed-effects model, a method that separates shared patterns from person-level and trait-level differences. Computer simulations varied group sizes and curve shapes. The model recovered the shared growth curve and trait-specific curves well. Its error ranges for trait differences were wide, yet still useful for decisions. With only a few readings per person, it forecast full curves for each person and trait. A real example used data on children's thinking skills.
pmc-13275986:
Qiong Li and co-authors report a 2026 study comparing two MRI methods for stomach cancer. Both methods use diffusion-weighted imaging, which tracks how water moves in tissue to reveal tumors. Judging how deeply a tumor has grown, called T staging, guides surgery, so image quality matters.

The newer method, with a long technical name shortened to FOCUS-MUSE, was tested against the standard method in patients with proven stomach cancer. Two radiologists scored the images, and the team measured clarity with several ratios. The new method produced sharper images and clearer tumor outlines across one hundred seventy-seven patients. Among patients with confirmed stages, it staged tumors correctly far more often than the standard method. Readers also agreed with each other well, the authors report.
pmc-13276186:
Shahenda Khalaf and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on whether a rock layer in Egypt's Western Desert could be a source of oil and gas. The Khatatba Formation, from the Jurassic period, holds dark shale in its Upper Safa Member. Source rocks cook organic matter into hydrocarbons over geologic time.

The team examined one hundred rock samples from four wells in the Obaiyed Field. Lab tests measured minerals and total organic carbon, the fuel content of the rock. Carbon levels averaged near two percent, a moderate to very good richness. Heating tests showed the organic matter is mature and mostly gas-prone. A method that estimates carbon from well logs matched lab values closely. The authors call the layer a fair to good source rock tied neatly to nearby reservoir sands.
pmc-13277386:
Amine Aiddi leads a 2026 study of dangerous Escherichia coli bacteria in Moroccan waters. Some E. coli strains resist many antibiotics and cause severe infections worldwide. The team collected water from seven rivers and three wastewater plants in eight cities between February and June 2024 and sequenced the full genomes of recovered bacteria.

Twenty-two isolates yielded thirteen strain types, led by three globally known high-risk clones. Most carried a gene that breaks down key antibiotics, and five carried genes that defeat last-resort drugs. The study is the first genomic proof that such clones circulate in Moroccan waters. Stronger joint human, animal, and environment monitoring is urgent, the authors warn.
pmc-13278586:
Sanjoy Kumar Mukharjee leads a 2026 genome study of a salt-tolerant bacterium that helps rice grow, tested as a candidate for climate-resilient farming. From 283 bacteria collected around rice roots, the team selected strain OSNO4 for deep profiling. Lab tests showed it frees phosphate and potassium, makes a plant growth hormone, fixes nitrogen, and forms protective biofilms.

The strain tolerated high salt, drought-like conditions, heat, and a wide acidity range, and it suppressed a rice fungus in dishes. Its genome held about four thousand five hundred predicted genes, including clusters for helpful compounds. Under salt stress, treated rice seeds germinated far better and grew stronger roots and shoots. Safety tests suggested a low-risk profile.
pmc-13279386:
Anne Neubert and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review, part two, of blast injury patterns. Part two covers landmines, unexploded ordnance, meaning old shells and bombs that still can burst, and terror attacks with suicide bombings. The team searched two databases in March 2025 for studies of blast harm in troops and civilians of all ages.

The full review held one hundred twenty six studies. This part weighs forty five terror studies and twelve mine studies. Mine studies from 1980 to 2006 held more than thirteen thousand people, mostly men in poor, post war lands. Leg harm and loss were most common, then eye harm. Terror studies held more than twelve thousand victims, mostly civilians. Limb harm led there as well. Clear patterns help medics plan triage and gear.
pmc-13279486:
Jeffrey Li and colleagues report a 2026 pilot study of cocoa extract in a zebrafish model of autism. Autism is a brain development condition with few drug options. Plant phenols, health linked plant compounds, may guard nerve cells. The team used valproic acid, a drug known to cause autism like traits in fish, to build the model. Cocoa extract rich in a phenol called epicatechin was the test treatment.

Fish got the drug, cocoa, both, or no treatment in four groups. The drug alone caused hyperactive acts and grave gut shape harm. Cocoa given with the drug eased both the acts and the gut harm. Broad chemical and protein scans showed drug linked breaks in nerve signals, cell power and cell defence. Cocoa moved many of those marks back toward normal. Early fish proof backs wider tests of food based nerve guards.
pmc-13280586:
Tarek Zieneldien offers a 2026 poem, The dose divided, on fractionated radiation therapy. Radiation comes in weekdays, hope measured out in calibrated light. Every morning, the body returns in nervous posture to the same unadorned white room and the same mask cooled against the face. The machine knows how to divide harm from healing so finely they nearly share a name. She lies while the beam is delivered, trespassing in exactness, as if the body could be persuaded one small portion at a time.

In the hall, an old woman folds her appointment card in something like a prayer. Outside, deadly nightshade petals gather in the gutter, purple as a bruise. She thinks of Avicenna crossing sandstorms by memory and vow, his companion lost on the road. By Friday, the chart calls it a fraction and the body calls it return. Fractals and an elsewhere of health close the poem.
pmc-13280686:
Stefanie Linnhoff and colleagues wrote a 2026 letter replying to a comment on their work on mental fatigue. Their study had pointed to a brain wave measure as a sign of fatigue. The sign appeared in both multiple sclerosis and long COVID, two very unlike illnesses. A fellow scholar praised the work but raised doubts about who was studied and what the sign means.

The authors agree that their group was small and alike in background, all from one center. They stress that the sign is an early clue, not a firm test. They also agree that fatigue can arise by unlike paths in unlike people. Wider and more mixed groups, they say, must test the sign next.
pmc-13280786:
Ayça Muhterem and colleagues tested an extra toothbrush in a 2026 study with dental students. A plain hand brush can miss plaque, the sticky film on teeth, in tight spots. Forty healthy students took part in a split-mouth test. For two weeks they brushed one side with a plain brush only. On the other side they added a small brush with one tuft of bristles. A blinded checker scored plaque and gum health.

Both sides got cleaner and gums got healthier in two weeks. Plaque fell by about the same amount on both sides. Gum health, though, improved more on the side with the extra brush. More than four in five students said they would keep using it. The authors say the small brush is a cheap add-on for hard-to-reach spots.
pmc-13280986:
Kefiyalew Jote and colleagues mapped gene variety in malaria parasites in a 2026 study from southern Ethiopia. Malaria still burdens health and income where it spreads fast. The parasite's variety helps it dodge the immune system and adapt to drugs. The team took blood from two hundred patients at clinics in two towns. Gene tests sorted the parasites by two surface protein genes, which come in many forms.

About seven in ten patients carried a single parasite strain. Tests found more than one hundred distinct forms of the first gene and even more of the second. Two form families turned up most often. The wide mix shows the parasite pool there is rich and shifting. The authors say such maps help track how malaria changes and how well control plans work.
pmc-13281886:
Qi Xu and colleagues reviewed tiny cell sacs in psoriasis in a 2026 paper. Psoriasis is a lasting skin disease of red, scaly patches driven by immune crosstalk. Cells trade messages in small sacs called exosomes. In sore skin, those sacs carry code scraps and proteins that skew immune cells. They fan skin cell swelling and keep a key immune loop running. The review follows the sacs from villains to tools.

Blood sac patterns may flag disease activity without a biopsy. They may also split plain psoriasis from its joint form. Sacs from stem cells, plants, and germs are being tested as cell-free care. Loading cargo, dressing their skins, and smart needle patches aim to sharpen them. Blocks remain: no standard making, unclear active parts, and thin trial proof. The authors urge shared rules and strict trials.
pmc-13281986:
Giovanna Pestana Silva and colleagues checked hearts in dogs of three body weights in a 2026 study. Dog obesity is rising and strains the whole body, yet its heart effects are murky. Thirty owned dogs were split into lean, overweight, and obese groups of ten. Each dog had a physical exam, a heart tracing, and a heart scan. Body scores and belly measures were logged. The team compared the groups on every measure.

Obese dogs panted and tired far more than lean ones. Their heart tracings showed longer signal times, a sign of slower conduction. The left upper chamber ran wider in obese dogs, and valve flaws were more common. Belly fat share rose as the waist-to-chest pattern shifted. Pump strength scores, though, did not differ between groups. The authors say fat reshapes the dog heart early, before frank failure. Routine heart checks for heavy dogs are their advice.
pmc-13282286:
Karla Susanna Tavares Grangeiro Belém and co-authors report a 2026 lab study on a new compound that may help antibiotics beat resistant Staphylococcus aureus. That bacterium pumps many drugs back out of its cells using efflux pumps, a key resistance trick. The team made a hydrazone compound, a type of chemical built here from the drug hydralazine, and tested it against pump-carrying strains.

Alone, the compound did not kill the bacteria at the doses tried. It also lowered the survival of immune cells as dose rose, a safety flag. Paired with antibiotics, though, it cut the dose needed in one strain and sharply lowered the dose of a pump test dye in another. Computer docking suggested it sits in the pumps' binding sites, blocking their action. The authors see promise as a resistance breaker to restore old antibiotics.
pmc-13282386:
Rehab Alharbi and co-authors report a 2026 study identifying a gene switch that marks a harmful blood vessel pattern in pulmonary arterial hypertension. That disease narrows lung arteries and is currently incurable. Vessel lining cells get injured, then repair excessively, worsening the narrowing. The switch, called KLF6, was higher in human disease tissue and in lab models than in healthy controls.

Switching KLF6 on reshaped gene activity in vessel lining cells, driving repair and new vessel growth. Its effects differed from two related switches. It also pushed neighbouring muscle cells in vessel walls to multiply, an effect blunted by two existing drugs. Data set and tissue mapping analyses found high KLF6 in lining cells, their precursor cells, and in a related lung condition of infants. The authors describe KLF6 as an orchestrator of the overgrown vessel pattern. They suggest it could become a target for slowing the disease.
pmc-13282486:
Seong Dae Yun and co-authors describe a 2026 imaging methods study on a new brain scan sequence that fixes a mismatch between functional and anatomical MRI images. Functional MRI, which maps brain activity, uses a fast method that warps images through magnetic field unevenness. Anatomical scans warp differently, so aligning the two is error-prone. An earlier sequence copied the functional warp into the anatomical scan, easing alignment but bending the reference image.

Correcting that bend needed extra data in the reverse direction, which lengthened scans. The new sequence captures the reversed data inside the same single acquisition, adding no scan time. The work focuses on technical build and validation for very fine, submillimetre functional imaging at high field strength. The authors say distortion-matched anatomy with built-in correction should sharpen where activity is localised in the cortex.
pmc-13282686:
Xun Wu and co-authors present a 2026 study on deaths and disability from fatty liver disease driven by high fasting blood sugar, in China and worldwide, from 1990 to 2021. The liver condition, shortened to MASLD, is now the commonest chronic liver disease. Using Global Burden of Disease data, the team tracked deaths and healthy years lost, then projected trends to 2046 with an age-period model.

In 2021 this cause accounted for about ten thousand deaths and over two hundred thousand lost healthy years worldwide. Age-adjusted rates rose significantly over the three decades, faster globally than in China. Burden was higher in men and climbed with age, peaking past eighty. Forecasts show absolute deaths and disability still rising by 2046 in both China and the world, driven by population ageing, even as age-adjusted rates are expected to fall, especially in women.
pmc-13282886:
Severe infections tied to modern myeloma immune therapies are pooled and weighed in a 2026 meta-analysis from Federico Spataro's team. The therapies include bispecific T-cell engagers and CAR-T cells for relapsed myeloma. Severe infection is a major safety concern in routine care.

The review pooled 16 real-world studies with 2,097 patients in total. About one in four patients had a severe infection classed as grade 3 or 4 in severity. Rates were higher with bispecific drugs than with CAR-T therapy in pooled results. Rates also varied by drug target. The authors stress careful infection control when these treatments are used outside trials.
pmc-13284086:
Fear of new foods ties to narrower diets in type 2 diabetes in a 2026 pilot study from Turkiye by Merve Sena Topkaya and colleagues. Food neophobia means avoiding unfamiliar foods and resisting new tastes. That reluctance may undercut varied eating and treatment follow-through.

Face-to-face surveys covered 35 patients and 35 healthy people at one hospital clinic. Scores captured food fear, diet variety, and treatment adherence in both groups. Higher fear scores linked to lower diet variety among patients with diabetes. Poorer treatment adherence also tracked with higher fear scores in patients. Fear levels alone did not split patients from healthy peers. Tackling food fear may widen diets.
pmc-13284486:
Yun Ouyang and colleagues map research trends on mitochondrial DNA and atherosclerosis in a 2026 bibliometric analysis. Papers from 2004 to 2025 were drawn from the Web of Science Core Collection and charts were built with CiteSpace software. The team tracked authors, institutions, and keywords to see how the field has grown and shifted.

A total of 341 papers were included, with yearly output rising over time in the authors summary. Ten keyword clusters emerged, led by oxidative stress, mitochondrial DNA copy number, and vascular disease themes. Work has moved from basic mechanisms toward clinical use. The authors call for stronger team links and deeper pathway work to support translation into care.
pmc-13284686:
Sang Eun Ha and co-authors test a plant extract on human skin cells in a 2026 laboratory study. Extract from Belamcanda chinensis rhizomes is rich in polyphenols, compounds linked to antioxidant action. The team named five main polyphenols by liquid methods and tested how the extract calmed inflamed keratinocyte cells.

In cells stirred by bacterial toxin, the extract lowered key inflammation drivers such as COX-2 and iNOS and shifted STAT3 and NF-kappaB signaling. Docking work showed the five compounds bound strongly to NF-kappaB targets. The authors conclude the extract shows antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects in cells, giving a base for drug work, though human testing has not been done.
pmc-13284886:
Yashendra Sethi and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, links between geomagnetic activity during auroras and human health, with a focus on the brain. Shifts in Earth magnetic fields have been tied to varied body and mind outcomes. The team searched peer-reviewed work in PubMed and Google Scholar on surgery, nerve, and mental health settings.

Reported links included more seizures in epilepsy, poor sleep that slows recovery, and thinking problems that could affect consent. Stress and anxiety may also rise during magnetic storms, adding risk after surgery, notably in older patients. The authors call for deeper work on mechanisms and for care guidance that accounts for geomagnetic conditions.
pmc-13285186:
Yunfei Wang and co-authors map gene splicing faults in esophageal cancer in a 2026 data study. Faulty splicing makes many protein forms from one gene and can drive tumor growth, yet its full pattern in this cancer was unclear. The team pooled gene data from five public sets and used network and motif tools to link splicing events to cell processes and drug response.

Thousands of changed splicing events were found, mostly in protein-coding and long non-coding RNAs in the pooled analysis. Events tied to cell cycle, immune response, fuel use, spread, and cell death. Eighty-five binding proteins stood out as hub factors. Two drugs, bortezomib and BI-2536, tracked strongly with the fault pattern and curbed cell growth in checks.
pmc-13285586:
A back pelvic joint slipped out while the front ring stayed whole in a 2026 case report by Leonardo Comerlatto and co-authors. Such back-only damage is vanishingly rare, since hard pelvic crashes usually break the weaker front first. A 15-year-old boy was hit in the back by a heavy metal frame and arrived with one-sided back joint dislocation.

Doctors eased the joint back shut and pinned it with a single thick screw through skin. Current grading schemes do not quite hold this pattern, the authors note. They urge careful checks of front ring soundness in high-energy back pelvic trauma, since missing a hidden break can doom fixation. The case adds a new pattern to the record.
pmc-13285986:
Nozomu Motono and colleagues report surgery for a chest infection in a man with advanced lung cancer in their 2026 case report. The 75-year-old had just learned that a squamous tumor filled his left lower lung lobe and nearby nodes. Three weeks after the biopsy that proved the cancer, fever signaled pus gathering in the space around the lung.

Surgeons used keyhole chest surgery to strip the infected peel from the lung, a step called decortication. Fluid tests grew MRSA, a drug-resistant staph germ, so antibiotics switched to a drug that covers it. Tubes came out a week after surgery, and he went home about a month after the operation. Scans six weeks later showed no return of the infection, which cleared the way for the planned cancer chemotherapy to begin.
pmc-13287186:
Luise Geithner and Michael Wagner used survey data in 2026 from very old adults in Germany to ask whether feeling disoriented by social change helps explain who stays socially active. Their model linked money, schooling, health, values, and relationships to participation, with that sense of disorientation placed in between.

All the main factors related to participation directly except income. Income instead worked largely through insecurity linked to feeling worse off than others. Schooling and health also showed small indirect paths. The authors conclude that support for participation in very old age should address material insecurity and lost orientation, not only practical resources and health limits.
pmc-13288886:
Alba Torne-Ruiz and colleagues gather review proof on hard veins in adults in 2026. Their work is an umbrella review. It searched five databases in July 2025. Only reviews from 2014 onward were kept. Each review's bias risk was graded.

Seven reviews made the cut. They sorted into three themes. Core marks of hard access were shared. Two or more failed tries counted. Veins unseen or unfelt counted too. A known history of trouble counted as well. Obesity and chronic disease raised risk. Past chemotherapy and hidden veins also raised it. Tools stayed weakly validated. Specialist teams and ultrasound formed the response kit.
pmc-13289186:
Tsz Wing Leung and colleagues track special glasses for short-sighted children in 2026. The lenses are called DIMS lenses. They slow eye growth in past trials. This study follows the first trial group. Follow-up runs past eight years.

Sixty young adults took part in all. Their mean age was near 20 years. Wear time averaged 9.4 years. Eye length grew far less with DIMS wear. The modeled cut was 65 percent. Prescription change showed no firm split, though. The gap puzzles the authors. No live control group was kept. More work must sort the mismatch out.
pmc-13289786:
Zhanyu He headed a 2026 first total synthesis of cortinarins, ring-shaped peptides from Cortinarius mushrooms linked to kidney harm after poisoning. Making them in the lab had never been done, blocking study of how they act. The team used iodine-driven linking of tryptophan and cysteine to form the signature bridge that closes the double ring structure.

Twisted forms of the peptides, called ansamers, appeared and were mapped with nuclear magnetic tests and computer motion models. Shape analysis showed turn-like folds in the rings. In kidney cells, the peptides moved a water channel protein in a way resembling a body hormone that controls water and salt, yet through a different route. Lab supply now enables drug lead work.
pmc-13290086:
Four antisense drugs approved in the United States for Duchenne muscular dystrophy are reviewed by Hidenori Moriyama and co-authors in 2026. The condition is a fatal inherited disorder in which the body cannot make dystrophin, a protein that muscles need.

The review follows eteplirsen, golodirsen, viltolarsen, and casimersen from their key trials through later updates, explaining how each drug skips a faulty exon to restore some dystrophin. Moriyama and colleagues also weigh the problems: hard trial design, gaps between animal results and patient benefit, real-world burdens, and narrow eligibility. They close with next-generation antisense drugs now in development and the lessons this field offers for other rare genetic diseases.
pmc-13290386:
Three robotic prostate surgery techniques end at nearly the same place for continence, but one gets patients dry faster, Shih-Hsuan Lin and colleagues show this in a 2026 comparison. Their retrospective study compares Retzius-sparing surgery with conventional two-layer and three-layer reconstruction after radical prostatectomy.

Seventy-nine patients at one tertiary center were grouped by technique, and pad-free recovery was tracked right after surgery and at one, three, and six months. By six months every group reached continence rates of at least 96.7%, with no clear winner among the three. The Retzius-sparing group did better immediately, reaching 89.5% pad-free while the other groups sat at 60.0%, though the one-month gap was not statistically secure. Bladder neck angles differed on imaging without changing long-term function, which the authors take as a reminder that continence has many drivers.
pmc-13290786:
Two acids from Antarctic lichens push leukemia cells toward death and stall their cycle, Fabrizia Brisdelli and colleagues report in a cell study from 2026. Lobaric acid was known to be biologically active, while rhizocarpic acid had barely been tested, so the pair were compared head to head in two leukemic cell lines.

In K562 and MOLM-6 cells, both compounds slowed growth and triggered caspase-dependent apoptosis. Lobaric acid raised the pro-death protein Bax in K562 cells, while rhizocarpic acid raised Bcl-2 there, and both cut STAT5 levels in MOLM-6 cells. Each acid also redistributed cells across cycle phases and shifted cyclin and CDK proteins. Brisdelli and colleagues frame rhizocarpic acid as a newly characterized player, with dose-response and animal work still ahead before any therapy talk.
pmc-13290986:
Yao Liu leads a 2026 genome study of the bHLH transcription factor family in longan, a tropical and subtropical fruit crop. Flower formation in longan is poorly understood at the gene level, so the team searched the full genome for family members and sorted them by structure and shared ancestry.

Altogether 126 family members were found and grouped with Arabidopsis relatives into 27 subfamilies. Segmental duplication, followed by strong purifying selection, appeared to drive the family’s growth over time. Promoter clues pointed toward a role in flower bud growth. One gene, DlbHLH8, stood out with a changing pattern that differed between two cultivars during flowering. That pattern makes it a lead candidate for later work on how longan flowering is switched on.
pmc-13291486: A correction notice from 2026 fixes a figure in a study by Valerie De Anda and colleagues on the archaeal roots of complex life. Evidence is limited to the correction notice itself. One label in Figure 4 sat at the base of the wrong branch. The label now sits on the Hodarchaeales branch, as it should. The corrected figure and legend are reprinted in the notice. The online version has been updated to match.
pmc-13291786:
Marc A Manzo and co-authors examine a 2026 medicolegal question: what do makers of hip replacement stems actually list as reasons not to use their implants? The team took the 11 femoral implants used most often in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland. They pulled contraindications and warnings from each maker's surgical guides, then weighed the findings against negligence and consent law in England and Wales.

Infection was listed as a bar for all 11 implants, and poor bone quality for nine. Two makers called obesity a contraindication, while four more flagged it as a warning. The authors note that many listed traits are common in hip patients, so use is not ruled out by good judgment. Still, once a maker publishes a warning, legal attention shifts toward the surgeon's reasoning.
pmc-13292686:
Fernanda Ramírez-Bravo and colleagues present a 2026 letter on peristomal bullous pemphigoid, a blistering autoimmune disease erupting around a colostomy site and easily mistaken for infection or contact dermatitis. Their patient was an 83-year-old man, three months past colorectal cancer surgery with a permanent stoma. Tense blisters began beside the stoma and marched toward his flank and navel.

Repeated antibiotic courses for suspected bullous impetigo changed nothing, which pushed the team toward the rare localized diagnosis. They took paired punch biopsies, one for direct immunofluorescence and one for standard staining from the blister's edge. The discussion weighs how cancer and bowel inflammation might expose shared antigens such as plectin, seeding cross-reactive autoimmunity against skin anchors BP180 and BP230. The authors urge clinicians to biopsy stubborn peristomal blistering rather than cycling antibiotics.
pmc-13292786:
Matthew Morse and a large public health team report, in 2026, on two Legionnaires disease cases tied to a vacation rental hot tub in New York. The cases came to light in mid-October 2024, and both guests had used the same tub.

Urine tests confirmed the illness, and Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1 was grown from sputum of one patient. Genome sequencing matched the strain to the rental hot tub, while taps and showers were also sampled. Health staff used a public nuisance law to require proper cleaning before the tub reopened. The report urges rental owners and guests to take hot tub hygiene seriously.
pmc-13293286:
Krishna B Singh and co-authors test, in a 2026 mouse study, whether sulforaphane, a broccoli compound, can prevent prostate cancer driven by the Myc gene. Population studies hint that eating broccoli links to lower risk, but no proven preventive drug exists.

Young male mice prone to this cancer got the compound by mouth three times a week for five weeks, with no weight loss or side effects seen. Early cancer in the prostate fell by about 54% with treatment, a drop the authors report. Treated mice also made fewer fats in the prostate and blood, with lower fat-building proteins. Blocking fat making may explain the benefit.
pmc-13293386:
Francesca Bettio and co-authors revisit, in a 2026 study, partner violence during COVID-19 lockdowns in Tuscany, Italy, asking whether harm grew and which shocks drove it. A large phone survey in 2021 anchors the work, drawn from a wider mixed-method project.

People reported that violence grew worse in frequency, severity, or both during the first lockdowns. Strain from caring for children at home had the largest link to harm, with job loss next in line. Crowded housing without privacy showed no clear link in their models. A graded harm measure, counting severity as well as occurrence, split apart effects that simple yes-no counts would blur.
pmc-13293786:
Yu Wang and co-authors hunt, in a 2026 study, for copy number variants in New Zealand dairy cattle using two kinds of DNA sequencing. These larger genome changes affect health and yield traits but are hard to confirm at herd scale.

Linked-read data from 37 cattle flagged 62,438 candidate regions. Depth-based typing in 2306 animals, checked against family inheritance, sorted real variants from noise. A total of 7218 regions passed a strict inheritance bar, and 82 of them were new to public records, counts the authors give. High-pass regions showed clean family patterns, giving breeders a trusted variant catalogue.
pmc-13293986:
Melanie K. Becher, Kaela Wilson, and Italo Mocchetti share a 2026 protocol that locates messenger RNA inside named neuron types in rodent brain tissue. RNA shows current gene activity, while protein staining alone spreads diffusely and blurs counts. Their method runs fluorescent in situ hybridization first, then antibody staining on the same section.

Target RNA appears as sharp dots, while protein fills cells or processes, so counts per cell type stay clean. Steps use RNAscope probes with signal amplification, blocking, and fluorescent secondary antibodies. The pairing lets researchers ask which exact neurons raise or lower a gene, with anatomy preserved.
pmc-13294286:
Thabelang Rabaholo and Moganavelli Reddy ask why men stop HIV treatment in a 2026 qualitative case study at a Seventh-day Adventist clinic in Maseru, Lesotho. Global stopping rates near 20% and far higher shares in Sub-Saharan Africa make the question urgent. Ten men aged 18 and older who were on antiretroviral therapy gave in-depth recorded interviews.

All ten had stopped treatment within the past year, 2023 in the study framing. Four linked driver groups emerged: personal struggles, money and job instability with transport costs, cultural and religious norms that discourage clinic visits, and rigid services with long waits. The authors urge male-focused delivery options.
pmc-13294386:
Zenghong Luo and coauthors delete a cell division exit gene in wheat scab fungus for a 2026 study. Fusarium graminearum blights wheat heads worldwide and poisons grain with deoxynivalenol. Its Mob1 protein, FgMob1, sits at spindle poles as part of the mitotic exit network first mapped in yeast, but fungal disease roles were vague.

Mutants missing the gene grew poorly, made fewer spores of both kinds, produced less toxin, and caused weaker disease. Nuclei piled up in threads and spores, confirming an exit role. Mutants also handled wall, membrane, and oxidative stress badly. One hub gene thus ties growth, reproduction, stress defense, and attack strength together.
pmc-13294686:
Illia Uharov and colleagues redescribe a Madagascan huntsman spider in a 2026 taxonomic article. The species, Damastes leo, was first named in 1903 and had been placed in its own genus, Megaloremmius. Only the female had been formally documented before this work.

Study of the first known male led the authors to move the species into Damastes as a new combination. The female gets a fresh, detailed account, the male is portrayed for the first time, and the first COI genetic record is supplied. Citizen-science photographs help map a range limited to rainforest remnants, where the species is endemic.
pmc-13295186:
Anna-Kristin Brettschneider and co-authors report newborn feeding at hospital discharge across Germany in a 2026 study. Exclusive breastfeeding rates in the country are low, prompting routine national collection of feeding data from 2021. The team used that first year of records to map patterns and risk links.

Data covered 656,907 newborns leaving maternity hospitals in 2021. About three quarters were fed only human milk at discharge, while a small share received formula alone. Babies born by caesarean section, as multiples, or to mothers with higher weight were less often fed only human milk. Rates also varied by region, with Berlin highest.
pmc-13295786:
Isabelle J Henskens and colleagues plan a rollout trial for a glowing dye in breast surgery in a 2026 protocol. Finding the first draining lymph node guides breast cancer staging, yet the standard radioactive tracer brings extra visits, radiation, and cost. Indocyanine green fluorescence shows nodes live without those burdens but has spread slowly.

Seven Dutch hospitals will switch in staggered order from the radioactive tracer alone, through a phase using both, to the dye alone. The main measure is how fully the dye-only phase takes hold in practice. Safety, costs, patient satisfaction, and rollout lessons are tracked together to guide nationwide adoption.
pmc-13295986:
Guoliang Wang and colleagues test, in 2026, adding kaempferol, a plant antioxidant, to frozen ram semen. Freezing and thawing damage sperm through oxidative stress, so the team try five doses in semen from Yuansheng Aite dairy rams and check movement, energy and cap integrity after thawing.

Movement measures shifted with dose in a curved pattern rather than a straight line. The lowest tested dose, 25 micrograms per millilitre, gave the best overall balance of movement, antioxidant strength and energy. Protein and chemical profiling pointed to adhesion, energy and carbon pathways. Fertility trials are still needed, the authors note.
pmc-13296486:
Yi-Chi Chen and co-authors build a learning model in 2026 that predicts the chemical fingerprints of PFAS, the persistent pollutants nicknamed forever chemicals. New variants appear faster than laboratories can measure reference spectra, leaving monitors blind to many forms.

Their network, retrained from a general model on PFAS data, beat rival predictors and found far more matches when searching samples. Applied to firefighting foam and groundwater, its virtual library flagged dozens of candidate chemicals, including very short and altered forms missed elsewhere. The tool is offered online for wider environmental screening.
pmc-13297286:
Ilaria Martelli and co-authors review, in 2026, how cancer-causing viruses corrupt RNA splicing, the editing step that decides which protein versions cells build. Nine viruses are classed as proven human carcinogens, blamed for a large share of cancers worldwide.

By hijacking splicing machinery, these viruses force out abnormal proteins, some directly cancer-driving, touching growth, spread and treatment resistance from first change to metastasis. The mechanism stays underappreciated beside better-known tricks such as disabling tumour suppressors. The authors argue fixing virus-skewed splicing opens fresh therapeutic chances that are worth pursuing further.
pmc-13297486:
A glowing molecule that switches off for copper and back on for sulfur compounds is the subject of a 2026 chemistry paper by Mingjie Wei and co-authors. Their coumarin-based probe, named XDP, was built to follow copper ions and biothiols one after the other inside a single system.

Copper binding at the probe's imine site quenches its fluorescence, giving a linear response from 1 to 80 μM and a detection limit of 0.108 μM. Biothiols such as glutathione then pull the copper away and restore the glow, detectable from 1 to 30 μM. Copper also triggers a visible color change readable by eye or phone camera, and the probe imaged both events in living cells and zebrafish.
pmc-13297786:
For cancer patients whose upper arm bone breaks from metastases, two operations reach similar long-term results by different routes. Giuseppe Rovere and co-authors compared them in a 2026 retrospective study of 48 patients treated between January 2015 and January 2025 at their center.

Twenty-six patients received an intramedullary nail and twenty-two a modular megaprosthesis after tumor removal. Nailing won early: function scores at one month were 78% versus 63%, with advantages lasting about two years. The prosthesis group caught up gradually, and outcomes converged by roughly 2 to 3 years. Complication rates were alike, although infections around the implant occurred only with prostheses, and survival did not differ.
pmc-13298086:
Face nerves long taught as separate actually trade fibers extensively, synthesize Alexandra Diana Vrapciu and colleagues in a 2026 narrative review. They gathered dissection, staining, and clinical studies on connections between the trigeminal nerve, which senses the face, and the facial nerve, which moves it.

Twenty peripheral connections were mapped, some found in nearly every cadaver and others varying from 29% to 86% depending on method. Tissue evidence confirms sensory and motor fibers swap between the nerves, which may supply position sense to facial muscles that lack their own sensors. Clinically, these links help explain spontaneous recovery after nerve injury, tumor spread along nerves, and conditions such as synkinesis.
pmc-13298286:
Soft gels are usually too weak for load-bearing jobs, but Mingzhen Wang and co-authors made one nearly a thousand times stiffer in a 2026 materials study. They packed silica nanoparticles into a polyampholyte hydrogel, then soaked the gel in a zirconium salt solution to add metal-coordination bonds.

The crowded particles and the mix of ionic and metal bonds worked together: the network dissipated energy while the aggregates carried load. The best gel reached a Young's modulus of 87.9 MPa and tensile strength of 7.9 MPa, some 976 and 8.8 times the plain gel's values. Soaking time, salt strength, and particle content all tuned the result.
pmc-13298486:
Routine blood tests might sharpen the hunt for significant prostate cancer, propose Fangming Wang and co-authors in a 2026 study of 542 men who underwent biopsy at a Beijing hospital. They combined blood counts, clotting tests, and biochemistry to build a new discrimination index.

The index blends PSA density, age, and a clotting-based score built from fibrinogen, platelets, and D-dimer. It reached an area under the curve of 0.821 overall, beating total PSA at 0.701, and kept its edge in the tricky PSA gray zone of 4 to 10 ng/mL, where its sensitivity hit 96.0% at the chosen cut-off. The authors suggest the index could cut missed cancers.
pmc-13299586:
Being born early leaves chemical marks on brain-related genes that are still visible decades later, show Carl Peter Vittrup Rasmussen and colleagues in a 2026 twin study. They examined DNA methylation in blood from 288 adults in 144 identical twin pairs whose birthweights differed, spanning a younger and an older cohort.

In the serotonin receptor pathway, younger twins showed a mixed pattern while older twins leaned significantly toward extra methylation, and one gene, HTR1A, flipped direction between cohorts. Glutamate receptor genes GRIA2 and GRIA4 were consistently undermethylated across both age groups. The authors read the results as long-lived epigenetic echoes of preterm birth in pathways central to brain development.
pmc-13299686:
Back to work after a bout of nerves or low mood is a deal struck anew each day, not a box ticked. Nandini Khatter and her team draw that line in a 2026 talk study. They spoke with three camps: staff who had been off sick, work guides who aid the way back, and staff chiefs who run the rules.

The chiefs spoke in steps and forms. Staff and guides spoke in heart terms: trust won back, give in the plan, and aid that did or did not show up. Where the camps' hopes did not meet, the way back felt hard and unsure. The team say a sound way back needs shop ways of life, chief acts, and a mind set to work, all in tune, not rule books alone. Aid must stay close, soft in form, and fit to each case.
pmc-13300686:
Body mass index hides more than it reveals in dialysis patients, Julia Lecyk and colleagues show in a 2026 study of ninety-nine people on maintenance hemodialysis. Bioelectrical impedance measured body makeup, while blood tests covered classic inflammation markers plus newer NETosis indicators such as citrullinated histone. Outcomes were tracked over twelve months.

BMI itself showed no tie to inflammation, yet visceral fat rose alongside IL-6 and C-reactive protein, and muscle mass pointed the other way. Patients dialyzed through catheters carried higher NETosis markers and lower albumin. Low albumin and high TNF-alpha each independently predicted death, tying access choice and body makeup to prognosis.
pmc-13301486:
A widely used bite-force scanner can flatter its own readings if the operator skips one setup step, Robert B. Kerstein warns in a 2026 comment on a study by Maga and colleagues. The target paper used T-Scan digital analysis to show that selective occlusal adjustment shortened disclusion time and balanced contacts in patients with temporomandibular disorders.

Kerstein argues the team never set per-patient sensor sensitivity before recording, so maximum bites oversaturated the sensors. Their figures show clusters of pink, saturated cells, which inflate force percentages and fake balanced distributions, he writes. Proper calibration keeps only one to three pink cells at full bite. The comment urges readers to discount the reported gains until recording technique is fixed.
pmc-13302286:
A past cytomegalovirus infection leaves faint fingerprints on the brain waves of people with schizophrenia, Mădălina Georgeta Sighencea and colleagues explore in a 2026 study. One hundred twenty-three patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders received clinical, cognitive, and lab assessments plus visual EEG reading. Blood tests sorted them by CMV antibody status for comparison.

Overall EEG organization did not split by virus status. Sharp-wave discharges appeared somewhat more often in patients without CMV exposure, independent of background rhythms, while virus-positive patients carried higher white cell counts. Patients showing sharp waves scored better on cognition and memory items. The authors frame these exploratory patterns as non-causal hints for longitudinal work.
pmc-13302986:
Choosing the solvent steers which crystal phase grows on a catalyst sheet, Yuntao Huang and colleagues demonstrate in a 2026 photocatalysis study. Titanium dioxide was grown directly on MXene nanosheets in a heated water-acetonitrile mixture. Adjusting the ratio between the two liquids selected either the anatase or the rutile form of the oxide, a long-standing control problem in heterostructure design.

Acetonitrile appears to coat the growing crystals and lock in the anatase phase. The tuned pairing separates light-generated charges more effectively and produces more singlet oxygen, the reactive species that chews through pollutants. The authors present solvent regulation as a simple dial for phase engineering in environmental catalysts.
pmc-13303086:
Sugar substitutes look broadly safe yet leave open questions, Stanislava Ivanova and colleagues survey in a 2026 overview. Searching four databases, the review covers how these sweeteners are ruled on and what studies say about hormones, gut germs, the brain, and behavior. Groups seen as more at risk, children and people with diabetes among them, get their own sections.

Some studies link sweeteners to changed insulin response and shifted gut germs, but results clash and proof for at-risk groups stays thin. Effects on nerves and hormone systems also remain unsettled. The authors call for ongoing human trials, market watch, and fresh safety reviews rather than a final verdict.
pmc-13303586:
Saveria Batti leads a 2026 laboratory study of fabrics containing germanium and their effects on inflamed blood vessel cells. Such fabrics are said to emit infrared radiation and negative air ions that may calm swelling and oxidative stress.

Human vein cells and immune cells were inflamed with standard triggers, then exposed to the fabric in single cultures, shared cultures, and a flowing 3D system. Cell survival stayed intact, harmful reactive oxygen fell in vessel cells, and several signaling proteins shifted in calmer directions. The layered models show how vessel and immune cells influence each other under fabric exposure.
pmc-13305486:
Zixiao Li and colleagues present a 2026 case of a blood vessel growth in the sacral spine canal that masqueraded as a nerve sheath tumor. Such cavernous hemangiomas in that spot are exceptionally rare and fool scans regularly.

A woman in her mid-fifties had one month of night pain and mild weakness in the left leg. Scans showed a brightly enhancing lump near a lower spine nerve opening, read as schwannoma. Surgery found a dark red, soft, vessel-rich mass instead, and quick tissue checks confirmed hemangioma. Pain eased greatly after removal, with full relief and clean follow-up scans.
pmc-13306786:
Vasilis Vasileiadis added scent delivery to a room-scale virtual reality cave in a 2026 study. Smell feedback lags behind sight and sound in immersive systems, especially in large CAVE rooms where almost no prior work exists.

The Scentree device releases scents in real time as users act, inside a themed experience called Smelling Ancient Greece. Feedback is framed as part of the story action, not background perfume. A user study with 51 people rated immersion, presence, realism and ease of use, supporting live scent as a workable design layer. Users in the trial gave the scent loop strong marks for feel and ease of use.
pmc-13307186: A 2026 retraction notice withdraws a 2022 article on facial emotion reading for crime investigation that fused two image methods. Publisher John Wiley & Sons acted after an inquiry found signs of systematic manipulation of the publishing process. Listed concerns cover scope mismatch, unclear research description, data availability gaps, poor citations, incoherent content and compromised peer review. The notice is brief and gives no replacement findings, so the original claims should no longer be trusted.
pmc-13307286:
Hui Yang catalogued ABI4 hormone-response genes in oilseed rape and tested their drought role in a 2026 study. Four copies were found in the elite ZS11 cultivar, each holding one conserved AP2 domain and promoters rich in stress switches.

Plants with extra BnaABI4-4 copies lost less water, held lower pore conductance and grew fewer stomata, surviving drought better in reported trials. Knockout plants showed the exact reverse pattern across the same measures. The gene acts through the abscisic acid pathway, making it a breeding target for water saving. Such pore control could cut water loss in dry fields while still letting the crop breathe well.
pmc-13307386:
Lingling Wang and co-authors survey in 2026 whether parents of children with special health care needs in Wuxi, China, will accept routine vaccines for their children. Their stratified survey gathered 904 parents or guardians and used group comparisons plus regression to weigh what drove the choice.

Most parents, 864 of those who took part, said they were willing to vaccinate their child. Willingness rose with parent schooling and with knowing about clinics that assess vaccine fitness for such children. Parent knowledge about vaccines also mattered in simple comparisons. Better outreach about those clinics could help close gaps in cover for a group at higher risk of infection.
pmc-13308186:
Sarah Samuelson and co-authors map in 2026 new ideas at work in Swedish primary care, as seen by centre managers across the country. Their mixed survey drew 392 replies from 1028 invited managers, with counts for scale and text study for free replies.

About 80 percent of managers told of a new product, process, or way of organising care at their centre. Most ideas were born inside the centre, and joint work stayed mostly internal, with outside partners in only a small share of cases. Leaders gave time and room for skill growth, yet tight budgets and output demands capped staff input. Broader links across sectors need system level plans, the authors argue, to spread gains.
pmc-13308386:
Dires Delessa Alemu and co-authors study in 2026 weight gain in adult tuberculosis patients during the first two months of care in East Gojjam Zone, Ethiopia. Their survey covered 619 adults at 31 public sites from June to August 2025, with talks and chart checks for each patient.

Weight rose for 428 patients, which is 69.1 percent of the group in the first phase of care. Full drug adherence, early start of care, extra food, three or more meals a day, good knowledge, and a hopeful stance all raised the odds of gain. Food aid and teaching thus stand beside drugs as core parts of strong tuberculosis care.
pmc-13309386:
Ridzky Firmansyah Hardian and colleagues present a 2026 study in rats on what makes brief electrical pulses injure the brain surface. Such pulses are used during brain surgery to check movement pathways. Old safety rules stress total charge, but high pulse rates may change what matters most.

Thirty-two rats received pulse trains that varied in current, pulse length, repeat count, and rest gap. Slices of brain tissue were then checked for lesion depth. Higher current and more repeats deepened injury, while total energy predicted depth better than total charge did. The authors argue that energy, not charge alone, should guide safe limits for this kind of monitoring.
pmc-13310686:
Tianyu Gao and co-authors chart a rare autoimmune brain disease in Chinese patients in a 2026 study. Anti-mGluR5 encephalitis attacks a brain receptor and most often travels with Hodgkin lymphoma, yet it makes up under 1 percent of reported autoimmune encephalitis cases worldwide. Asian data were especially thin.

Eight patients at one referral center between 2019 and 2025 were joined with 31 published Chinese cases, giving 39 in the combined summary. Mean onset age was 42.5 years across the group, with thinking problems the top first feature at 61.5 percent, ahead of behavior change and seizures. Tumors were found in a share of cases, and antibody testing patterns in fluid and blood were compared. The authors set regional benchmarks for recognition.
pmc-13310786:
Wenni Dai and co-authors review ketone bodies and kidney disease in a 2026 paper. Ketones serve as backup fuel and also shape cell signals, swelling, and organ cross talk. Kidney disease is common and deadly, and faulty energy use sits at its core, so ketone paths draw growing interest.

Care paths under review include low carb ketogenic diets, diabetes drugs that raise ketones, and direct ketone drinks. Each path may help or harm the kidney based on dose, timing, and illness type. Past work links ketones to slower harm in some settings. Clear rules for safe use are still lacking, and trials must sort benefit from risk.
pmc-13310886:
Hajed M. Al-Otaibi and Malik A. Althobiani survey nicotine pouch use among adults who once smoked cigarettes in a 2026 study. Pouches are sold as a cleaner option than smoking, yet use habits in former smokers are little known. The team asked about daily amount, timing, craving, and views on quitting help.

Answers covered 693 adults in the final count, with 560 current pouch users who had quit smoking and 133 current smokers. Over two fifths of users took at least ten pouches a day, and most took the first within half an hour of waking. Heavier past smoking linked to heavier pouch use. Many users rated pouches as highly effective for quitting.
pmc-13310986:
Shujie Fu and colleagues test dragon fruit flower extract against acute lung injury in mice in a 2026 study. The dried flower has a long folk use for lung ills, yet proof for sudden lung injury was lacking. A bacterial toxin model was used to probe gut and lung links.

Dosed mice showed less lung swelling, less tissue harm, and calmer swelling signals. Gut barrier protein rose, gut germ mix shifted, and helpful short acids grew. Moving gut germs from dosed mice to fresh mice carried much of the lung gain, which backs a gut lung path. Gene and network maps pointed to key targets for checks.
pmc-13311086:
Iftikhar Ahmed and co-editors open a 2026 collection on germ based cleanup of heavy metal pollution. Metals such as cadmium, lead, and mercury persist in soil and water for decades and climb food chains. Standard fixes cost much, burn energy, and can spawn fresh pollution, which drives interest in living methods.

Germs can bind, store, transform, or free metals through distinct chemical tricks. Gene tools and synthetic biology now let teams design strains with stronger cleanup powers. Studies in the set test those paths in soil and water settings. Safe field use needs checks on strain spread and metal fate after capture.
pmc-13311186:
Brendan Layton and co-authors compare 90 day complications by sex in anemic hip replacement patients in a 2026 study. Low blood counts raise risk after hip surgery and hit women more often, yet sex splits inside anemic groups were rarely tested. Matched records were used to compare matched men and women.

The matched group held 45,788 anemic adults who had first time hip replacement. Women faced higher rates of readmission, wound opening, urine infection, and transfusion. Men faced higher rates of vein clots and acute kidney harm. Death, sepsis, lung infection, and joint infection showed no clear sex split. Sex aware risk plans are backed.
pmc-13311786:
Mohammad Asghari-Jafarabadi and co-authors re-analyze the ENIGMA-II trial in a 2026 study of lasting pain after surgery and quality of life. Lasting post-surgical pain is common and has many drivers.

The analysis covered 2999 trial patients with twelve-month follow-up. A grouped lasso method picked predictor sets, and a structural model then explored paths among pain history, lifestyle, surgical factors, and outcomes. Pain before surgery showed the strongest tie to lasting pain in the model. Accuracy stayed moderate, and the authors stress the work is exploratory, not proof of cause. Better sorting of high-risk patients remains the goal.
pmc-13312786:
Guang Du and co-authors introduce, in a 2026 study, a model that reads online course reviews across languages while respecting cultural context and the skills learners believe they gained. Reviews of massive open online courses carry emotional verdicts on quality and job value, but standard sentiment tools flatten how different groups express opinions and never tie feelings to named skills.

Their model, CA-MuSiC, treats language, platform, and subject field as stand-ins for cultural context, a limit the authors state openly. It grounds opinions in outside skill references, blends extraction with generation, and bootstraps extra labels from a teacher ensemble. Across three benchmarks, including an English-Chinese set, it beat rival methods on structured sentiment and skill-linked scoring tasks. The authors frame reviews as evidence about perceived skill growth, useful to learning analytics.
pmc-13313186:
Fei Lu and fellow authors review Z-nucleic acids, rare forms of DNA and RNA that twist to the left instead of the right, in their 2026 paper. Two proteins with Z-binding parts, ZBP1 and ADAR1, sense these odd shapes, and their roles in health and disease have long been a puzzle.

The review draws on mouse genetics, using knockout mice and mice with changed Z-binding sites, to show what these sensors do. The evidence casts Z-nucleic acids as key triggers of planned cell death, swelling, defense against viruses, and attacks on tumors. That same sensing can also drive diseases of excess inflammation. By weighing both sides, the review helps readers see when blocking or boosting this system might help patients.
pmc-13314286:
Xueqiang He and colleagues report a 2026 case of a homemade magnet tool used to pull swallowed blades from a child throat and chest. A 13-year-old girl with an emotional disorder came in with chest pain after swallowing blades for 7 hours, by the times given in the report.

Scans showed a metal body low in the neck beside the food pipe, plus air leaks in both lungs coverings, the chest center, and under the skin. The team drained both sides of the chest, eased the skin air, and gave anti-infection care first. Through a scope they then removed the blades from a complex hole joining the food pipe to the chest center, found 15 cm from the teeth as stated in the report. The case shows a low-cost magnet trick for a rare and risky removal.
pmc-13314486:
Yanling Yao and co-workers track soy isoflavones in the diet and later diabetes in Chinese adults in their 2026 study. Whether these plant compounds guard against type 2 diabetes over years was still open.

The team drew on the China Health and Nutrition Survey from 1997 to 2015 and enrolled 14,652 adults, as counted in the report. Diet was gauged by three days of recalls plus food weighing. Over a mean follow-up of 10 years, a total of 1051 new diabetes cases arose, as stated in the report. Higher intake of total isoflavones and of subtypes such as daidzein and glycitein tied to lower risk in fully adjusted models, with trend values kept in the report. The long view from a big national cohort strengthens the case for soy foods in prevention.
pmc-13315186:
Fei Chen and a large team report a lab study from 2026 comparing guided and freehand ways to find root canals in pulled human molars. Three dynamic navigation systems, using infrared or visible light tracking, were tested against freehand work done with a microscope and scan images.

Ninety-six molars were split evenly into four groups. Navigation cut angle error to about 0.6 degrees, compared with about 11 degrees freehand, and entry and target errors were also much smaller. Guided work removed less tooth structure as well. The results support navigation for hard canal cases, where saving tooth tissue and hitting the canal matter.
pmc-13316086:
Han Wang and co-authors tested in 2026 whether glowing dye imaging can reveal leftover giant cell tumor of bone during scraping surgery. Finding hidden residual tumor inside the cavity is crucial, since missed tissue can regrow, so indocyanine green near-infrared imaging was used after standard curettage under white light.

Data from 20 patients with at least two years of follow-up were reviewed. All tumors took up the dye, and only one patient, or 5 percent, had a local recurrence. Overall accuracy for spotting residual tumor was 68 percent, with both false positive and false negative results reported against biopsy checks.
pmc-13316186:
Chrysoula Kourtidou-Papadeli and co-authors report EEG evidence in 2026 that graded extra gravity reshapes resting brain networks in people with a nerve inactivity profile, mostly multiple sclerosis. Long inactivity and low sensory input alter large-scale brain wiring, and spinning in a short-arm centrifuge can deliver controlled gravity without voluntary movement.

Brain waves were recorded before and after repeated centrifuge sessions. They were rebuilt at cortex level with a standard imaging method. The pilot study tests whether balance and body sense input from extra gravity can nudge brain change linked to inactivity. That would offer a passive route to network change.
pmc-13316286:
Abigail Low led a small 2026 pilot trial testing whether online group talk therapy for poor sleep can work for women treated for cancers of the reproductive organs. Sessions ran weekly over video in a small group format.

Five patients joined and four finished the program, with three of them attending at least four sessions. Connection quality, joining in, and patient ratings all met the preset goals for a workable program. Sleep severity scores fell by more than six points by week six and stayed lower through 24 weeks of checks, while night waking also dropped. Other sleep and life quality scores barely moved. The team reads the early signs as support for a larger trial and wider access.
pmc-13316786:
Yanliang Ji and co-authors built a 2026 prediction model that fuses brain scan signals with routine clinical data to forecast recovery after ischemic stroke. The target was poor function at ninety days, defined on a standard disability scale.

The single-center study covered 562 patients scanned one to seven days after symptoms began, split into training, tuning, and test groups. In the held-out test set, the fused model scored the highest discrimination figure, 0.951 in the reported analysis, beating the scan-only model clearly. Against strong clinical models, though, its extra gain looked limited on calibration and benefit curves. The authors ask for outside testing and recalibration before any bedside use.
pmc-13316986:
Bastien Petit and colleagues report a 2026 discovery from a Chilean fungus, Anthracophyllum discolor, a little-studied mushroom relative from Patagonia. Fungi hide vast chemical wealth, and this genus had never been mined, so the team grew it and screened its products.

They found anthracaurisin A, the first known fungal nor-sesquiterpene dimer, with strong cell-killing power in dishes and in living tests. Alongside it came one new and several known illudin compounds, whose exact 3D shapes the team pinned down. The work shows that even obscure mushroom genera can yield drug-like molecules, strengthening the case for wider fungal collecting and screening.
pmc-13317386:
Muhammad Daud and co-authors rank, in a 2026 study, eight alfalfa varieties for salt tolerance, a growing threat to forage farming as soils turn saltier. They grew each variety at four salt levels and read shape, water, and chemistry traits together.

Strong salt slashed plant height, weights, and leaf counts by roughly half or more across the board, while cell damage markers climbed steeply and defense enzymes surged. Combined scoring named variety V5, A'erjienong, the most tolerant and V4, Fudina, the most sensitive, with a few enzyme and pigment traits carrying most of the signal. Breeders gain both parent picks and a screening recipe for future salt-hardy forage lines.
pmc-13317586:
Dong Fan and co-authors show, in a 2026 study, that plumbagin, a plant compound from Plumbago roots, kills nonfunctioning pituitary tumor cells by forcing ferroptosis, an iron-driven death. These tumors, among the most common in the skull, rely on surgery today, so drug options are prized.

In cell and ball-of-cells models, plumbagin beat the standard drug temozolomide at stopping growth. It turned down a protective pathway, Nrf2 and FTH1, while raising NCOA4, the ferritin eater, so free iron piled up and fats burned in the pattern of ferroptosis. Computer docking and dynamics helped pick the targets before bench checks confirmed them. The plant compound earns a place on the candidate list for these stubborn tumors.
pmc-13318686:
Vanitha Innocent Rani leads a 2026 randomised study of knee pain treatment. The trial pairs cold therapy with the Graston Technique, a tool-based soft tissue method. Participants had non-traumatic knee pain. The question was whether adding cold improves pain and daily function.

One hundred adults aged 31 to 50 joined the trial. Half received Graston work alone, and half received cold packs afterwards. Everyone had ten daily sessions over two weeks. Both groups improved clearly by the end. The combined group gained more, with a pain drop of 2.18 points against 0.56 in controls on the scales used. Daily task scores also rose more, and pain relief tracked closely with better function.
pmc-13318786:
Yilian Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 study building a screening chart for carotid plaque from routine health check data. Finding plaque early supports prevention of cardiovascular disease. Their model adds a combined index of triglycerides, glucose, and waist-to-hip ratio. That index aims to capture insulin resistance plus central obesity.

The development group held 4,992 people from a health examination cohort. A further 3,812 people formed a later-time validation set. The combined index alone reached an AUC of 0.689 for spotting plaque, beating the standard index. A chart using eight routine measures reached 0.85 in the later validation set, with good calibration. The authors stress it flags current plaque, not future events, and needs outside testing.
pmc-13319086:
Bofei Liu and colleagues present a 2026 retrospective study of Brucella infection spreading to the testis and epididymis in men in Northwest China. Records came from the regional infectious disease hospital in Ningxia. The window ran from January 2021 to December 2023. Among 1,188 male brucellosis inpatients, cases with confirmed genital involvement were compared with the rest.

Seventy-two men, 6.06 percent of the cohort, had the genital complication. After adjustment, four factors stayed associated with it. Fatigue and back pain were reported less often in affected men. Higher white cell counts and positive blood cultures were more common. Platelet counts and symptom duration lost significance after adjustment. The authors read the pattern as a distinct local form of the disease, needing prospective study.
pmc-13319186:
Timur I Bikulov and colleagues present a 2026 method for telling magnetic nanoparticles apart by their magnetic moments, aimed at multiplex medical assays. The standard rebuild from a static magnetisation curve has limited resolving power. Their approach probes higher-order responses head-on using two excitation tones at once. A purpose-built setup reads the mixed signals in sync.

Spectral patterns separate amplitude effects from rate effects, clarifying where each nonlinearity comes from. Tests on shop-bought particles compared the method with standard techniques. A two-particle mixture was measured with only 8.9 percent deviation from the true ratio. The particles' average moments differed threefold, with no prior knowledge supplied. The authors see room for three independent contrast channels. The method may also reveal how particles interact inside mixtures.
pmc-13319486:
Fangqing Liu and Yixuan Li pool trial proof on gentle ear nerve pulses and thinking skills in a 2026 review. The method sends mild pulses through the skin of the ear to reach a major nerve linked to alertness. Past small trials gave mixed scores by skill type, so a pooled count was used to weigh the overall gain.

Fifty three studies were found across seven databases, and 30 gave data from more than 1500 people for the pooled count. Scores rose overall, with clear gains for planning and flexible learning and smaller gains for memory and focus. Stronger pulse levels gave larger gains. Brain scans in future trials could show how the pulses work.
pmc-13319886:
Zeffry Alkatiri and co-authors study how market led growth has split urban space in Batam, Indonesia in a 2026 article. The island city was set up in 1973 as a state planned factory zone meant to rival Singapore and has since become a showcase of market led city growth in the region. How state power, foreign cash, and daily life jointly shape its streets was the core focus.

Four weeks of field work and eighteen deep talks were paired with policy and plan records. Factory zones, road corridors, and gated housing sit apart from informal worker housing that lacks formal status. Even so, those informal areas push back by building their own ways of living and shared life. The case shows how growth can split a city while local life resists.
pmc-13320286:
Weipeng Zhang and co-authors test needle pulses at a leg point for nerve linked erection failure in a 2026 rat study. Pelvic surgery often severs the fine nerves that drive erection, and drug care helps such cases poorly. Rats with both nerves crushed showed lasting overdrive of one nerve branch and shutdown of its partner branch in the organ, a skew that tracked with scar buildup.

Gentle electric needle care at the leg point rebalanced the two branches, restored function, and eased organ scarring. Tissue scans showed a rise in a building block for the key erection gas signal, made by an enzyme rich in vessel lining cells. Blocking that build path wiped out the gain, while topping up the block restored it.
pmc-13320386:
Elizaveta Klockenbring and co-authors present a soil germ data set from a French farm test site in a 2026 data article. The site trials green farming with no pest sprays across four cropping plans that vary tillage and nitrogen use. Soil germs steer nutrient flow and crop health, so their makeup was read by gene scans across many plots and years.

Samples came from 42 plots split into subplots, gathered from 2018 to 2021, and 640 samples yielded usable gene reads before quality checks trimmed the set. Cleaned data hold more than ten thousand germ groups with names, counts, and rich plot facts in shared formats, plus ready made objects for a common stats tool. The set aids method tests and fair contrasts with other soil studies.
pmc-13322486:
Christine Grellmann Schumacher and co-authors test musical auditory training for tinnitus in a 2026 randomised trial. Tinnitus, ringing with no outside source, can burden daily life, and training that engages hearing may reshape brain responses. Twenty adults with tinnitus for at least six months and normal hearing were split into two groups of ten.

Over eight sessions in four weeks, one group did active musical training while the other watched audiovisual material passively. Both groups felt some gain, but only the training group showed wide brain response change plus steady drops in tinnitus loudness, discomfort, and handicap scores. Passive exposure gave a narrower brain change alone.
pmc-13324486:
Hwa-Young Lee and colleagues test a curcumin nano-liposome product in mice with drug-induced memory loss, in a 2026 animal study. Scopolamine blocks acetylcholine signals and mimics early features of Alzheimer disease.

Male mice took the oral product for 30 days at 250, 500, or 1000 mg per kilogram, then received one scopolamine injection. Maze and open field tests showed better learning and memory after treatment. The product also steadied acetylcholine levels and enzyme activity, cut oxidative stress, and calmed inflammation in the hippocampus. Gene shifts included lower App and Bace1 and higher Adam10 and Bdnf. The authors note blood and brain curcumin levels went unmeasured, so claims stay limited to the tested product.
pmc-13324786:
Olivia Briceño, Iris P. Guzmán-Guzmán, and Malén Massot-Cladera open a 2026 editorial on immune aging and chronic inflammation. Aging weakens immune defense, a change called immunosenescence, and stirs steady low-grade inflammation, termed inflammaging, raising risks of cancer, autoimmunity, and infection.

The editorial introduces a research collection on diet, lifestyle, and treatments that might steady the aging immune system. Highlighted work covers a broad review of the mechanisms, treadmill training that eased muscle inflammation and restored insulin sensitivity, and activity effects in cancer patients. Other pieces address master athletes, gut health, and mind-body care. The editors argue joined-up habits may keep immune resilience longer.
pmc-13325386:
Ni Deng and colleagues probe how cannabidiol acts on melanoma cells grown with T cells in a 2026 multi-omics study. CBD spares the high of cannabis yet shows cancer and immune effects whose full wiring is unclear.

At 10 micromolar, a dose below blanket toxicity, CBD pushed melanoma cells toward death while T cells stayed alive and released more IL-2. Gene and protein readouts lit up the integrated stress response, centered on EIF2 signaling. Both data layers converged on immune cell trafficking, with adhesion proteins such as ICAM1 and ITGB1 rising. The pattern frames CBD as a possible helper beside standard melanoma immunotherapy.
pmc-13326486:
Xibing Rao and co-authors move a stress gene from a wild sugarcane relative into Arabidopsis to test its protective power in a 2026 study. Erianthus fulvus shrugs off cold and drought that hurt farmed sugarcane.

The gene EfMYB124 switches on under cold and dry stress. Plants carrying it showed milder visible damage under both stresses than plain plants. Their antioxidant enzymes and proline shot up faster, while the damage marker MDA fell. The gene also tuned known cold and drought response genes, including CBF1 and RD29A, and quieted several ABA signal genes at rest. The results nominate EfMYB124 for sugarcane breeding programs.
pmc-13327886:
Adolfo Renzi sets out a new staging and decision plan for obstructed defecation in a 2026 article. The syndrome, trouble emptying the rectum, underlies up to half of functional constipation cases and falls mostly on middle-aged women. Care once treated it as a simple mechanical blockage, fixing any bulge or prolapse found.

Many patients stayed symptomatic after sound repairs, pushing the field toward a wider idea Renzi calls ineffective defecation syndrome, where a descended pelvic floor wastes the force of straining. The proposed algorithm stages how damage spreads across sites as the condition evolves, then matches surgery to the exact topographical damage found. One operation for all is rejected in favor of site-specific choices.
pmc-13327986:
Kun Zhang and co-authors single out a monocyte type driving inflammation after traumatic lung injury in a 2026 study. Chest trauma often deepens into acute respiratory distress syndrome, which kills many patients and lacks targeted drugs. Single-cell data from trauma patients' blood, lung macrophage data, and a mouse injury model were combined.

One monocyte subgroup marked by ISG15 and STAT1 grew after trauma and pushed a storm of inflammation, and the gene PIM1 stood out as shared across blood and lung data. Genetic analysis backed PIM1 as a causal risk factor for the distress syndrome, acting through the JAK2, STAT3, and PIM1 chain. The approved JAK2 blocker fedratinib reversed the harmful gene pattern in their drug screen.
pmc-13328186:
Lingyi Chi and co-authors compare irrigation fluids for keeping neurons alive in a 2026 cell study. Artificial cerebrospinal fluid is used in brain surgery, but whether it beats plain saline or phosphate buffer was unproven. Mouse hippocampal HT22 cells were kept in each fluid, with standard medium as control, and survival, death markers, and mitochondria were checked.

The artificial fluid preserved viability best and cut cell death, holding mitochondrial shape and voltage steady, lowering the Bax to Bcl-2 death ratio, and taming reactive oxygen and calcium swings.
